issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Verifyit declares `requires-python = ">=3.11"` (`lib/verifyit/pyproject.toml`), and its runtime imports `enum.StrEnum` (`lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/grade.py:15`, `spec.py:17`, and four grade modes) and `tomllib` (`spec.py:15`, `modes/grade_json_schema.py:15`). The task-curation grading harness runs the staged runtime through the grader machine's own `python3` (`taskcompendium.runtime.grading._verifyit_reward`), so every grader machine below Python 3.11 fails grading with an import error instead of a verdict.

Task-curation workspace tasks whose source environment lowers onto a Python 3.10 base hit this at rollout: the Daytona census validates the machines, setup completes, and then the verifier returns `infra_error`:

```
File "/tests/.taskcompendium-runtime/verifyit/grade.py", line 15, in <module>
    from enum import StrEnum
ImportError: cannot import name 'StrEnum' from 'enum' (/usr/local/lib/python3.10/enum.py)
```

This affects the DCAgent python-tests family, where 7 of 10 sources lower onto `python:3.10-slim` bases (curriculum-easy, pymethods2test and its large cut, unitsyn-python and its large cut, e2egit and its large cut); their workspace-image graders run the image's Python 3.10.

Reproduce:
1. Convert a real `DCAgent__exp_rpt_curriculum-easy` row through `convert_python_tests` (the grader environment inherits the workspace image).
2. Grade an empty submission with `grade_empty_in_sandbox` against a Docker machine created from `RegistryImage(grader.docker_image)`.
3. Observe `infra_error` with the `StrEnum` import error above; on Python 3.11+ bases the same path returns `graded` with reward 0.0.

Expected: verifyit's runtime runs and returns a verdict on the grader machines the catalog's declared environments produce, including Python 3.10 workspace images, or the catalog refuses to declare a grader machine whose interpreter cannot run the runtime.

Evidence: end-to-end run over real TaskTrove rows on 2026-11-19 (multifile python:3.11 and stack-pytest/nl2bash ubuntu:24.04 graders return graded verdicts; the 3.10 cases stop at the import).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 ## Research

`_verifyit_reward` launches the grader machine's `python3`, while Verifyit declares Python ≥3.11 and imports `StrEnum` and `tomllib`. That explains the reported Python 3.10 import failure. On current `main`, the DCAgent converter gets a separate grader environment from its conversion context, and the catalog declares `GRADER_PACKAGES` on a Python 3.12 base; the reported `/tests/.taskcompendium-runtime` path is absent from this checkout. No open PR references #11721.

Relevant code: [grader command](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/grading.py#L366-L378), [Verifyit Python floor](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/verifyit/pyproject.toml#L6-L12), [Python 3.11 imports](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/spec.py#L13-L17), [converter environment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/tasktrove/python_tests.py#L167-L175), [catalog grader image](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/tasktrove/python_tests.py#L385-L398).

## Proposed Fix

1. Reproduce with a pinned affected row and record the resolved `grader.environment`, grader image digest, `python3 --version`, and runtime staging path. Compare them with the catalog's Python 3.12 grader image to locate where the workspace image became the grader image.
2. Correct that environment selection so Python-tests tasks keep their Python 3.10 workspace but grade in the declared Python 3.12 grader image. Add a qualification check that rejects a resolved grader interpreter below Verifyit's supported floor before admitting tasks.
3. Add a regression using a Python 3.10 source Dockerfile and a separate supported grader environment. Verify an empty submission and an oracle submission return verdicts, then rerun the affected safe tests and one real Daytona row.

This needs a traced image-selection fix and a grader-image run before a PR; changing Verifyit's Python floor alone would leave its 3.11-only imports broken.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
Resolution landed on `atlas-env-audit` (landing in progress):
- `requires-python` lowered to `>=3.10`; a version-gated `verifyit.compat` provides `StrEnum` and the `tomli` fallback for `tomllib` on 3.10 machines; `grade_judge` uses `timezone.utc`.
- `render_spec` keeps `tomli_w` host-side (staging-only), so the staged runtime imports nothing beyond the declared pytest packages on any machine.
- Behavior tests run the staged entry under Python 3.10 and 3.11 on a real DCAgent row and assert the scored negative verdict; the hidden-pytest graders install `tomli==2.5.0` behind a `python_version < "3.11"` marker on 3.10 machines.

Its Daytona-unsafe class is different (unresolved Docker build contexts refused by `require_resolved_environment`, recorded as `daytona_execution_failures=13562` in its declaration) and needs the environment build-and-pin path, not this grader-environment inheritance fix. Its current pin stays.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
🤖 Candidate inference starts before a hosted judge's checkpoint is prepared. With a warm candidate and a cold judge, candidate accelerators remain reserved while the judge's CPU prepare job downloads its checkpoint.

Prepare the candidate and hosted judge checkpoints together before starting either inference service. Preserve independent serving configurations, immutable model revisions, and target-cluster/region cache placement. A preparation failure should prevent accelerator submission for both services.

Done when a regression test starts with a warm candidate and cold hosted judge and shows both preparation steps finish before either serving job is submitted.

Follow-up to https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10277#discussion_r4519907770 and #9233.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

[`run_evaluation_steps`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dffdeb25457b7a4c8815bfca9c0358d6cf5dc1ec/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L602-L672) opens the candidate inference session before it constructs the hosted judge config. In [PR #10277](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10277), each `remote_inference` call prepares its model and then submits its accelerator job, so a cold judge prepares while the warm candidate is already serving. That PR owns this code path and remains open for review.

**Relevant code**
- [`runner.py#L648-L671`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dffdeb25457b7a4c8815bfca9c0358d6cf5dc1ec/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L648-L671) — candidate starts before judge config
- [`iris.py#L732-L759`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dffdeb25457b7a4c8815bfca9c0358d6cf5dc1ec/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py#L732-L759) — preparation precedes serving per session
- [`iris.py#L783-L830`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dffdeb25457b7a4c8815bfca9c0358d6cf5dc1ec/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py#L783-L830) — prepare jobs inherit each model's placement

# Proposed Fix

Extend #10277 so the eval runner constructs both inference configs, pins each Hugging Face revision, submits both sets of CPU preparation jobs to their respective serving placements, and waits for every preparation result before opening either inference session. Keep the candidate and judge serving configs independent; on any preparation error, terminate outstanding prepare jobs, record the infrastructure failure, and submit no accelerator jobs. Add a regression using a warm candidate and cold hosted judge that observes both preparations completing before either serving submission, plus a judge-preparation failure case. This belongs on #10277 rather than a parallel implementation PR.

issues.author: asartran
issues.body:
The marin unit test `tests/rl/test_rl_launch_documents.py::test_rl_launch_documents_load_with_the_vendored_launcher` takes 37 s at the median (55 s at p90, 114 s max) across 306 CI runs from Nov 15-18, which makes it one of the two slowest test files in the marin unit suite. CI deals test files to four marin shards, and the shard holding this file is often the last to finish, so it sets how long many PRs wait.

Almost all of that time is the SkyRL-side check, not the environment build. Timed on a development machine at `main` with a warm SkyRL environment:

| Stage | Time |
|---|---|
| Render the 103 launch documents (`render_launch_census`) | 5.5 s |
| SkyRL launcher subprocess loading the 103 documents (`tests/rl/launch_document_loader.py`) | 42.6 s |
| Build SkyRL's CPU environment from an empty uv cache | 10.9 s (0.5 s warm) |

Each `launch_config.load_launch_config` call composes the full SkyRL training config through Hydra (`_compose_source_recipe` -> `compose_skyrl_config` -> `hydra.compose`), with most of the time in OmegaConf deep copies, so the check costs about 0.4 s per document. It grows with every new launch document.

Done when:
- the test's CI time no longer grows with the number of launch documents, or stays under about 10 s on a GitHub `ubuntu-latest` runner, while still checking that every launch document loads with the vendored launcher (for example in the nightly slow job if not on every PR).

comments.body:
🤖
# Research
The test renders every launch document, then the loader calls `load_launch_config` once per document. Source recipes enter `_compose_source_recipe`, which composes a full SkyRL config for each call; 103 documents therefore add roughly 43 seconds to the PR unit shard. The scheduled `slow` job already runs tests marked `slow`.

**Relevant code**
- [`test_rl_launch_documents.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/rl/test_rl_launch_documents.py#L18) — full census test
- [`launch_document_loader.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/rl/launch_document_loader.py#L27) — per-document load

- [`unified-unit.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/unified-unit.yaml#L129) — nightly slow job

Split the test so PR shards render and check the full document census, while the nightly slow job loads every document with the vendored launcher. This removes the repeated Hydra composition from PR unit shards and preserves the full load check each night.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Summary

- **Motivation:** In an RL pass-rate screen on SWE-smith tasks, 575 of 1,024 Snowball tries had a broken tool call, and 524 of the 576 malformed spans were Pi `edit` calls. The 10/05 SFT data has almost no edit calls in Pi's nested shape.
- **Goal:** Stop Snowball from writing malformed JSON for Pi's nested `edit` tool by adding correct examples to its SFT data.
- **Data:** 1,000 synthetic Pi edit exercises built from open TMax code, each checked to restore the target file exactly, plus held-out exercises for testing. Later runs use a grown set of 5,536 exercises.
- **Method:** Short SFT runs from the 10/05 SFT with and without the slice, scored on a targeted eval (apply the model's edit and compare with the target file) and on Micro210.
- **Results:** In the FP32 from-base pair (one training run per arm), replacing 41 of 4,800 rows with edit-call exercises scored 120 of 855 on the edit-call test (higher on 10 of 11 tasks) and Micro210 score mass 97.39 / 99.33 (mean 98.36 of 440), against 63 of 855 and 87.30 / 87.28 (mean 87.29) for the control; native equal-20 overlapped across repeats (20.21% vs 19.12%), AIME24 and OlympiadBench accounted for 11.00 of the 11.07 mass points (the other 18 sources netted +0.07, with tool-use sources not clearly improving), and both arms sat far below the 2026-11-18 from-base control (145.01) and 10/05 (175.75). Earlier 15-update FP32 continuations from 10/05 scored 284 to 293 of 855 against 224 for 10/05 (issue 11687), and a partial Mochi screen found far fewer broken edit calls (7 of 358 against Snowball's 524 of 1,093) but ended undecided.
- **Conclusion:** On a weak baseline (one run per arm), the edit-data run scored nearly twice as high on the edit-call test with no measured cost to general ability, so we keep the edit-call rows in the mix. The effect size on a healthy model and any gain on real agent tasks are not yet measured, and earlier BF16 runs through 2026-11-18 carried the BF16 stored-parameter caveat (issue 11687).

## Description

Pi's edit tool takes `{"path": …, "edits": [{"oldText": …, "newText": …}, …]}`, a list of objects inside the arguments object. The 10/05 SFT data has about 2.7M flat `str_replace_editor(command, path, old_str, new_str)` calls and essentially no Pi-shape edits.

Measured in the screen above:
- 1,093 edit calls; 523 failed `json.loads`.
- 362 of the 524 broken edit spans parse after one insertion at the JSON error offset: `]}` for 259, `}` for 103. This is a syntax-only check. It does not show that the repaired edit applies or fixes the task.
- 14 of the 575 broken-call tries still scored 1, so a malformed final call does not always mean a failed task.

Examples are viewable without login in the public trace viewer: https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/193c0a18-17c8-4348-9df3-765f3811a5d5/ (run "Pass-rate 43604"). Missing `]}`: attempts [`010d96c8…`](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/193c0a18-17c8-4348-9df3-765f3811a5d5/#attempt=010d96c8bd03428fb13da34e880a3a73) (step 18) and [`0288247e…`](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/193c0a18-17c8-4348-9df3-765f3811a5d5/#attempt=0288247ea31c47e48cbb5c7ee3b6a467) (step 11). Missing `}`: [`04741406…`](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/193c0a18-17c8-4348-9df3-765f3811a5d5/#attempt=04741406ca5a4ff38401423e48ccd4ad) (step 18). The viewer shows only this screen and the edit-exercise training rows. It reads from temporary storage: the traces expire about 2026-11-28 and the exercise data about 2026-12-18, so the links are not durable.

An A/B with a flat replacement edit tool (16 tasks × 2 arms × 4 tries) solved 20/64 vs 7/64 for Pi's native tool. Malformed calls not caused by the output cap were 3 vs 25. A larger confirmation (128 tasks × 8 per arm) is pending review. Third-party harnesses fix their own tool schemas, so a flat tool would only help our own harness.

The SFT training data's tool calls are well-formed: 452 of 47,399,691 assistant call spans failed a delimiter and `json.loads` check, across 51 scanned sources.

## Hypothesis or Goal

The model learned the flat edit shape in SFT and miscounts brackets in Pi's nested shape. Adding valid nested-edit calls to SFT should cut the malformed-edit rate without lowering other scores.

## Status

- E12-B data built: 1,000 train / 100 val / 100 test synthetic Pi edit exercises from TMax code (ODC-BY), 1–4 edits per call, 393,750 supervised tokens in train. Each edit was checked to restore the target file exactly. [Manifest](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Farm-b-20261114-r1%2Fmanifest-r1.json) (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/arm-b-20261114-r1/manifest-r1.json`).
- 1 h version: three 15-update arms (general-only control, E12 full, E12 attention/head only) trained, exported and scored on Micro210. Results below.
- 8 h version: C150 recipe plus a grown E12-B set (~6k rows, at most 4 passes per row, about 0.8% of supervised tokens), against the existing C150 arm. It waits for the 1 h readout.
- Mochi: in its BFCL ×5 Pi traces, 1,445 tool calls parsed, and at most 3 messages left tool-call-like text unparsed. BFCL rarely uses `edit` (7 calls, none with more than one edit), so this does not test the nested-edit problem.

Readout: malformed-edit rate on Micro210's Pi trials, the Micro210 score paired by task, and the retention panel. Carry the slice into the next SFT stage if the malformed-edit rate falls by at least half against the matched control with no Micro210 or retention loss.

## Results (1 h version, as of 2026-11-17)

All three arms start from the 10/05 weights and run 15 updates of 32 × 262,144 tokens. In the two edit arms, the E12-B slice is 0.68% of supervised tokens: all 1,000 train exercises, seen twice. All Micro210 numbers are single runs; two runs of the parent differ by about 5 tasks (2.1 points).

| Model | Micro210, equal weight over 20 sources | vs parent run 1 | Held-out E12 edit loss (100 test rows, update 15) | Malformed `edit` spans in Micro210 Pi traces (about 100 records; one outlier record excluded) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10/05 parent, run 1 / repeat | 49.39 / 47.32 | 0 / −2.1 | not measured | 16 |
| General-only control | 43.57 | −5.8 | 0.0294 | 14 |
| E12 attention + head only | 46.52 | −2.9 | 0.0294 | 20 |
| E12 full | 42.48 | −6.9 | 0.0018 | 3 |

- **The control loses about as much as the full arm**, so the Micro210 drop comes from the continued training itself, not from the edit data. One untested difference: E12 restarted at LR 2e-5 with fresh optimizer moments, while 10/05 ended its decay at 5e-6. A rerun of the control at 5e-6 and a zero-update export control are being prepared.
- **The edit data taught the format only when all weights trained.** The full arm's held-out edit loss is 16× lower than the control's. The attention + head arm did not change.
- **Not shown yet:** that real edits improved. The malformed counts are witness counts, not rates. The excluded full-arm record alone holds 8,166 malformed spans (see the comment of 2026-11-17 07:34 UTC). A behavioral test is being built: each model answers the 100 held-out test prompts, and the returned edit is applied with Pi's edit function and checked against the target file.
- The pre-stated carry rule (malformed-edit rate at least halved, with no Micro210 or retention loss) is **not met**: the full arm loses 6.9 points.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

- 2026-11-16: Do not train on the screen's own successful calls; those tasks are the readout panels.
- 2026-11-16: Keep Pi's native edit tool for reported benchmarks.

## Conclusion

1. Evaluate the control, full-slice, and attention/head arms on the same task and attempt set with the pinned Pi policy. Report malformed edit JSON failures per edit attempt, trials ending on a malformed call per trial, and output-cap truncations separately.
2. Publish paired Micro210 scores, scored and unscored counts, and retention results for each arm, with run and checkpoint IDs.
3. Apply the decision gate already stated in this issue. If an arm qualifies, compare the planned longer C150 treatment with its matched control, then record the result and recipe decision here.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Protocol FAIL; original preregistered confirmation claim FALSE.** The run completed, but the strict tool-contract check failed. The numbers below are descriptive, not a confirmed flat-edit effect or a promotion decision.

We compared Pi’s native nested edit arguments with a flat replacement on the same 128 SWE-smith training tasks, eight attempts per arm: 2,048 assignments. There were 2,024 verified binary outcomes and 24 masked/unknown outcomes, which were not counted as failures.

| Descriptive reading | Control wins / known | Flat wins / known | Complete task profiles | Flat-minus-control task-profile difference | Conditional 95% interval |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| As recorded | 161 / 1,011 | 307 / 1,013 | 120 | **+14.38 percentage points** | +10.21 to +18.85 |
| Two affected attempts excluded | 161 / 1,011 | 305 / 1,011 | 118 | **+14.30 percentage points** | +9.96 to +18.75 |

The second reading removes two verified flat-arm wins from the pooled sensitivity only: nominal denominators become 1,024 control and 1,022 flat. The 13 control and 11 flat unknowns remain unknown. For the separate balanced eight-per-arm task comparison, the two affected task profiles become incomplete and are omitted; their other 30 outcomes remain pooled. The original endpoint is unchanged. These intervals condition on the observed complete task profiles; they do not cover excluded-task uncertainty, shared-run dependence, training-repeat variation or population generalization.

**Why strict confirmation failed:** two flat-arm attempts contained 65 requests using the native nested edit schema. Contracts were checked in 1,015 attempts per arm: zero affected control attempts and two affected flat attempts. Unchecked attempts and incomplete guard exposure are not assumed clean.

**Supported explanation:** in both cases, the outer agent ran `pi submit` through its bash tool. Pi 0.87 treats `submit` as a prompt, not a submission command. The resulting recorded requests use the default native tools; the outer flat extension was supplied through explicit CLI flags that the child commands omitted. The parent’s flat requests resume afterward with its prior context preserved. Pinned source and retained command/request/tool-result ordering support a recursive CLI invocation explanation, rather than an established parent compaction switch. Captured OS ancestry, every child setting/binary, original HTTP traffic and the effect of those calls on reward were not proved. This explanation does not repair the protocol failure.

Independent review reproduced the archive/grid joins, counts, bootstrap intervals and both sensitivities. Cost was **26.20 requested H100-hours**, not a utilization or invoice measurement. Native jobs and containers completed; exact GPU Pod absence/provider release has not yet been established. No new run, harness change or training-data promotion follows from this result.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Mochi nested-edit screen: the frozen test ended undecided (coverage hold). It shows neither "slice needed" nor "no slice needed". The descriptive numbers, over selected evidence-complete pairs and retained returned spans, are much lower for Mochi than for Snowball, but they cannot decide the 5% line.

## Result

The screen ran Mochi SFT step 400407 on the same 128 SWE-smith tasks × 8 tries as the Snowball pass-rate screen. Setup: Pi 0.87.0, the nested `edit` tool, one DP16 GB200 serve in cw-us-east-08a, 32 trials at once, a 900 s agent cap and no retries.

The frozen rule sorts each of the 1,024 assigned pairs into one of three classes:
- BAD: a broken tool-call body under a verified request contract.
- CLEAN: fully recorded, no broken call, and a clean ending.
- UNKNOWN: everything else.

It decides "slice" at 205 BAD and "no slice" at 973 CLEAN.

| Run (same 128 tasks × 8, same readout code) | BAD / CLEAN / UNKNOWN of 1,024 | Frozen result | Agent timeouts (of readable) | Evidence-complete pairs (of readable) | Broken call / evidence-complete | Broken **edit** first / evidence-complete | Broken returned spans |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Snowball SFT `grug-datakit-sft-262k-20261005-ac60d940-r1` (run 43604; finished historical run) | 575 / 317 / 132 | same rule applied retrospectively: B ≥ 205 | 19 / 1,016 (1.9%) | 892 / 1,016 (87.8%) | 64.5% (61.3–67.5) | 58.7% (55.5–61.9) | 582 / 35,041 (1.66%); edit 524 / 1,093 |
| Mochi SFT step 400407 (stopped early) | 19 / 147 / 858 | undecided (coverage hold) | 289 / 464 (62.3%) | 166 / 464 (35.8%) | 11.4% (7.5–17.2) | 3.6% (1.7–7.7) | 22 / 10,040 (0.22%); edit 7 / 358 |

## Stop

At 06:15Z we declared a value stop: after the second interim look, continue only if B ≥ 100. That look had B = 18. We cancelled the screen at about 06:42Z, with 469 of 1,024 attempts recorded. This stop rule is separate from the frozen rule, and every unfinished pair counts as UNKNOWN.

## How to read it

- The Snowball row reruns the same frozen code on run 43604's retained traces. Its 575 BAD tries are exactly the 575 reported above. It is a finished historical run, not a complete capture: 132 pairs are UNKNOWN.
- Mochi's UNKNOWN pairs are 555 assigned pairs with no retained attempt record, 171 unmappable records, 124 incomplete request/turn records, 3 timeout endings and 5 unreadable records.
- No-slice was out of reach once the timeouts piled up. A timed-out try can never be CLEAN under the frozen rule, and 289 timeouts alone cap CLEAN at 735.
- The intervals are nominal 95% Wilson intervals over each run's evidence-complete pairs. They do not account for which tries finished or for dependence within a task, and they are not calibrated for the 1,024. Mochi's evidence-complete pairs contain no timed-out try, so they may lean towards shorter episodes.
- The span column counts broken tool-call bodies among the calls the model returned, using lexical tool names. It is not a prevalence of executed calls.
- The runs differ in model and serve, so this table compares descriptions and does not give a causal effect.

## Timeout-aware sensitivity

This was declared after the first look and is descriptive only. It checks the proved prefix of each timed-out try for a broken call. It found none in the 289 eligible timeouts, so the witness count stays at 19 of 1,024.

## Cost

76.07 GB200-hours over six serve starts, from Iris task durations × 4 GB200 per task. The CPU-only screen drivers are not included. The total uses unrounded durations; the rounded rows below sum to 76.08.

| Start | GB200-h |
|---|---:|
| r1 | 2.86 |
| r2 | 9.21 |
| r3 | 3.61 |
| r4 | 1.01 |
| r5 | 3.01 |
| r6 | 56.38 |

r5's serve was ready, but its screen failed at worker start-up: the local-machine factory found bubblewrap blocked on that CPU pod (see issue 10692).

## Follow-up

What a cleaner Mochi test could try (hypotheses; nothing built):
- A longer agent cap, to test whether more attempts finish and satisfy the capture checks.
- Higher trial concurrency, for better use of the serve. In the run's first 35 minutes, mean inter-token latency was 141 ms (about 7 tok/s per sequence) at 32 concurrent trials. Higher concurrency may slow each sequence further, and it is not shown to improve completions.

Two retained-trace snapshots, taken about 15 minutes apart after the stop, agree exactly. That is an observation, not proof of final retention. Private traces are not published. Leftover Daytona sandboxes were not observed; they were created with a 360-minute lifetime.

🤖
## Result

On `eval-r2`, pooled exact-file scores over sampled seeds 1–5 were **0.497 for E12 full, 0.262 for 10/05, 0.271 for C-replay r3 and 0.263 for C-e12**. Each uses one trained export and one serve for those five seeds. The recipes differ in data, LR, grouping, clipping and state; the cause of the score differences remains unknown. Reviewed parent/F/Hb Micro210 results are available separately (`505ed09b`); C-arm readouts remain pending.

## Edit-call test and recipes

`eval-r2` has 171 prompts from 11 tasks; `eval-r1` has 300 from 88 tasks and overlaps added TMax-correction tasks. Those arms use `eval-r2` only. Every 10/05-derived row carries **“TMax exposure of the base mix unverified.”** `exact_ts` means the edited file matches its target after stripping line-end spaces/tabs; byte equality agreed in the original single-pass cells. These are file-edit scores, not program-test scores. Seed 0 came from separate earlier serves; pooled intervals are descriptive task bootstraps.

| Arm | Added edits in 480 packed rows | Effective LR | Routed experts / stacked RMS | State | `eval-r2` seed 0 | Pooled seeds 1–5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| 10/05, new stack | No continuation | Last-stage LR unverified | Reference checkpoint | Reference | 0.292 | 0.262 (0.193–0.311) |
| F | General only | 5e-6 | Adam / MuonH | Fresh | 0.298 | Unmeasured |
| Hb | General only | 5e-6 | MuonH / Adam | Fresh | 0.287 | Unmeasured |
| E12 full pilot | 16 E12-B r1 positions | 2e-5 | Adam / MuonH | Fresh | 0.544 | 0.497 (0.429–0.561) |
| C-replay r3 | General only | 5e-6 | MuonH / Adam | Carried | 0.287 | 0.271 (0.202–0.319) |
| C-e12 | 41 grown E12-B positions | 5e-6 | MuonH / Adam | Carried | 0.281 | 0.263 (0.201–0.305) |

F and the pilot have nominal linear late decay outside the 15 observed updates. E12 full served 1,000 exercises twice, contributing 0.68% of target tokens; C-e12 served 5,536 once, contributing 1.97%. E12 full used per-group clipping; C-e12 used one global clip. A matching group map does not imply the same optimizer implementation. This is not an isolated data, LR or state comparison.

Within-serve exact-score ranges were 0.234–0.281 / 0.462–0.538 / 0.251–0.310 / 0.240–0.292 for 10/05 / E12 full / C-replay r3 / C-e12. Fixed-setup serve-to-serve variation remains unmeasured. The old-stack 10/05 seed-0 score was 0.292 (build and settings differ); Qwen3.6-35B-A3B scored 0.713 as a separate-system reference. Pooled jobs: `edit-call-eval-base-1005-noise-r2-20261118`, `edit-call-eval-e12-full-noise-r2-20261118`, `edit-call-eval-c-replay-r3-noise-20261118`, `edit-call-eval-c-e12-grown-noise-20261118`.

Applied-but-wrong files were the largest original sampled failure class: 75 / 80 / 77 / 49 / 77 / 75 for 10/05 / F / Hb / E12 full / C-replay r3 / C-e12. The line-diff audit found wrong replacement text, missing edits, partial edits, wrong-region heuristics, extra changes and blank-line-only differences. For 10/05 / E12 full / Qwen, blank-line-only counts were 15 / 10 / 24 of 75 / 49 / 33 applied-but-wrong cases. These are structural labels; blank lines can affect quoted content.

## Training-data audit

- The sampled general replay had 9,104 recognized native calls and **zero declared Pi-style nested edits**. Six legacy flat-edit calls were positive-weight targets valid under their own schema. Fourteen calls violated declared schemas; five more failed only the no-extra-keys policy. Zero nested-edit targets is not a zero-percent failure rate.
- Prepared E12-B r1 / grown / teacher-r4 files had 1,000 / 5,536 / 5,347 supervised nested edits with no identified schema malformation. Terminus instead expresses shell commands in JSON-in-text `keystrokes`: all 5,436 replay responses parsed and all 8,957 command entries passed their strict schema; five responses lacked `plan`, with one further closed-key-only root failure. Pi-equivalent shell effects were not established. Compactions request Markdown summaries.
- These bounded samples do not estimate corpus prevalence or attest the original 10/05 consumed stream. Raw-cache masks and historical worker segmentation remain unverified. Reviewed audit fingerprints: `94ec60d2`, `7075a74b`.

## Carried state and Hb/F

Both C arms completed 15 updates with audited restored state and active carried Adam state. On r3, the step-15 MuonH buffer difference from Hb projected **0.877** onto the expected decay-only carried component; this is not a retained-buffer fraction. C-e12 used the same restore recipe, but its step-15 buffer was not measured separately. On six expert/shared-MLP leaves, r3–Hb weight difference was **0.13% of Hb's own weight-change norm**, not the all-MuonH statistic. Adam leaves differ. The shared endpoint pattern below limits this weight comparison's ability to distinguish run-specific carried-state effects; their effect on weights remains unresolved. Training jobs: `e12-carried-replay-eager-20261118`, `e12-carried-e12-eager-20261118`.

F/Hb used the same 480 packed rows and 15 updates at 5e-6; Hb also had a first-update state round-trip. Step-15 eval loss was **0.495029271 / 0.495384425** for F/Hb. Their single sampled edit scores were **0.298 / 0.287**, with 24 / 29 unparseable edit-tag responses. The edit-file scores alone do not identify an optimizer-quality effect; the separate reviewed Micro210 readout covers parent/F/Hb.

## Parameter precision

**Single runs per recipe; BF16 parameter storage with no FP32 master; 27/27 parameter leaves (67,078,882,816 values); step 15 against the 10/05 BF16 start.** Updates cast back to BF16 with round-to-nearest. The sealed Mochi source recipe uses FP32 parameters on device; live-worker binding is unverified. The original native 10/05 checkpoint stores FP32 parameters. The G5r2/G20r2 full 27-leaf close was separately verified against its independent original scan.

| Arm / routed-expert optimizer | All-parameter changed % | Expert `w_down` changed % / large-value count | Output projection changed % | Token embedding changed % |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Hb / MuonH 5e-6 | 8.375 | 8.387 / 1,627,374,248 | 0.351045 | 0.398317 |
| C-replay r3 / MuonH 5e-6 | 8.369 | 8.382 / 1,627,374,248 | 0.370503 | 0.199260 |
| C-e12 / MuonH 5e-6 | 8.369 | 8.382 / 1,627,374,248 | 0.370643 | 0.199546 |
| G5r2 / MuonH 5e-6 | 8.374 | 8.386 / 1,627,374,248 | 0.348707 | 0.399694 |
| G20r2 / MuonH 2e-5 | 9.072 | 9.076 / 1,627,374,251 | 1.39586 | 1.59808 |
| F / Adam 5e-6 | 15.504 | 15.640 / 1,670,372,923 | 0.349185 | 0.398359 |
| E12 full pilot / Adam 2e-5 | 55.282 | 56.350 / 10,499,230,101 | 1.39602 | 1.59853 |

“Large-value count” means changed values whose start magnitude was ≥1e-3. Count equality alone does not establish element identity. A separate comparison verified **identical changed positions and bit-identical new values on all 1,627,374,248 such positions** across Hb, r3, C-e12 and G5r2, despite different data, state history and launches. These shared endpoints cannot distinguish run-specific learning. G5r2/G20r2 also had **identical new values at 100% of their shared large-value changed positions**; about **65% moved away from zero and 35% toward it**, consistently across 6,656 expert matrices. This is not a uniform rescale. The AdamH output projection does not show this MuonH pattern. Scan fingerprints: `8c2d1df1`, `ff569acd`, `2b5c6102`, `9c081004`, `a8f45bf2`.

Across 18 MuonH leaves, r3/Hb tangential displacements were **3.857**. The nominal accumulated LR-scaled step length, **15 × 5e-6 × starting L2 = 0.188**, uses idealised norm-preserving updates: the **20.5×** ratio is a reference-scale comparison, not a bound on realised BF16 motion. Tangential-change cosine was **0.99999**; **0.0053** is the L2 norm of the r3−Hb tangential-delta difference divided by Hb's tangential L2. On the audited expert-branch path, each update ends with BF16 weight-group renormalisation. A **one-step CPU toy** of that formula changed **6.33%** of large values at LR zero. Rounding from renormalisation could account for some or much of this pattern; the contribution and whether the learning signal survives are unmeasured. These runs measure their BF16 screen recipes and leave effectiveness under Mochi's FP32 parameter policy unresolved. E12 full also differs in LR and expert optimizer, so its higher edit score does not identify a cause.

## Next comparisons

The initial zero-LR run stalled before completing an update. G0r2 completed its first call at **10:55:18Z**; **no reviewed step-15 zero-LR weight comparison is available yet**. Through that first call, the observed EAGER (CUDA module loading)/autotune-0 set with a state rebind had **six first-call completions and one stall**, not a controlled success-rate estimate; the earlier [issue 11646 correction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11646#issuecomment-6976136441) covered the five/one snapshot. G5/G20 edit-call comparisons and FP32-policy twins need separate readouts; the FP32 policy also changes gradient and moment dtypes.

- **Answers are shorter overall.** Mean response length is 8,196 vs 13,919 tokens, and shorter in 15 of 20 sources. Examples: DS-1000 4,695 vs 45,836, and BixBench 8,675 vs 38,023.
- **Some length numbers are mixed.** GSM8K is longer on average (2,083 vs 418), but only because of repeat 1 (3,900 vs 266 in repeat 2). SWE-bench Verified length-cap stops overlap across repeats (75% mean, 90% and 60%, vs 60% mean, 40% and 80%).
- We have not read transcripts.

## Known differences from the earlier control

- The new run starts from an FP32 upcast of the pre-train base.
- Seven special-token head columns were reseeded at the start.
- The training lineage is different.
- Optimizer: routed experts moved from Adam to Muon-H. The `.weight` and RMS-norm leaves moved from Muon-H to Adam. Per-group clip 1.0 became global clip 1.0. `expert_normalization` is `all_experts`.

The cause of the drop is not established. These differences are the ones we know. We have not tested which of them matters.

## Coverage

- Nine broader-suite import failures remain unresolved. They are outside the 20-source Micro210 and are not counted as passing.
- Excluded trials are not imputed.
- The packet has no H100-hour accounting and no per-trial UID join against the comparators.
- Effective renderer: the independent tools tokenizer, with `enable_thinking` true. This is configuration evidence, not a capture of runtime requests.
- Both evaluation coordinators succeeded, and every child ran with one attempt.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Four `long-context/*` branches implement the context-parallel gaps #8374 lists for Grug main: a `context` mesh axis, context-sharded queries in the production FA4/CuTe attention path, a token-axis policy for MoE routing and loss under a sharded sequence, and an opt-in Transformer Engine CP backend. An integration branch composed them and trained the hero shape at sequence 262144 on one NVL72 rack (EP16xCP4, global batch 16, 4.19M tokens/step) from the hero's step-6000 checkpoint: 8.78% MFU, 113.5 s/step, peak HBM 127.6 of 138.2 GiB, and a drop fraction of 18% that was still rising. The hero's 1.15/1.15 capacity factors, tuned at sequence 4096 with batch 1024, do not carry to 262K at batch 16.

## Description

The 535B-A23B campaign (#8435) plans context extensions to 65K and possibly 262K; #8374 tracks the blockers and names four gaps in Grug main. Each gap has its own branch with a spec, implementation, an independent code review, and a fix round; specs and implementation notes live under `.agents/projects/` on each branch.

* [`long-context/mesh-context-axis`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/long-context/mesh-context-axis): `(replica_dcn, data, context, expert, model)` compact mesh via `compact_grug_mesh(context_axis_size=...)`, ported from the finished 262K TPU CP4 run (commit `b2cf4fe1aa` on `june_tpu_67b_a2b`). Checkpoints record no mesh, so pre-context checkpoints restore onto the 5-axis mesh unchanged.
* [`long-context/fa4-sequence-sharding`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/long-context/fa4-sequence-sharding): all-gather-KV context parallelism in the FA4/CuTe path. A runtime `q_offset` kernel input supplies the causal frontier (the kernel derives it from the local query index), the shard_map transpose provides the dK/dV psum over `context`, and the backward query-tile range is clamped to close an out-of-bounds LSE/dPsum read for key CTAs past a shard's queries. 19/19 GPU tests on GB200 at seq 512 / cp 2, including the hero tile config.
* [`long-context/moe-context-sharding`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/long-context/moe-context-sharding): the flattened token axis is sharded over `("replica_dcn", "data", "expert", "context")` and each context shard routes its tokens independently; EP drop psums, both QB estimators, and the fused cross-entropy loss reduce over spec-derived token axes.
* [`long-context/te-cp-backend`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/long-context/te-cp-backend): opt-in `gpu_te_cp` backend whose striping matches TE v2.17's `reorder_causal_striped` source. Runtime is blocked by the cuDNN `BAD_PARAM` in #8141, and no shipped variant can select it yet: a homogeneous layer scan cannot give TE a static per-layer window.
* [`long-context/262k-rack-experiment`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/long-context/262k-rack-experiment): merges the four, ports the bench launcher flags (`--seq-len`, `--restore-from`, `--context-axis-size`, `--expert-axis-size`, `--qk-mult`), and adds what composition required: composite `("expert", "context")` parameter sharding, a context-sharded residual stream, a left-halo `short_conv` wrapper, and a `MeshConfig` fix for global batch below the device count.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Measure whether the hero shape trains at 262144 sequence length on GB200 and what it costs in memory, throughput, and routing drops from a real checkpoint. This covers gates 1-2 of the early-cooldown list and the docs-per-shard routing risk #8374 calls the unresolved model-quality question.

## Status

Probe complete. Run `lc262k-ep16cp4-08251450` restored the 535B step-6000 checkpoint in 3.5 minutes and trained to the 6100 stop step on one rack; the job sealed `succeeded` with one preemption. Steady state over steps 6000-6012, from raw timestamps: 113.5 s/step, 37,042 tokens/s, 8.78% MFU, peak HBM 127.63 GiB against a 138.22 GiB limit, loss 1.416 median.

`moe/drop_fraction` was 0.18 median (0.081 sender, 0.101 receiver), rising 0.168 to 0.207 over the window. `capacity_overflow_rate_mean` tracks it exactly, so the loss is capacity clipping, not transport. Baselines: 3.5% drops on the live 4K hero, 1.7e-4 on the 4K one-rack restore arm. At batch 16 each expert coordinate routes one 65,536-token document instead of sixteen independent 4,096-token sequences, and expert load within one document is correlated enough that the fixed per-expert capacity clips it.

Caveat: the LR heuristic reads `HERO_MODEL.max_seq_len` (4096), so the probe applied ~6.9e-5, about 2% of the checkpoint's rate. The run measures throughput, memory, and routing; it does not diagnose 262K training stability.

## Links

* Plan and full run record (three failed attempts and their fixes): [`.agents/projects/20260824_262k_rack_experiment.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/long-context/262k-rack-experiment/.agents/projects/20260824_262k_rack_experiment.md)
* W&B: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc262k-ep16cp4-08251450
* Blocker tracker: #8374. TE/cuDNN toolchain: #8141. Hero campaign: #8435.

## Decision Log

* All-gather-KV FA4 is the production CP path; TE stays an opt-in seam until the #8141 toolchain is fixed.
* Parameters, their fp32 pinned-host masters, and Muon state shard over composite `("expert", "context")` so CP does not multiply per-rank optimizer memory; without this, EP16xCP4 needs ~1072 GB/node of host memory against ~850 available. Muon's Newton-Schulz derives its layout from the parameter instead of a hard-coded spec.
* The residual stream is context-sharded end to end, unblocked by a `kernel_size - 1` left halo (carrying neighbour segment ids) above the unchanged `short_conv` Pallas kernel. This took the rack step from an uncompilable 350 GiB/device to 127.6 GiB, and the d768 ladder at seq 262144 / cp4 from 19.71 to 13.59 GiB.
* `--schedule-steps 4470000` holds the mixture's simulated-epoching budget at ratio ~1 so no cell slices empty at sequence 262144.

## Conclusion

The hero shape compiles, restores, and trains at 262K on one rack with 10.6 GiB of HBM headroom. Routing capacity is the open problem: 18% of assignments drop under the 4K-tuned capacity factors, and the rate was still rising when the probe ended.

comments.body:
🤖 Handoff.

**State.** The five branches are pushed and review-complete: each went through a spec, implementation, an independent code review, and a fix round, with the full CI suite green on every tip (1964 passed on the integration branch). No PRs are open; that was deliberate while the campaign ran. The probe sealed `succeeded` and the numbers in the body are final.

**Blockers.**

* Routing: 18% drops, still rising, under the 4K-tuned 1.15/1.15 capacity factors. This blocks real 262K training in the current configuration.
* Stability is unread: the LR heuristic computes from `max_seq_len` 4096, so the probe applied ~2% of the checkpoint's LR. A stability read needs the heuristic computed at the real sequence length, or an explicit resume-LR config the way the 67B cooldowns used `GrugMoeMuonHResumeConfig`.
* TE runtime: `gpu_te_cp` cannot execute until the #8141 cuDNN `BAD_PARAM` toolchain issue is fixed. Not on the critical path; FA4 all-gather-KV is the working production path.

1. Upstream to main as reviewed PRs: mesh, then FA4, then MoE, then TE. The integration-only commits need proper homes: the `MeshConfig` fix and launcher flags belong with the hero launcher; composite parameter sharding, the context-sharded residual, and the `short_conv` halo belong with the FA4/MoE material.

Measured but unfixed performance items: the MoE flatten costs context-group all-to-alls each layer (shard_map over the 3-D activation is the recorded alternative); the cross-shard dK/dV reduction happens in bf16 and its error grows with the CP degree (compare against cp1 before long training); the composite parameter spec triggers ~1 GB/rank/step of involuntary SPMD rematerialization copies.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
Marin has no way to mark a test as needing a GPU, a minimum device count, or a specific accelerator. Some accelerator tests skip invisibly in CI as a result, and the two that need real device topology were written outside pytest entirely.

`tests/test_utils.py` provides `skip_if_no_tpu` and nothing equivalent for GPUs or device counts. The root `pyproject.toml` markers are `slow`, `integration`, `data_integration`, `cluster`, `requires_cluster`, `docker`, and `manual`; none describes hardware. `tests/cluster/conftest.py` names two clusters, `MARIN_TPU_CLUSTER` and `MARIN_GPU_CLUSTER = "cw-us-east-02a"`, with no entry for the GB200 cluster `cw-us-east-08a`.

Two tests in `lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py` check the ragged all-to-all MoE backend against a dense reference and run nowhere:

```
uv run python -m pytest lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py -rs -k "ragged or granular or clip"
...
SKIPPED test_moe_mlp_ep_backends_match_dense_value_and_gradients_when_available[ragged_all_to_all]
SKIPPED test_moe_mlp_reports_positive_drop_count_in_ragged_a2a_when_over_capacity
5 passed, 2 skipped
```

They skip on `requires an even number of >=2 devices`, and forcing two CPU devices hits the next guard, `ragged_all_to_all is not implemented on XLA:CPU`. Every job in `.github/workflows/` runs on `ubuntu-latest`. The five that pass cover lowering, offset arithmetic against a NumPy simulation of the collective, and capacity clipping in isolation. None runs the real collective or the SM100 expert kernels.

The root `addopts` does not include `-rs`, so these skips never appear in CI output. A green run with full coverage and a green run with no ragged coverage look identical.

Both files that need real accelerator topology avoided pytest. `lib/iris/tests/e2e/gpu_gang_smoke.py` is a standalone `__main__` script with `--target kind|coreweave` and `--i-understand-the-cost`; it mock-labels kind nodes to simulate an NVLink domain instead of requiring one. `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ragged_ep_check.py` (PR #8549) submits a 4-GPU GB200 job, computes a pass/fail verdict, and raises on failure, but sits under `experiments/` with no scheduled caller.

Two cases need different mechanisms. A test like the levanter one needs N local devices inside the pytest process. A test like `ragged_ep_check` needs no local hardware: it submits a job whose constraint rides in `ResourceConfig.with_gpu("GB200", count=4, ...)`, so what it needs is a cluster fixture and a way to declare that the run is expensive.

#7242 delivered `tests/cluster/`, the `cluster` marker, and `marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` for smokes that submit real jobs. It left open which hardware a test needs and what a test that cannot get that hardware should do.

Done when:

- A test can declare a local device requirement and skip with a named reason instead of an ad-hoc in-file guard.
- Skipped tests are visible in CI output.
- A job-submitting test can target the GB200 cluster through a fixture, and its cost is expressible on the test rather than only in the workflow.
- One existing case is ported as the reference: the levanter ragged EP tests, or `ragged_ep_check.py`.

It says `tests/cluster/` "covers submitting a job to a standing cluster" and that the gap is a GB200 lane and a cost tier on the existing workflow. The workflow no longer exists. #8605 deleted `.github/workflows/marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` on 2026-08-22, and its commit message gives the reason:

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Correcting my comment above, which was too absolute. "No workflow runs the `cluster` marker" is accurate; "accelerator tests have no automated vehicle" was not.

Scheduled GPU work does run. `marin-canary-ferry-coreweave.yaml` fires daily at 10:00 UTC against `cw-us-west-04a`, sets `CANARY_ACCELERATOR: gpu`, and runs `python -m experiments.ferries.canary_ferry` on 8x H100 through Iris, with `scripts/ci/validate_canary_metrics.py` asserting the result. That is a real accelerator smoke on a daily cron. It is not pytest and carries no marker.

`iris-smoke-coreweave.yaml` looks like a second GPU lane and is not one. It runs `pytest tests/test_integration_test.py -m integration` on PRs touching `lib/iris/**`, and the workflow comment says it submits "against the shared H100" — but the jobs `tests/integration_test.py` submits are `ResourceConfig.with_cpu()` with `require_accelerator=False`. It exercises a CoreWeave-hosted controller, not a GPU.

The deleted `marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` had two jobs, not one. `marin-tpu-smokes` ran on the schedule; `marin-gpu-smokes` was `if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.run_gpu`, so it never ran on a cron at all. The 38 timed-out scheduled runs the deleting commit cites were the TPU job. Standing-cluster GPU tests were therefore never automatic, before or after #8605.

So the gap this issue describes is sharper than "no runner": **no pytest marker anywhere selects GPU work.** The `cluster` marker has no workflow, and the `integration` marker runs only CPU jobs. Every GPU assertion in CI today lives in the canary ferry, outside pytest.

Two facts worth having when someone picks this up. The canary already parameterizes the accelerator (`CANARY_GPU_TYPE`, documented as "H100, GH200, B200", plus `CANARY_GPU_COUNT` and `CANARY_GPU_REPLICAS`), so scheduling GPU work of a given shape from Actions is solved machinery rather than something to build. And `marin-canary-ferry-coreweave.yaml` and `iris-smoke-coreweave.yaml` share the concurrency group `iris-coreweave-ci-shared` because they contend for one host, so any added lane needs a capacity story and not only a config entry.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Build RiffleEval as a paired long-context evaluation of coherent stream tracking. Each base item keeps the source text, question, answer, distractors, and token budget fixed while changing document chunks from blocked to riffled order. The primary result is the per-item riffle penalty, sliced by foreign-chunk interference count and token distance.

UncheatableEval is a candidate source feed after revision pinning, token-length filtering, license review, and safety filtering. Its current Marin integration is unsuitable: it downloads a stale GitHub fork whose records are capped at 5,000 characters and supplies no questions or evidence annotations. For v0, use frozen natural documents with exact-answer factual overlays; evaluate a filtered UncheatableEval `-Long` subset as one source arm, beginning with English Wikipedia and permissively licensed documents.

## Description

Long-context evaluations such as NIAH often test retrieval of one conspicuous item from a large context. RiffleEval tests whether a model can maintain several ordered information streams whose chunks repeatedly alternate across a 32K–64K prompt, then reconstruct facts within one stream.

For source document \(D_i = [C_{i,1}, \ldots, C_{i,n}]\), generate a legal merge that preserves chunk order within each source. Every chunk receives an opaque, per-example stream ID and ordinal. Questions and evidence annotations are created and verified against the clean document before riffling.

Each base item produces these conditions:

1. Clean target document, for source-task competence.
2. Blocked full context, with the target and distractor documents contiguous.
3. Riffled full context, with identical content and prompt budget.
4. Adjacent-evidence control for multi-evidence items.

The v0 task families are single-stream exact QA and two-evidence within-stream integration. Cross-stream joins and continuation NLL remain follow-ups.

The proposed context-length and stream-count matrix is not a full Cartesian product. With 4K–8K source documents, 32K supports roughly 4–8 streams and 64K supports roughly 8–16 streams. Larger documents or additional filler semantics would be required to hold stream count fixed while scaling total context. The generator must reject infeasible cells instead of silently repeating or padding sources.

## Hypothesis or Goal

At fixed content and question difficulty, riffling causes a measurable accuracy loss beyond the loss caused by the same blocked distractors. The loss increases with the number of intervening foreign chunks after controlling for absolute token distance. Better long-context checkpoints should move the retention curve toward larger interference counts.

## Status

Background research is complete. No implementation or model run has started.

### Proposed v0

- 250–500 verified base items, expanded into deterministic paired variants.
- 32K and 64K contexts; feasible 4/8/16-stream cells; approximately 512-token chunks.
- Exact short answers with one-evidence and two-evidence overlays.
- Opaque opening and closing markers with tokenizer-balanced random IDs.
- Random and same-domain distractors.
- Native-model score with tools disabled.
- Exact match, per-item riffle penalty, blocked-to-riffled penalty, and retention curves by token distance, interference count, evidence count, and active streams.
- Target-stream extraction and oracle-evidence diagnostics to separate stream selection from reasoning.
- Frozen generator version, seed, source revision/hash, tokenizer, prompt, and structural metadata for every item.

### UncheatableEval corpus decision

Use it as an optional source-discovery and freshness feed. Do not use the published collection as the sole corpus or reuse `experiments/datasets/uncheatable.py`.

The current upstream `-Long` snapshots contain 7,500 records across 15 categories and retain source URL, date, category, `content`, and `untruncated_content`. They provide recent natural interference, but no question, answer, stable ID, evidence span, or hop graph. The dataset card declares no dataset license, and source rights differ by document. AO3 has safety concerns; arbitrary GitHub files need license and secret checks; BBC is a poor redistribution default; PDF extraction can corrupt arXiv text. Freshness only protects models whose training cutoff predates the crawl.

A derived arm must:

- pin the Hugging Face revision and content hash;
- filter on benchmark-tokenizer length, language, quality, and safety;
- record URL, collection date, source category, license, and transformed-text hash;
- begin with English Wikipedia and individually cleared permissive sources;
- exclude BBC and AO3 from v0;
- generate exact-answer overlays and frozen evidence spans against the exact transformed text.

## Background Research Brief

- Effort / stop rule / date: medium; 2026-08-24; stopped when the internal, benchmark, corpus, and contradiction passes no longer changed the v0 recommendation.

### Current Marin context

- #7638 owns RULER integration. RiffleEval should not duplicate its eval harness work.
- #4736 specified the closest reusable data contract: frozen long-document QA items with exact answers, evidence spans, and length bins.
- #7181 found that retained MRCR context reduced final-turn PPL from 21.0855 to 10.4012 at 8,192 tokens. Its extraction PR #7203 closed unmerged, so it is prior evidence rather than current infrastructure.
- #5825 previously built 32K/64K long-document PPL slices; the implementation was later removed by #6633.
- No existing issue or implementation tests repeated switching among several coherent streams.

### External prior art

- [RULER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654) varies context length and task complexity across multi-needle retrieval, variable tracking, aggregation, and QA. RiffleEval adds coherent natural streams and a paired blocked/riffled intervention.
- [MRCR/Michelangelo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) shows that repeated, similar requests and ordinal selection are harder than unique needles. RiffleEval should include similar competing streams and report random/noise floors.
- [NoLiMa](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167) shows that lexical overlap makes retrieval easier and normalizes long-context scores to short-context competence. RiffleEval should vary lexical overlap and reject items with weak clean-document accuracy.
- [BABILong](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/c0d62e70dbc659cc9bd44cbcf1cb652f-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf) distributes multi-fact synthetic tasks through natural books. RiffleEval adds several foreground streams, explicit stream identities, and the same task before and after structural transformation.
- [LOFT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13121) found that marker and prompt formatting materially affect retrieval. Marker tokenization and query placement must be fixed or explicitly ablated.
- [UncheatableEval](https://github.com/Jellyfish042/uncheatable_eval) evaluates rolling internet text by NLL. Its freshness method is useful for source discovery; it does not provide RiffleEval annotations.

### Contradiction and shortcut pass

- Random riffles and IDs prevent fixed-order contamination but do not prevent a model from answering public facts from parametric memory. Synthetic counterfactual overlays provide the durable control.
- Opaque IDs expose segmentation but do not prevent keyword search within the target stream. Lexical-overlap and near-neighbor distractor slices remain necessary.
- “Uniform-ish” legal merges do not independently control gap length. Sample examples from explicit interference-count and token-distance strata.
- Marker token lengths can differ across tokenizers and become an unplanned treatment. Balance marker encodings and store their token counts.
- Native QA generation from unannotated documents can admit one-passage shortcuts. Require evidence spans, clean-document verification, and minimal-evidence ablations.

### Recommended next experiments

#### 1. Validate the paired structural signal at 32K

- Minimum experiment / baseline: 100 overlay items, four streams, 512-token chunks; clean, blocked, and riffled conditions on two representative models with different long-context capability.
- Expected signal / falsifier: a nonzero blocked-to-riffled penalty that grows across interference buckets while clean accuracy remains high. Near-zero penalty, floor-level clean accuracy, or prompt-format sensitivity larger than the treatment falsifies the current setup.

#### 2. Add two-evidence integration and 64K

- Minimum experiment / baseline: two controlled facts in widely separated chunks; adjacent-evidence and oracle-extracted-stream baselines; feasible 8/16-stream cells.
- Expected signal / falsifier: two-evidence retention degrades faster than one-evidence retention while oracle extraction recovers most accuracy. Failure of the oracle indicates base reasoning or question-construction problems.

#### 3. Compare source pools

- Minimum experiment / baseline: matched overlays over a pinned filtered UncheatableEval `-Long` arm and one stable, license-cleared long-document corpus.
- Expected signal / falsifier: model ranking and riffle penalty remain stable across source pools. Large domain-specific reversals require a multi-corpus benchmark or removal of the unstable source.

### Source ledger

| Source | Type | Location | Claim used for | Confidence | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RULER | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654 | complexity axes and baselines | high | nearest variable-tracking precedent |
| Michelangelo / MRCR | paper and official code | https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640 | repeated similar needles and order | high | conversation format differs from riffled documents |
| NoLiMa | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167 | lexical-overlap shortcut and retention normalization | high | single-association retrieval |
| BABILong | paper | https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/c0d62e70dbc659cc9bd44cbcf1cb652f-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf | distributed multi-fact reasoning in natural text | high | one background stream |
| LOFT | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13121 | formatting and identifier sensitivity | high | fixed retrieval corpora |
| UncheatableEval | official repo and dataset | https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-07-Long | source schema, freshness, and corpus limitations | high | no dataset-level license or QA annotations |
| Marin #4736 | GitHub issue | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4736 | QA manifest and evidence schema | high | closed before implementation |
| Marin #7638 | GitHub issue | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7638 | active RULER scope | high | avoid duplicate harness work |
| Marin #7181 | GitHub issue | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7181 | paired MRCR PPL result | high | extraction PR closed unmerged |

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates: #7638, #4736, #7181, #5825

## Decision Log

- 2026-08-24: scope v0 to paired single-stream exact QA and two-evidence within-stream integration at 32K/64K.
- 2026-08-24: treat UncheatableEval as an optional filtered source arm; reject the current Marin handle and the unfiltered published corpus as the canonical benchmark source.
- 2026-08-24: defer cross-stream joins, continuation NLL, and 128K+ until the primary structural signal is validated.

## Conclusion

Open. Advance to implementation if the 32K pilot produces high clean accuracy, a reproducible blocked-to-riffled penalty, and a stable ordering across source pools and marker templates.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
## TL;DR

`telemetry_v1` retained 643.5 million rows and 14.94 GiB across 28.54 hours on 2026-08-21, an observed fill rate of 12.57 GiB/day. Levanter supplied 66.2% of rows and node telemetry supplied 28.0%. This experiment will reduce duplicated and low-value writes, retain priority training metrics separately, and validate the result on copied production shards before a production PR.

## Description

Finelog's inherited 15 GiB per-namespace local-cache cap leaves about 28.6 hours of `telemetry_v1` queryable on local storage at the measured rate. A current 704-process Levanter run publishes `step` from every process. Node agents publish about twenty device series per GPU every 30 seconds. vLLM and Iris controller snapshots publish cumulative histogram buckets every 15 seconds.

The detailed commands and raw measurements belong in `.agents/logbooks/telemetry-volume.md` and the linked Loom artifacts. Production objects are read-only inputs; local shard copies stay outside the repository.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Route cheap, frequently queried training metrics to a 50 GiB priority namespace; route other telemetry to a bulk namespace; remove replicated Levanter progress; and reduce the cadence of high-volume bulk snapshots. The combined treatment should cut compressed bytes/day while increasing the locally queryable priority window.

## Status

Phase-a attribution is complete. A 10.08 GiB sample of 110 production Parquets is being copied for byte-level cadence and namespace experiments.

## Links

* Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/telemetry-volume.md`
* W&B Report: none
* Important updates: Loom artifact `telemetry-influx-phase-a`

## Decision Log

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 In-progress, multi-module experiment with validation pending on copied shards — not opening a PR, since that would preempt the very treatments this issue is set up to measure. Three grounding notes so phase-b lands on real code:

**"Levanter publishes `step` from every process" — confirmed root cause.** `TelemetryTracker._publish` gates tracker metrics on `publish_tracker_metrics = (process_index == 0)`, but `log()` writes `step` and `progress_time_seconds` through `_set` *before* that gate, and `runtime_telemetry.configure(...)` runs on every process. So all 704 processes emit those two series, consistent with Levanter's 66.2% row share.
- [`telemetry.py#L200-L207`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/telemetry.py#L200-L207) — unconditional `_set("step"/"progress_time_seconds")`
- [`telemetry.py#L167-L169`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/telemetry.py#L167-L169), [`#L241-L247`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/telemetry.py#L241-L247) — process-0 gate that `step` bypasses

Gating those two writes on `self._publish_tracker_metrics` is the minimal "remove replicated Levanter progress" treatment (<20 lines).

**Priority vs bulk namespace — the enabling mechanism already exists.** `StoragePolicy(max_bytes / max_segments / max_age_seconds)` is applied per namespace at register time, so the 50 GiB priority namespace is a producer-side namespace split plus a policy value — no server change.
- [`policy.py#L28-L46`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/src/finelog/policy.py#L28-L46) — per-namespace caps on `RegisterTable`

**Cadence knobs are already configurable.** Node/probe intervals are plain parameters, so reducing bulk-snapshot cadence needs no new plumbing.
- [`prometheus.py#L128`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/telemetry/prometheus.py#L128) — `poll_interval`
- [`probes/runner.py#L184`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/telemetry/probes/runner.py#L184) — probe `interval`

Happy to carve any single treatment into its own PR once phase-b picks winners.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 The [production-sample analysis](http://127.0.0.1:7878/s/l7xftsek/artifacts/telemetry-volume-mitigation-analysis) is complete.

The selected producer policy reduced the 10.08 GiB sample by 68.6% compressed bytes and 68.1% rows. The resulting priority tier projects to 2.09 GiB/day, or about 24 days under a 50 GiB local-cache budget. A 60-second compaction policy saved 63.9% and changed five-minute GPU-utilization means by 1.12 percentage points on average and 6.43 at p95. A 300-second policy saved 74.7%, with p95 utilization error of 28.1 points.

The implementation keeps priority training and Zephyr progress in `telemetry_v1`, routes bulk records to `telemetry_bulk_v1`, lowers the high-volume producer cadences, and leaves generic compaction downsampling for a metric-family-aware follow-up.

comments.body:
🤖 Update: the two-tier `priority`/`bulk` namespace proposal in the earlier comment is superseded. The implementation now routes records to semantic children such as `telemetry_v1.node_agent`, `telemetry_v1.levanter.core`, `telemetry_v1.levanter.extra`, `telemetry_v1.iris.rpc`, and `telemetry_v1.vllm`. `telemetry_v1` remains a logical rollup over every child and the legacy physical table during migration. Cross-child window queries remain enabled because the rollup executes them correctly and now has regression coverage.

The child retention budgets sum to 50 GiB. Producer-side suppression and cadence results are unchanged: the 10.080 GiB replay fell 68.6% in compressed bytes. Generic compaction downsampling remains deferred pending per-family reducers and a recent unsampled horizon.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
## TL;DR

On the same data (Experiment 2's 216 pinned SFT chat caches, 234,383,016,035 real tokens after 262,144-token left-slicing), Levanter's sequential packer produces 1,035,158 sequences at 13.6267% padding with the 64-segment cap. A bounded-window first-fit lookahead packer removes 42% of that padding (970,215 sequences, 7.8451% at window 64) with local reordering and a few CPU-seconds of packing cost. What remains is set by the segment cap, not document order: raising the cap is a separate lever (cap 128 + lookahead → 2.45% chat padding, cap 256 → 1.33%, uncapped → 0.98%). Recommendation: adopt the lookahead packer as an opt-in option (PR #11379), decide the segment cap separately in Experiment 3, keep replay leaves streamed.

## Description

Experiment 2 SFT packs whole conversations into 262,144-token sequences on 216 chat leaves (`pack=True` → at most 64 segments per sequence); 1,711 pretraining-replay leaves run as a continuous stream (no packing, documents cross sequence boundaries with EOS). Conversations are never split, so each sequence pads the tail it cannot fill. The question: how much of that padding is recoverable by a better packer on the same data, at what cost?

Method: per-document token lengths were re-extracted offsets-only from the pinned caches (every cache verified against the Experiment 2 census receipts: rows, tokens, per-cache length-vector SHA-256; totals 21,245,136 traces / 234,420,759,584 tokens). Packing strategies were simulated offline on CPU; no model, no training run, no source data change. Pretraining-replay leaf caches were extracted the same way from the pinned spec (388 leaves, 35,255,949 documents, 38,826,415,376 tokens).

Run-wide composition context for interpreting the totals:

- 128-sequence prefix estimates from the native loader: 22 replay / 106 chat; 30,847,679 real tokens of 33,554,432 positions (8.07% padding overall; chat 9.74%; replay 0%).
- Expected composition (weights × component stats), phase 0: replay 20.47% of positions, 22.33% of real tokens, 29.92% of loss-bearing tokens; chat assistant tokens are 67.34% of chat real tokens. Phase 1 (from step 8000): replay 20.37% / 22.22% / 29.79%.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Measure, per packing strategy, the pad fraction overall and per source, packed sequences (equivalently optimizer updates at batch 8), segments per sequence, reorder distance against the source order, packing compute/memory cost, and determinism/resumability; and quantify how much padding the 64-segment cap versus document order causes.

## Status

Complete. Strategies measured at capacity 262,144, cap 64, packing within each child cache, `slice_strategy="left"` for over-long documents. Real tokens are identical in every row; positions and padding vary.

| Packer | Packed sequences | Positions | Pad fraction | Relative change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| sequential (Levanter's current, baseline) | 1,035,158 | 271,360,458,752 | 13.6267% | — |
| lookahead w=8 | 979,589 | 256,793,378,816 | 8.7270% | −39.4% |
| lookahead w=64 | 970,215 | 254,336,040,960 | 7.8451% | −42.4% |
| lookahead w=256 | 968,405 | 253,861,560,320 | 7.6729% | −43.7% |
| lookahead w=1024 | 967,574 | 253,643,718,656 | 7.5936% | −44.3% |
| window FFD w=64 | 1,063,698 | 278,842,048,512 | 15.9442% | worse |
| window FFD w=1024 | 999,300 | 261,960,499,200 | 10.5273% | worse |
| window BFD w=1024 | 999,291 | 261,958,139,904 | 10.5265% | worse |
| global best-fit-decreasing | 989,596 | 259,416,653,824 | 9.6500% | worse |
| lower bound (cap 64) | 961,454 | 252,039,397,376 | 7.0006% | floor |

Segment-cap binding (definition: a 64-document pack that still had room for the next document): 143,933 of 1,035,158 packs (13.904%); 46 of 184 SFT components bind, led by math_v2/low, instruction_following_chat_v2, identity-data, ultrachat (≥99.4%). With the cap, 99.9% of the lower-bound padding comes from the 39 cap-bound sources; per-source group split: cap-bound sources 45.75% → 45.72% padding (unchanged by any packer), non-cap-bound sources 8.29% → 1.06%.

Reorder distance (share of documents moved / mean displacement in positions): lookahead w=8: 14.5% / 0.31 (max 29); w=64: 35.2% / 1.55 (max 63); w=1024: 53.1% / 12.37; global BFD: full re-sort. Because cross-document attention is blocked, reordering changes sequence/batch composition, not per-document computation; source composition per sequence is invariant and per-batch composition is unchanged in distribution; under fixed per-sequence mixture weights, per-source real-token shares shift at most +0.37 pp.

Packer cost (single CPU core, all 21.2M documents): sequential 1.5 s; lookahead w=8/64/256/1024 = 7.0/10.5/22.2/70.1 s; window FFD/BFD 42–54 s; global BFD 50 s. Memory O(n) (two int64 arrays; ≤58 MB on the largest cache). All strategies are deterministic and rebuild identically from the cache after a restart.

Segment-cap axis (chat pad fraction, sequential → lookahead w=64): cap 64: 13.6267% → 7.8451%; cap 128: 8.9632% → 2.4478%; cap 256: 7.9986% → 1.3325%; cap 512: 7.8221% → 1.1293%; uncapped: 7.6911% → 0.9787%. Cost of a larger cap: no training-path array is shaped by `max_segments` (segment ids and FA4/CuTe bounds are per-token `[B, S]` int32/bool; short-conv kernels likewise), so raising it costs zero training memory; only eval per-segment metrics allocate a `(max_Segments, Pos)` mask. Chat fully streamed (documents crossing sequences) would be 894,348 sequences / 0.0116% padding — the absolute floor, at the cost of cross-conversation attention.

Replay leaves: streamed continuously in the consumed configuration, 148,311 sequences, 0.1348% padding (2,699 documents exceed 262,144 and are split, not truncated). Packing replay with the chat packer would instead produce 579,303 sequences at 76.21% padding. Combined consumed-configuration view: chat sequential + replay stream = 310,239,297,536 positions at 11.9359% padding; chat lookahead w=64 + replay stream = 293,214,879,744 positions at 6.8228% padding.

Validation: the offline simulation matches Levanter's reference `pack_documents` exactly on 200 randomized inputs × 3 segment caps, and the PR's lookahead implementation produces exactly the same packs as the simulation on five real caches (largest 3.6M documents, plus segment-cap-bound and small caches).

## Links

* Full report: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/benfeuer/sft-new-mix-candidate/packing-ablation/REPORT.md` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/benfeuer/sft-new-mix-candidate/packing-ablation/REPORT.md))
* Result JSONs (per-strategy/per-cache/per-source, cap sweep, cap binding, replay side): same prefix ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/benfeuer/sft-new-mix-candidate/packing-ablation/))
* Opt-in packer implementation: PR #11379
* Experiment 2 census inputs: `artifacts/experiment2/population-262k-final/truncation-census.json` (216 chat caches) and the pinned spec's `pretrain/*` replay components

## Decision Log

* 2026-11-13: measured; baseline reproduces the Experiment 2 population census exactly (1,035,158 sequences, 13.6267%). Windowed decreasing and global BFD rejected (worse than lookahead under the segment cap). Lookahead packer implemented as opt-in; Experiment 2 keeps its current packer.
* 2026-11-13: replay leaves confirmed continuous-stream in the consumed config; `pack: 262144` literals in the pinned component JSONs are historical and unconsumed.

## Conclusion

Packing efficiency on this corpus is bounded first by the 64-segment cap and second by document order. A bounded-window lookahead removes 39–42% of chat padding at trivial cost with local reordering, and reaches within 0.85 pp of the cap-64 floor. The remaining ~7% padding under the current cap requires raising the segment cap (a data/training decision, zero training-memory cost) rather than a different packer. Replay stays streamed.
