issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Research abstention behavior for the cold-start SFT recipe: the model declines or flags uncertainty when it does not know, and still answers when it does. This is a child of #8089.

Candidate inputs: [nvidia/Nemotron-RL-QA-Abstention-v1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-RL-QA-Abstention-v1) (CC-BY-4.0, queued for Atlas ingest as an SFT candidate), converted to SFT with teacher responses. [AbstentionBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ymerkli/AbstentionBench) is a candidate evaluation and must stay out of training.

Done when:

- The intended abstention behavior is specified for unanswerable, underspecified, false-premise and answerable questions.
- Candidate supervision and evaluation cases measure both over-abstention and missed abstention.
- Any new source is registered through the datakit SFT workflow, so its Atlas variant carries the `sft` tag.
- The cold-start recipe records the selected behavior and its acceptance test.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

Effort: low (issue, checkout, related PRs, dataset cards). [Nemotron-RL-QA-Abstention-v1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-RL-QA-Abstention-v1) contains 3,150 RLVR prompts and answer keys but no assistant responses; its boxed `[IDK]` instruction is not yet a cold-start conversational SFT target, and 450 questions come from HotpotQA. [AbstentionBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ymerkli/AbstentionBench) supplies `should_abstain` labels across 19 splits and must remain evaluation-only. No QA abstention recipe or acceptance evaluation appears in this checkout; [#11658](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11658) is defining versioned SFT mix handles, while [#11730](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11730) covers the separate tool-call abstention case.

**Relevant code**
- [`experiments/sft/launcher.py#L116`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L116) — pinned SFT dataset component.
- [`experiments/datasets/instruction.py#L135`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/datasets/instruction.py#L135) — chat source adapter.
- [`experiments/sft/configs/delphi_1e22.py#L121`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/sft/configs/delphi_1e22.py#L121) — existing recipe declaration.

# Proposed Fix

Proposed behavior contract:
- Unanswerable or unknown: state the missing knowledge and stop before an unsupported factual claim; offer a source or tool when useful.
- Underspecified: ask for the specific missing detail; answer any part that is invariant to that detail.
- False premise: correct the premise, then answer the corrected question when possible.
- Answerable: give the supported answer directly. An unnecessary refusal or clarification is a failure.

Plan:
1. Freeze a held-out evaluation before making training data: use pinned AbstentionBench splits plus a small reviewed set with all four behaviors and matched answerable controls. Keep every evaluation prompt and answer out of teacher generation and training; audit overlap with the NVIDIA source, including its HotpotQA component. Record baseline rates for unsupported answers on unanswerable prompts, clarification on underspecified prompts, premise correction, false abstention, and answer accuracy, by domain and thinking mode.
2. Pin and audit the NVIDIA source revision and row-level licenses. Generate teacher SFT responses from its prompts, verify answer-bearing responses against the provided answer key, and review uncertainty responses. Add independently sourced, matched unanswerable, underspecified, false-premise, and answerable cases; the NVIDIA release alone does not supply supervised abstention decisions. Reject examples that teach boxed output or blanket refusal outside that format's intended use.
3. Register the accepted source and transform through the datakit SFT workflow, verify that its Atlas variant has the `sft` tag, and include its immutable revision and mixture weight in the versioned cold-start recipe. Coordinate the factuality and grounded-answer boundaries with [#11824](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11824) and [#11825](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11825).
4. Run a matched control and treatment from the same parent checkpoint and training budget. Proposed acceptance gate: reduce unsupported answers on unanswerable prompts by at least 5 percentage points; improve clarification and premise-correction rates; allow at most a 2-point rise in false abstention and a 2-point drop in answerable accuracy. Report per-split counts and paired confidence intervals, then record the selected behavior, data pins, and gate results in the recipe. These thresholds are proposed before a baseline exists and should be frozen before the ablation.

This needs data curation, teacher generation, a held-out evaluation, and a training comparison; there is no isolated small fix to submit as a PR yet.

issues.title: [sft] Establish abstention behavior

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Micro210 and Mini840 select few tasks per benchmark, so answer keys can be highly imbalanced, and a constant reply can score far above chance. On Micro210, `B` scores 50% on GPQA Diamond (5 of 10 keys are B), `I don't know.` scores 40% on MMLU-Pro (4 of 10 keys are I, picked up by the last-capital fallback), and TruthfulQA keys are all A (#11827). Those three benchmarks then cannot separate a trained round from a constant (contributor analysis on #11337: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11337#issuecomment-7041057634). Random guessing as an extractor fallback is acceptable; the defect is the key distribution.

Done when:
- The next Micro210 and Mini840 policy versions select tasks so that no answer label in any multiple-choice benchmark exceeds a stated maximum share (for example 1.5× uniform), with a fixed seed.
- The policy build fails if a benchmark violates the bound, and a test covers it.
- A constant-reply floor check (the `trivial_replies` replies from #11222 plus each single letter) runs on every new version and reports each benchmark's best constant score.
- The new versions get new policy hashes; existing records keep their old hashes.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The archived selector interleaves benchmarks and existing strata but does not see answer keys; `collect_release_sources` copies that selection before fetching its source specifications, and `build_release_dataset` publishes the resulting 210-task prefix and 840-task set. The selection builder is archived outside `main`, while `main` pins a frozen Micro210 policy by digest. TruthfulQA accepts every position marked true, so its all-A prompt ordering (#11827) must be fixed before a label bound can pass; the open trivial-reply launcher (#11222) also refuses judged tasks.

**Relevant code**
- [`methods.py#L36-L73`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5b53a4d12e9f55bb2c629c7423a00974ec1df4d7/experiments/evaluation/mini_policy/methods.py#L36-L73) — archived seeded selector.
- [`collect_release_sources.py#L36-L61`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5b53a4d12e9f55bb2c629c7423a00974ec1df4d7/experiments/evaluation/mini_policy/collect_release_sources.py#L36-L61) — selection precedes source collection.
- [`build_release_dataset.py#L373-L416`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5b53a4d12e9f55bb2c629c7423a00974ec1df4d7/experiments/evaluation/mini_policy/build_release_dataset.py#L373-L416) — nested release and manifest.
- [`micro210_policy.py#L14-L65`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/28c399d23300c030d424b106d2ad0a24703daaf0/experiments/evaluation/micro210_policy.py#L14-L65) — old and current content-pinned references in #11120.
- [`trivial_replies.py#L105-L134`](https://github.com/XiaoyuanWang111/marin/blob/772913f85b6287269989a2c208a62e87defc321a/experiments/evaluation/trivial_replies.py#L105-L134) — standard driver and unsupported grader paths in #11222.

# Design

1. Bring the archived release selector and validation into a maintained evaluation path. Before drawing tasks, build a source-revision-pinned answer-key manifest for every eligible multiple-choice candidate; the current collector only materializes already-selected tasks. Keep the existing benchmark budgets, repetitions, source identities, and Micro210-as-Mini840-prefix rule. Use a fixed seed and deterministic candidate ordering to satisfy a published per-label cap, initially `count(label) <= floor(1.5 * tasks_in_benchmark / option_count)` for both prefixes. Preserve existing strata as a secondary selection criterion. Fail with benchmark, label counts, and available-pool counts if the cap cannot be met.
2. Coordinate with #11827 to shuffle TruthfulQA choices with a fixed per-task seed before deriving label counts. Count every position accepted by its generated-choice grader, since a task may have more than one true answer. Do not certify a label distribution from only the first true position.
3. Add a release test on pinned source fixtures that checks both cohort sizes and nesting, deterministic selection, per-benchmark bounds, and an infeasible-pool failure. Gate the built Parquet and manifest with the same checks. Publish new immutable Mini840 and Micro210 dataset revisions and a new Micro210 policy URI, revision, byte size, and SHA-256; retain all historical references and records under their existing hashes.
4. For each new version, score the five plain `trivial_replies` responses from #11222 plus every single letter present in a multiple-choice prompt through the version's prepared tasks and actual graders. Extend the constant-model runner for judged and agentic paths that #11222 does not support, then publish each benchmark's best reply, score, scored/assigned count, and archive link. Make the floor report and complete benchmark coverage required release artifacts.

Open question: the pinned candidate manifest must establish whether the proposed 1.5× cap is feasible for TruthfulQA's multiple accepted positions; if not, report the minimum feasible cap and choose a stated bound before building the new version.

issues.title: [eval] Balance answer labels in Micro210 and Mini840 task selection

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
TruthfulQA generated-choice prompts in Micro210 and Mini840 always list a true answer first, so a constant reply of `\boxed{A}` scores 100%. The prompts take options in `mc2_targets` order, and that order starts with a true answer in every row of `truthfulqa/truthful_qa` (10 of 10 Micro210 tasks, 41 of 41 Mini840 tasks, 817 of 817 dataset rows). Model scores on this benchmark measure position bias, not truthfulness. Found in the contributor analysis on #11337 (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11337#issuecomment-7041057634).

Reproduce:
1. Load `open-athena/Marin-Micro-Eval-210` at revision `4564ed081c316bc3231ae5c3a53a46b39248c819`, `data/validation.parquet`.
2. For each `truthfulqa` row, decode `config.json` from the verifier resources and read `spec.doc.mc2_targets.labels[0]`.
3. Every value is 1 (true).

Expected: each task's options are shuffled with a fixed per-task seed, so the true answers are spread across positions. The full policy's MC2 likelihood scoring does not depend on order and needs no change.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

## Research

The released TruthfulQA generated-choice tasks preserve `mc2_targets` order in the solver prompt and verifier config. [The source-row audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11337#issuecomment-7041057634) found a true option A in 817/817 source rows, 10/10 Micro210 tasks, and 41/41 Mini840 tasks; `\boxed{A}` scores 100% on Micro210. [Micro210 preparation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/28c399d23300c030d424b106d2ad0a24703daaf0/experiments/post_training/long_loop/evaluation.py#L46-L72) selects released task JSON and rebinds grader resources without changing the prompt. [The canonical launcher](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0b7a195773d08c4bccdb185da029acb0cb8f7c20/experiments/evaluation/micro210.py#L53-L68) verifies prepared bytes against a frozen policy hash. The [full-policy MC2 importer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0b7a195773d08c4bccdb185da029acb0cb8f7c20/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evaluation_harness.py#L131-L136) uses choice likelihoods and needs no prompt shuffle.

## Proposed Fix

1. Inspect a released TruthfulQA task and its verifier, then add a versioned, deterministic permutation keyed by stable task ID in the generated-choice release path. Permute displayed options and the verifier's `mc2_targets` choice/label pairs together; serialize matching task and rollout specs.
2. Rebuild versioned Micro210 and Mini840 tables and Micro210 prepared inputs. Publish source revisions, task checksums, and new policy hashes. Keep existing artifacts and score records pinned to their old hashes. Coordinate policy-reference updates with [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120) and [#11818](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11818), which already modify the release and policy paths.
3. Test repeatable shuffles, preservation of every choice/label pair, and prompt-to-verifier agreement with a real verifier on tasks with multiple true answers. Audit all released TruthfulQA rows and report label-position counts plus the constant-A score for both panels. [#11829](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11829) owns the separate task-selection balance bound.

issues.title: [eval] TruthfulQA choice prompts always put a true answer first

issues.author: chrismc91
issues.body:
The eval launcher (`python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch`) always serves the candidate model itself, with vLLM or Levanter on a GPU or TPU ([`ServeBackend`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/model_config.py#L25-L29)). Adding a curated benchmark takes several rounds of 20-item smoke runs to check prompt rendering, answer extraction and grading. Each round waits for an accelerator, often for hours, before any item runs. The same check against a hosted OpenAI-compatible API needs only a CPU worker.

[`experiments.evaluation.task_driver`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/experiments/evaluation/task_driver.py) already runs a published corpus against any OpenAI-compatible URL. A 20-item ChemBench run against `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-super-vl:free` on OpenRouter graded all 20 items. It finished 14 minutes after submission (11 minutes of evaluation) and cost $0. The driver runs outside the launcher, though. It writes no `record.json`, so `cli scores` and EvalDash cannot read the run, and the corpus root, run config and tokenizer are assembled by hand. Its remote mode also connects straight to the CoreWeave controller, which needs `kubectl` and a CoreWeave kubeconfig; the launcher routes through the `marin` hub instead.

The launcher could accept a hosted candidate: a model whose requests go to an external endpoint, for curated chat-generation benchmarks. Curated judges already work this way. Run settings name a `judge_endpoint` and a `judge_api_key` secret reference. The launcher resolves the key at submission and adds the host to the job's egress allowlist ([launch.py#L300-L307](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/experiments/evaluation/launch.py#L300-L307), [#L705-L706](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/experiments/evaluation/launch.py#L705-L706)).

These parts of the launch path assume a served model:

- `build_evaluation_batch` pins Hugging Face weights, selects an accelerator, decides request seeding from platform and backend, and derives the records prefix from the accelerator ([launch.py#L368-L545](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/experiments/evaluation/launch.py#L368-L545)).
- The orchestrator starts an inference job, polls its health, and resolves its endpoint through Iris ([runner.py#L84-L143](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L84-L143), [#L698-L723](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L698-L723)).
- The evaluator reads the context window from vLLM's `max_model_len` field in `/models` and fails without it ([dataset_evaluator.py#L55-L59](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/dataset_evaluator.py#L55-L59)).
- `record.json` requires a model `serve` and `resource_hint` block and a GPU or TPU `HardwareRef` ([records.py#L240-L246](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/lib/evalrecords/src/evalrecords/records.py#L240-L246), [#L482-L491](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/lib/evalrecords/src/evalrecords/records.py#L482-L491)). EvalDash indexes backend, platform and accelerator.
- Every chat request sends `extra_body.chat_template_kwargs`, and `top_k` and `seed` when set ([rollouts/evaluation.py#L114-L137](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/lib/marin/src/marin/rollouts/evaluation.py#L114-L137)). OpenRouter accepted these in the ChemBench run above; other providers are unchecked.
- Likelihood and completion protocols need echoed logprobs and `/completions`, which hosted APIs generally do not offer.

| Option | Shape | Size | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | A separate `HostedModel` config type (base URL, provider model ID, key as a secret reference, tokenizer, context window), and an endpoint protocol that the runner accepts in place of `RemoteInferenceSession` | ~400–600 lines | One launch command for smoke and full runs; needs an evalrecords and EvalDash representation for API-served runs |
| B | A `ServeBackend.EXTERNAL` value on the existing `ModelConfig` | smaller | The vLLM serving fields, resource hints and accelerator selection each need a backend check; records carry serve and hardware values that do not apply |
| C | A launcher command that wraps `task_driver`: it resolves corpora and settings, submits the worker through the hub, and writes a minimal record | ~150–250 lines | Cheapest; adds a second record writer and still needs the record decision |

Option A fits best. It would start with curated chat-generation benchmarks and reject Harbor, likelihood and completion protocols at launch. Harbor needs separate work, because its OpenCode agent config hardcodes `apiKey: "EMPTY"` and a `hosted_vllm/` model alias ([trial_driver.py#L319](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py#L319), [#L365](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py#L365)).

Open questions for the launcher and evalrecords owners:

- How should a record mark an API-served run (for example `HardwareRef(platform="api", accelerator=<provider>)`)? Should these runs use a separate records prefix so they never mix with fleet results in EvalDash?
- OpenRouter can route one model ID to different upstream providers. Should records keep the requested and returned model and provider for each request?
- The worker loads a Hugging Face tokenizer for every run ([task_worker.py#L64](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b8a591ea535b9403ebc76f43dc0c652a6d4f1e0b/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/task_worker.py#L64)). Open-weight models have one; are closed models out of scope?
- Should hosted candidates and curated judges share one endpoint and secret type?

Related: [#4827](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4827) separated serving from evaluation behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, but its external-API path relied on LiteLLM, which [#10471](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10471) removed. [#10818](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10818) scoped free-tier OpenRouter use and noted its daily request cap, provider routing and data-retention terms.

Done when:

- `cli launch --model-config <hosted model> --evals <curated chat benchmark> --limit 20` runs through the standard orchestrator and worker with no accelerator job.
- `record.json` identifies the run as API-served, with provider and model ID, and `cli scores` reads it.
- The launcher resolves the API key from a secret reference, as it does for judge keys, and the key never appears in records or logs.
- Harbor, likelihood and completion protocols fail at launch with a clear error.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

On current `main` (`f79686b`), a curated evaluation already sends requests through an OpenAI-compatible URL, but `build_evaluation_batch` first pins weights and chooses an accelerator, and the runner always prepares a candidate inference session. `task_driver.py` can use an external URL but does not write the shared run record. No open PR found in the duplicate-work check implements hosted candidates; #11818 changes judge serving only.

**Relevant code**
- [`launch.py#L368-L553`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f79686b2185c57d2db32569d9c27f2bcebd04e76/experiments/evaluation/launch.py#L368-L553) — candidate resolution and record identity
- [`runner.py#L617-L769`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f79686b2185c57d2db32569d9c27f2bcebd04e76/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L617-L769) — unconditional inference startup
- [`dataset_evaluator.py#L30-L130`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f79686b2185c57d2db32569d9c27f2bcebd04e76/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/dataset_evaluator.py#L30-L130) — context lookup and CPU worker
- [`records.py#L228-L264`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f79686b2185c57d2db32569d9c27f2bcebd04e76/lib/evalrecords/src/evalrecords/records.py#L228-L264) — served-model record shape
- [`results_db.py#L354-L369`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f79686b2185c57d2db32569d9c27f2bcebd04e76/infra/marina/apps/evaldash/results_db.py#L354-L369) — hardware-dependent index

# Hosted candidates through the shared launcher

A hosted candidate should use `cli launch --model-config ... --evals ... --limit 20` and produce the same curated result artifacts and `record.json` as a served candidate, with no inference job. The first implementation should support curated `chat_generation` protocols with a pinned Hugging Face tokenizer. Harbor, text completion, likelihood, and policy finalization should fail during launch validation.

## Design

1. Add a distinct `HostedModelConfig` with a type tag, endpoint URL, provider, requested model ID, secret reference, tokenizer ID/revision, explicit context window, generation settings, and concurrency. Extend model-config loading and `LaunchSpec` to accept either model type. Reject accelerator, platform, serving-instance, and federated-cluster overrides for hosted candidates. Do not run weight pinning or fleet selection for this variant.
2. Resolve the API key at submission, pass it through the Iris environment to the curated CPU worker as a secret, and add the endpoint host to the orchestrator/child egress allowlist. Give the runner a hosted endpoint context that skips inference preparation and job health polling; keep the existing corpus dependencies, result paths, evaluator, and record writer. Use the configured context window because hosted `/models` responses need not contain vLLM's `max_model_len`.
3. Validate every selected benchmark protocol before submission. Build hosted chat requests without vLLM-only fields such as `chat_template_kwargs` when empty; reject a benchmark's required sampling option if the provider configuration cannot send it, instead of silently changing the protocol. Apply the existing per-model concurrency limit and report provider 429/transport failures as coverage errors or run failures.
4. Extend `ModelRef` with a hosted identity containing provider and requested model ID; make `hardware` absent for hosted records and keep the served record shape readable. Neither the key nor its secret reference belongs in the record, cache identity, or logs. Record returned model/provider per request when the API supplies them, leaving missing values unknown. Give hosted runs a dedicated default records prefix, add it to EvalDash ingestion, and update its nullable index fields and run detail display to show provider/model instead of an accelerator. Keep hosted runs outside policy cohorts. `cli scores` should read their record URI unchanged.

## Costs and checks

This changes the persisted record contract and EvalDash index/UI, so it needs a migration and reads of both old served records and new hosted records. Add focused tests for launch validation, no inference submission, secret omission, worker request shape, record round-trip, `cli scores`, and EvalDash ingestion. Then run one 20-item hosted smoke evaluation through `marin` and confirm it writes a readable record with only CPU jobs; compare its scored item count with the standalone driver run before treating scores as comparable.

## Open questions

- Should the initial hosted record retain only the requested model/provider when the API omits returned identity, or should that prevent comparison in EvalDash?
- Should candidate and judge endpoints share a configuration type beyond their existing `SecretSpec` keys? The proposed first release keeps their runtime contracts separate.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Regional Micro210 CPU admission fails with `google.auth.exceptions.DefaultCredentialsError` when resolving the judge credential on CoreWeave. The task has no Google Application Default Credentials. The evaluation runtime, `experiments/evaluation/micro210.py::run_micro210`, contains the same failing Secret Manager call.

Reproduce on source `40a3109be5b16819b5aff500848a30f0a0aaac60`:
1. Submit the long-loop round runner to CoreWeave with `--round experiments/post_training/long_loop/rounds/mochi-base-eval.yaml --through eval --run` and a fresh run version.
2. After input validation, the coordinator resolves the policy credential `gcp-secret://projects/hai-gcp-models/secrets/TOGETHER_API_KEY/versions/1` inside the task. Policy `2026.11.20-together` requires that exact version; an ambient `TOGETHER_API_KEY` cannot replace it.

Expected: resolve the pinned credential on the submitting client and deliver it through Iris secret files, so workers can authenticate without GCP credentials.

CPU admission `/benfeuer/mochi-micro210-admission-20261120-5c` reproduced this call and failure without allocating GPUs. An evaluation failure on this source has not been observed because admission blocked submission. The fix belongs on the shared long-loop branch, tracked in #11120.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The round runner builds a Micro210 step, then submits an Iris coordinator through `_coordinator_request`; that path only forwards ambient environment variables. `run_micro210` resolves the policy's pinned GCP secret inside the coordinator, where Google ADC is absent.

**Relevant code**
- [`cli.py#L106-L139`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/40a3109be5b16819b5aff500848a30f0a0aaac60/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/cli.py#L106-L139) — coordinator credential delivery
- [`micro210.py#L164-L190`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/40a3109be5b16819b5aff500848a30f0a0aaac60/experiments/evaluation/micro210.py#L164-L190) — worker credential lookup
- [`judge_config.py#L54-L70`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/40a3109be5b16819b5aff500848a30f0a0aaac60/experiments/evaluation/judge_config.py#L54-L70) — pinned version

# Proposed Fix

Carry the judge's secret reference as runtime execution metadata; resolve it on the submitting client into Iris's named secret map and read that file in `run_micro210`. The pinned source takes precedence over any ambient `TOGETHER_API_KEY`; admission and evaluation use the same delivered credential. Target #11120 so the round runner receives the fix without a parallel long-loop implementation.

issues.author: chrismc91
issues.body:
EconEvals ([#11614](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11614)) scores each answer with a gpt-oss-120b pairwise judge against a fixed baseline answer, and the judge favors longer answers. On `econevals-sampled-o3`, each doubling of the candidate's length relative to o3's adds about 0.22 to an item's win rate. Nemotron 3.5 Super writes longer answers than o3 on 78% of items and leads Muse Glimmer 30B by 0.21, but on the 170 questions where their answers are of similar length its lead is 0.015. The judge cannot yet tell padding from more complete answers, so the raw score partly ranks models by verbosity.

The SOTOPIA length control (`length_controlled_scores` in `vendor/harbor/src/harbor/metrics/sotopia.py`) applies unchanged to these per-item scores. It fits a logistic model with model, item and length-deviation terms over a comparison cohort and predicts each answer at the item's median length. On the three sampled runs it gives:

| Model | Raw | Length-controlled | Median words |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron 3.5 Super | 0.628 | 0.521 | 1,207 |
| Muse Glimmer 30B | 0.420 | 0.469 | 856 |
| Snowball v0.1 | 0.211 | 0.249 | 602 |

Options to compare:
- Reuse the SOTOPIA cohort fit. A model's corrected score then depends on a pinned set of comparison runs, and the fit lives in Harbor.
- Arena-Hard-style style control, which regresses each verdict on length and markdown differences against the baseline answer and needs no cohort.
- Remove the bias at the judge: a stronger, non-OpenAI judge or a prompt that discounts length, checked against a blinded human or model review.

Done when: the options are compared on the sampled runs for at least these three models, including how each ranks models against a blinded review of length-matched and length-mismatched pairs, and one is chosen for EconEvals' headline score, with a follow-up PR or a recorded decision not to adjust.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

[PR #11614](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11614) is approved but still open. Its sampled o3 suites fix six questions per category, and the pairwise grader retains both order verdicts and weights. The existing 40-pair blinded review covers Glimmer versus o3 only, so it cannot compare corrections or judge changes across the three models.

**Relevant code**
- [econevals.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1f2fa91109758e9b6c2fa5561c0faeb5975e817a/experiments/evaluation/benchmarks/econevals.py#L95-L168) — pinned samples and weighted score protocol
- [grade_judge.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1f2fa91109758e9b6c2fa5561c0faeb5975e817a/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_judge.py#L526-L560) — two-order verdicts and game weights
- [evalchemy.yaml](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1f2fa91109758e9b6c2fa5561c0faeb5975e817a/experiments/evaluation/configs/evalchemy.yaml#L54-L85) — current judge and suite bindings

# Proposed Fix

1. After #11614 lands, pin the three sampled-o3 run IDs and export each question ID, category, candidate and baseline answer, both judge verdicts and weights, and grading failures. Reproduce the raw and SOTOPIA-controlled scores in this issue before comparing methods.
2. Build a new blinded review set from all three models: 25 pairs per model from the closest length-ratio quartile and 25 from the furthest quartile, balanced across DWA and occupation (150 pairs total). Have two independent reviewers judge answer quality with model identity hidden; record disagreement and adjudicated labels. Keep the earlier 40 Glimmer pairs as a pilot, outside this comparison.
3. On the same pinned answers, compare the SOTOPIA cohort fit with an item-level correction using candidate-versus-o3 length and markdown differences. Fit correction coefficients outside the review set, test the cohort fit's sensitivity to its member runs, and rejudge the review pairs in both orders with a stronger non-OpenAI judge and a prompt that asks whether added detail improves completeness.
4. Report held-out pair agreement, score error, order disagreement, and the three-model ranking for every option, with uncertainty from a category-stratified bootstrap. Choose the headline score only if the review supports it; otherwise record a decision to retain the raw score. If the score changes, open a focused implementation PR with `Fixes #11839` and update Evaldash and evaluation docs.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Staged Hugging Face evaluation models can inherit RunAI-streamer loader options even when vLLM selects its `auto` loader. vLLM then rejects the RunAI-only `distributed` option after staging and loading the model configuration.

Reproduce:
1. Register a staged Hugging Face model with `load_format=auto` and `model_loader_extra_config={"distributed": true}`.
2. Start the model through the evaluation vLLM path.
3. Observe the `auto` loader reject the `distributed` option.

Expected: loader-specific options are coupled to their matching load format and are omitted when staged HF models use `auto`.

The Snowball evaluation canary first reproduced this after local-path normalization succeeded and `GrugMoeForCausalLM` was resolved. The catalog regression is in commit `d08ef276c5`.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Both Mochi Micro210 evaluations at run version `2026.11.20.5` failed before scoring: vLLM selected `auto` but received `distributed`, `concurrency` and `memory_limit` loader options. The sealed launch configs for versions `2026.11.20.4` and `.5` both use `model_loading=stage_local` and omit `load_format`. The [original profile](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d31b241b65b/experiments/post_training/long_loop/rounds/mochi-sft-eval.yaml#L67) already contains this mismatch; no loader change between sources `c06e1faf8d` and `6fcaecc8f3` caused it.

[Serving qualification 502](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fbenfeuer%2Flong-loop-anchor-mochi-near-window-serving-2026.11.20.502) used `model_loading=stream`, which [selects RunAI at runtime](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6fcaecc8f3/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/entrypoints/main_base.py#L165). The fix on #11120 will explicitly select `runai_streamer` for the staged local exports and reject RunAI options without a matching loader during preflight. RunAI [supports local safetensors files](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/models/extensions/runai_model_streamer/).

Fresh run version `2026.11.20.6` will receive an exact no-run comparison against `.4`: add only the explicit loader selection within the engine settings, preserve all three loader options, and preserve compilation and CUDA graphs. The full base and SFT evaluations will validate runtime loading; no extra serving smoke will run.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
Add small structural evals for basic agent behavior. The [BixBench trace audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6300963037) found answers left in chat instead of the required file, and simulated tool execution with no actual tool calls. The audit does not isolate model behavior from serving, tool parsing, or harness behavior.

Cover four checks:

- Required-file submission: when instructed to write an answer to a path, verify that a nonempty file exists in the actual task environment. An answer in chat or a claimed write does not pass.
- Actual tool execution: verify a real tool invocation and its execution status for tasks that need one. Tool-call markup, invented tool responses, or a narrated shell session do not pass. Distinguish missing/invalid invocations, executor failures/timeouts, and successful execution.
- Thinking disabled: verify the emitted response respects the supported `thinking=false` setting. Define the prohibited reasoning-channel output or delimiters under the pinned template; this checks observable output, not internal reasoning. Keep extraction/serving errors distinguishable from model violations.
- URL loading: when a task explicitly requires information at a supplied URL and a retrieval tool is available, verify an actual retrieval attempt. Record tool/network failures separately from failure to attempt retrieval.

Done when:

- Each check has minimal tasks and positive/negative grader fixtures, including narrated execution and missing-file cases.
- Results separate protocol compliance, submission completeness, and answer correctness. Passing the structural check alone must not imply a correct answer.
- Traces retain the request settings, raw response, parsed tool calls, execution events, and checked artifacts needed to locate failures.

Scope is evaluation additions; training interventions are separate.

Related: #10060 (output-contract validation), #10061 (tool-protocol syntax and localized supervision).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The [BixBench audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6300963037) found 156/205 tasks without the required answer file and a trace that narrated shell execution with no tool event; the evidence does not isolate model output from parsing or execution. Harbor keeps a trajectory but maps verifier reward to one `correct` value, leaving no separate protocol, submission, and answer labels. The duplicate preflight found no PR for these four checks; [#10045](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10045) covers BFCL training and syntax diagnostics.

**Relevant code**
- [`trial_driver.py#L316-L352`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py#L316-L352) — validates one Harbor dataset and agent.
- [`runner.py#L126-L145`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L126-L145) — reads trial result and trajectory path.
- [`runner.py#L172-L189`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L172-L189) — equates reward with `correct`.
- [`eval.py#L111-L141`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py#L111-L141) — sample and metric contract.
- [`eval.py#L288-L342`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py#L288-L342) — flattened trajectory fields.

# Design: agent protocol probes

Add a versioned four-task diagnostic through the evaluation launcher. Pin the model revision, chat template, tool schema/parser, agent/runtime revision, request settings, and task content. Use Harbor's existing local dataset path for sandbox checks; use a dedicated single-turn request to the same served endpoint for `thinking=false`, so the grader can inspect the exact request and response independently of an agent's final message.

1. **Required file.** Ask for a short known answer in `/workspace/answer.txt`. The verifier reads that path in the task environment after the agent stops and records existence, byte count, and content hash. Score file presence separately from matching the known answer; chat text or a claimed write cannot satisfy presence.
2. **Tool execution.** Ask the agent to obtain a per-trial nonce with an exposed shell tool. Record the raw generated response before tool parsing, parsed calls, dispatch/start/end events, and exit status. Label missing or invalid invocation, executor error/timeout, and successful execution separately. A narrated shell session, tool-call markup in ordinary text, or invented tool response must fail the execution check.
3. **Thinking disabled.** Send `enable_thinking=false` only for a pinned template that supports it. Define forbidden reasoning fields and template delimiters for that template; inspect the raw HTTP response and parsed message. An unsupported setting, server error, or extraction failure gets its own status, never a model-violation label. This measures emitted output only.
4. **URL loading.** Supply a task-local HTTP URL serving a per-trial nonce and make a retrieval tool available. Score a request observed by that endpoint or an executor-recorded retrieval attempt. Record no attempt, retrieval/network failure, and successful retrieval separately; compare the answer to the nonce independently. The local endpoint avoids public-site availability as a source of false failures.

Store one versioned evidence bundle per trial with request settings, raw response, parsed calls, execution events, URL access log, and checked file metadata. Archive it alongside the existing raw trajectory through `EvaluationStore`; link it from the sample's grading detail. Export `protocol_compliance`, `submission_completeness`, and `answer_correctness` as distinct numeric metrics; keep `not_evaluable` and its reason in grading detail when a prerequisite failed. Keep `EvalSample.correct` for answer correctness when assessed, and report each rate with its denominator; a structural pass alone cannot raise answer accuracy.

## Validation

Write grader fixtures before implementation. Include positive cases for all four checks: file submission, executed tool call, no emitted reasoning, and successful URL retrieval. Negative cases cover missing and empty files; answer only in chat; a fully narrated fake tool transcript; malformed call; dispatch failure and timeout; URL answer without retrieval and retrieval failure; reasoning-field and delimiter leaks; and a serving/extraction error. Assert both the label and the retained evidence for every fixture. Run the checked-in Harbor config through preflight and one capped end-to-end diagnostic suite covering all four checks on the pinned reference setup before using model comparisons. Keep [#10060](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10060) and [#10061](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10061) separate: they cover general output contracts and tool-call syntax/training.

## Open question

Do the pinned Pi/Harbor/vLLM versions expose the pre-parser generated text and executor lifecycle? The current archive records parsed tool calls and observations, but does not establish those boundaries. If either is unavailable, add capture there before grading that failure class, and mark earlier traces `not_evaluable`.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The [design comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10393#issuecomment-6302257478) covers the cause: Harbor maps verifier reward to a single `correct`, and ATIF trajectories record parsed tool calls and observations but no executor lifecycle or pre-parser text. No open PR covers these checks.

- [`runner.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py) — one reward per trial.
- [`trajectory.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trajectory.py) — the trajectory archive the evidence bundle sits beside.
- [`eval.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py) — `EvalSample`, `Grading.detail`, and `EvaluationStore.add_artifact`.

# Proposed Fix

This PR adds the grader layer in `marin.evaluation.protocol_probes`: a versioned evidence bundle, one typed spec and grader per check, the four minimal tasks, archiving that stores the bundle and links it from the sample, and denominator-aware rates for `protocol_compliance`, `submission_completeness`, and `answer_correctness`. Fixtures cover every positive and negative case listed in the design. When a prerequisite is missing, such as no captured executor lifecycle, the result is `not_evaluable` and never a model violation. A follow-up will connect the tasks to Harbor runs and the served endpoint once the capture question is settled.

issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

comments.body: Comparing our scaling law to prior runs. The main differences here is that the May recipe is at compute optimal, this run is at ~12x overtrained, and the 67B-A2B scaling law was at 100x overtrained. This will be good metric to monitor for issues. Drop rate jumps to 10 pct at very start, then drops to 0, then climbs to ~4pct over the run. Slightly increasing as we scale. Predicting we wont have that 10 percent spike for the hero, because our warmup (1 percent) will cover a much larger number of steps since the hero is at a higher step count. comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

comments.author: MythosAd
comments.body:
Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. comments.author: yonromai
comments.body:
🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

<details><summary>Evidence and reproduction</summary>

### Source and code identities

- Observed production source: [`e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83)

The earlier fixed-evaluation `a1` runs omitted each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. They are superseded by the corrected `a2` runs above. The separate evaluation-path problem is tracked in [#9352](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9352).

### Saved-input accuracy

The fixture contains 324 valid layer-15 entries representing 32 byte-distinct activation vectors. The production-shape probe tiles the entries to 65,536 rows and preserves their captured frequency.

| Arithmetic | Score RMS error | Maximum error | Top-8 order versus FP64 reference | Isolated forward | Isolated backward |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Current BF16 output, then FP32 cast | `0.0074565` | `0.0311123` | 80/324 entries changed | 14.07 ms | 14.43 ms |
| BF16 operands, FP32 accumulation/output | `0.00002808` | `0.00007003` | all 324 matched | 14.07 ms | 14.48 ms |
| FP32 operands | `0.00000416` | `0.00002373` | all 324 matched | 18.20 ms | 23.26 ms |

The isolated timing covers only the saved-input router dot and gradient. It is not a whole-step measurement.

| Mean expert-count CV | 0.097451 | 0.098131 | +0.000680 |

The corrected Paloma macro losses were `2.22016478` for the current continuation and `2.22088742` for the preferred continuation. The runs used current router arithmetic for both checkpoints and applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias state. This common policy removes evaluation-time router rounding as a direct difference. It also evaluates the preferred-trained checkpoint under arithmetic different from its training policy, so the sign is not a clean estimate of long-run preferred-policy quality.

comments.author: mindscanlabs
comments.body:
**An independent forecast of the final loss, with a law found from the data (no fixed form)**

I forecast the run's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss`: the last eval logged in the lineage at step 387,000 or later, as W&B records it (expected at 16K packing). I used only public W&B data, up to step 302,999 (snapshot of 2026-10-21, 22:58 UTC).

| forecast | data | value | 90 % interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | ladder + the hero's own evals | **1.979** | [1.965, 1.994] |
| B | ladder only | **1.935** | [1.915, 1.963] |

**Method in brief.** NAI, the symbolic-regression system I develop, finds a law L(C, fraction of training) from the table, with no form given: no floor and no power law are assumed. C is your lm_head-excluded compute.
- B is the ladder-only law at the hero's compute and the end of training.
- A adds the hero's post-swap 4K evals to the table and takes the level from its 16 evals at 16K.
- The intervals are NAI's forecast band, nominally 90 %.

B is 0.10 below the Aug 19 pre-registration from the same ladder, because the law NAI found has no fixed floor.

The formulas are sealed. Their SHA-256 digests and the scoring rules, fixed in advance: https://github.com/mindscanlabs/NAI-track-record/blob/main/forecasts/marin-535b.md

I'll post the formulas and the scored comparison after the run ends. Thanks for running this in the open: it makes a forecast like this possible.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body: A measurement for anyone checking forecasts made while the evals packed at 4K (Marin's Aug 19 forecast of 2.039, and mine in #9977): the switch to 16K lowered the Paloma macro by about 0.031 on nearly the same weights. The `qk16k-a1-step252k` arm restored step 252,000 with the hero's post-switch settings (16K, `qk_mult` 1.48) and logged 2.0929 and 2.0926 at steps 252,049 and 252,099, against 2.1234 for the hero's 4K eval of that checkpoint, logged at step 251,999. With `qk_mult` left at 1.3 (`qk16k-a0-step252k`), the drop is about 0.028. The hero's own step from 254,999 to 257,999 looks smaller (0.024) because WikiText's dip at 254,999 lowered the last 4K eval; without WikiText it is 0.032 over those 3,000 steps. So a 4K-era forecast scored against the 16K final value, as in H1 and H4 of the forecast linked above, starts about 0.03 high from the packing change alone. The offset may also drift over the remaining 16K training, so if it's cheap, one 4K eval of the final checkpoint would let these forecasts be checked at the 4K packing they were built on. How I'll compare the forecasts at the end, fixed before phase 2, is in [this addendum](https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/phase2-plan-2026-10-22/addenda/2026-10-22_phase2_plan.md).

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body: A heads-up for the hero's planned 262K extension (#10618): with evals packed at the training context, Paloma's PTB and WikiText-103 val sets are each shorter than one 262,144-token sequence, so they yield no eval data ([`tokens // seq_len`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py#L93)). Their losses are then logged as 0.0 and the Paloma group macro skips them ([eval.py#L634-L636](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L634-L636)), so `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` silently becomes a 14-subset mean: at current values a jump of about +0.06 (about 3%), enough to trip `eval_regressed`. The top-level `macro_loss` instead averages the zeros in ([eval.py#L611](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L611)), about −0.14 on the hero's 23 tags. The 67B's 65K→262K switch, with the same tokenizer and Paloma files, shows both: from step 155,999 ([65K run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step141k)) to 156,000 ([262K run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep1_ctx4_bs256_seq262144_ctxext_step156k)), `eval/paloma/macro_loss` rose 2.1774 → 2.2150 while the other 14 subsets moved +0.0004, and `eval/macro_loss` fell 2.0260 → 1.8607 (2.0379 without the zeros). Either fix is small: mask zero-token tags in the top-level macro as the group macros already do, or keep all 16 subsets by setting `GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len` (#9890) to 65,536 for the 262K phase.
