comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The `json` convention supports text and number tasks, but `extract_answer` parses the entire reply and requires `answer` to be a string. [PR #9608](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9608) replaces that extractor with `JsonAnswer.extract` and keeps both restrictions; it is active and owns the same code path.

**Relevant code**
- [`submission.py#L116-L121`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/submission.py#L116-L121) — JSON instruction omits the wire contract.
- [`submission.py#L200-L229`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/submission.py#L200-L229) — current parse and string check.
- [`#9608 submission.py#L106-L118`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a68f23a756528a8a1ae28366839b5714f70f40cf/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/submission.py#L106-L118) — replacement extractor has the same gap.
- [`#9608 grading.py#L94-L105`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a68f23a756528a8a1ae28366839b5714f70f40cf/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/grading.py#L94-L105) — grade boundary has `answer_type`.
- [`verifyit extract.py#L22-L25`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/extract.py#L22-L25) — existing fence helper also accepts embedded blocks.

# Proposed Fix

Land this in #9608: pass `specification.answer_type` to convention extraction, unwrap one Markdown fence only when it encloses the full reply, then parse through `_json_submission`. For number tasks, accept a JSON integer or finite float (excluding booleans) and convert it to text for numeric grading; keep nonempty strings for text tasks. Add grading regressions for fenced `{"answer":42}` yielding reward 1.0, plus trailing prose, boolean, nonfinite, and numeric answers to text tasks yielding submission failures.

Consumed Adam LR 5e-5, cosine schedule, betas 0.9/0.95; serialized-chat assistant loss; sequential packing capped at 256 documents; continuous causal replay |

RL consumes exactly 32 SWE + 32 non-agentic groups per update, eight samples per group (512 trajectories), with maximum staleness of two optimizer updates. Its explicit budget is 10 h from the first completed optimizer step, with a 1,800-second drain margin. Validation and native saves occur every two updates. Selection uses an EMA with span five (alpha 1/3) and requires all 120 validation tasks scored; selected step 20 scored 120/120. Retention is last three plus protected best. Reproduction requires fresh output versions, the frozen inputs, Marin storage access and configured secret bindings (`HF_TOKEN`, `WANDB_API_KEY`, `CW_KEY_ID`/`CW_KEY_SECRET`, `DAYTONA_RL_API_KEY`, `DAYTONA_EVAL_API_KEY`, `DAYTONA_TARGET=us`, `TOGETHER_API_KEY`). 🤖

## 10/05 Micro210 baseline

Evaluation-only entry for the frozen 10/05 model; this does not introduce a new SFT or RL training recipe.

Micro210 is Marin’s mixed reasoning, knowledge, coding and agentic evaluation suite.
This recipe supports 200 distinct tasks across 20 sources (Tau3 excluded), expanded to 440 assignments, including 100 Pi assignments.

## Model and evaluation policy

Model: [open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05/tree/ac60d9401820953943f5a56e06f36e13c86b12d6), immutable revision `ac60d9401820953943f5a56e06f36e13c86b12d6`. The three runs evaluate this same model in existing region-local storage, with no additional training.

The runtime separately selects [marin-community/marin-tokenizer-tools](https://huggingface.co/marin-community/marin-tokenizer-tools/tree/3f6879acdaf3dae7874b2d48c7d11b9d8c6faf09), revision `3f6879acdaf3dae7874b2d48c7d11b9d8c6faf09`, with no explicit template override and thinking enabled. The model’s embedded tokenizer provenance is not the selected runtime tools revision.

Current harness: 16 global Harbor slots (four rollout workers × four), one 8 H100 policy worker (TP1/DP8/EP8, max_num_seqs 8) and an independent 8 H100 M3 judge (TP8). Policy/judge caps are 21,600 s; root cap is 25,200 s. Native Pi 0.87; context 65,536, 16,384 generated tokens per turn, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95. Compilation and CUDA graphs remain enabled. These role budgets are not asserted identical to every historical recipe in this issue.

Pinned policy image request: `13519c59442bd70ed5ec2902869f15094992d6849d7e34e353f1338dec7ff5f8`. The region-control policy image matched that request; its CPU/judge/broker task image was `b5b474d80ca79f996049cc0cf700ab93ab2d41a4d9b8a91afc43ce11bf44d974`, matching the observed cw-us-east-02a reference. Policy/judge runtime pins are `39e62869693c` / `01911be34fac`; judge model revision is `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba`. Images and pins do not independently attest imported module bytes or platform equivalence.

All three produced suite Parquets are 16,401,114 bytes with SHA256 `00cdda0654be66060d3ff77b6b44e3dc6fa470e50625ef61ef24b5d9c778bef7`. Produced-byte/order identity is not live runtime consumption or complete assigned-UID coverage proof.

## Scores and coverage

Native equal-20 is recomputed from the 20 native source averages, whose denominators include excluded assignments. Available-only means omit excluded outcomes. Scores are heterogeneous partial-credit means, not pass@1.

| Run | Region | Native equal-20 | Available equal-20 | Pooled available | Scored / assigned | Unknown | BFCL /10 | Eval H100-h |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Run 1 (44627) | cw-us-east-02a | 49.39% | 49.39% | 41.44% | 440 / 440 | 0 | 8 | 26.35 |
| Run 2 (44628) | cw-us-east-02a | 47.32% | 47.42% | 40.91% | 433 / 440 | 7 | 5 | 28.43 |
| Region control (44633) | cw-rno2a | 47.98% | 48.44% | 40.31% | 436 / 440 | 4 | 7* | 26.04 |

Run 2 has one BixBench and six TB2 unknowns. The region control has one BFCL, one BixBench and two TB2 unknowns. Its BFCL slice has seven known score units from nine scored assignments plus one unknown, giving assigned-score bounds 7–8/10. Unknown outcomes are not known zero or failure.

| Run | Native score mass /440 | Assigned-pooled bounds |
|---|---:|---:|
| Run 1 | 182.338705602 | 41.4406–41.4406% |
| Run 2 | 177.120042792 | 40.2546–41.8455% |
| Region control | 175.750812947 | 39.9434–40.8525% |

The two cw-us-east-02a runs differ by 5.22 task-equivalents (run 2 minus run 1: -5.218662810; unknown-outcome bounds [-5.218662810, +1.781337190]). This is one observed same-configuration evaluation repeat difference of about five tasks, not a calibrated eval-noise estimate, universal tie band, confidence interval or independent training-seed replication. comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 On Canonical Micro210, a constant reply scores above Round 3 on TruthfulQA and GPQA Diamond, and 40% on MMLU-Pro. I graded the 140 prepared answer-only tasks, rebuilt with #11120's `prepare_micro` (sha256 equal to `prepared_rollouts_sha256` in #11686), with Round 3's tokenizer, context and output limits. The five replies of the `trivial_replies` launcher in the open #11222 (empty, `hello`, `0`, `I don't know.`, the prompt repeated) went through `run_evaluation`. Single letters went through the rows' own rollout specs.

| Benchmark | Constant reply | Score (%) | Round 1 | Round 2 | Round 3 | Base | Snowball v0.1 |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TruthfulQA | `\boxed{A}` | 100 | 70 | 80 | 70 | 20 | 90 |
| GPQA Diamond | `B` | 50 | 56.7 | 56.7 | 43.3 | 33.3 | 66.7 |
| MMLU-Pro | `I don't know.` | 40 | 70 | 70 | 60 | 40 | 90 |
| IFBench | `hello` | 10 | 40 | 40 | 30 | 0 | 40 |

The other ten answer benchmarks score 0 for every reply. The six agentic benchmarks were not run.

- TruthfulQA: the generated-choice prompts list the options in `mc2_targets` order, which starts with a true answer. Option A is true in every task: 10 in Micro210, 41 in Mini840, 817 rows of `truthfulqa/truthful_qa`. A seeded shuffle of each task's options would remove this. The full policy's MC2 likelihood scoring does not depend on order.
- MMLU-Pro: without `answer is (X)` or `Answer: X`, the extractor takes the last standalone capital A-J, so `I don't know.` counts as option I, the key of 4 tasks.
- GPQA Diamond: 5 of the 10 drawn keys are B.
- IFBench: the prepared rows grade it with the `evalchemy` wheel of `runtime-v4`, whose IFBench checkers are byte-identical to `vendor/evalchemy` before #10423. In one of the 10 tasks (key 278, the capitals of European countries north of 45°) a correct reply cannot pass: the checker's list leaves out Kyiv, so the 28 correct capitals score 0 and the 27 without Kyiv score 1.

This does not show that a round guesses. On these 10 tasks, the three benchmarks cannot tell a round from a constant below the floor. They carry 8.7 of Round 3's 41.07 points. Without them, Rounds 1-3, the base and Snowball v0.1 average 49.8, 44.7, 38.1, 13.3 and 40.3%.

Launcher floors rerun with `trivial_replies` on #11222's head over a TaskSpec corpus of a benchmark's prepared tasks. The TruthfulQA count needs only the dataset (`uv run --with pyarrow --with huggingface_hub python check.py`):

```python
import base64, json
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

path = hf_hub_download("open-athena/Marin-Micro-Eval-210", "data/validation.parquet", repo_type="dataset",
                       revision="4564ed081c316bc3231ae5c3a53a46b39248c819")
labels = []
for row in pq.read_table(path).to_pylist():
    if row["benchmark"] == "truthfulqa":
        files = json.loads(row["task_spec"])["resources"]["verifier"]
        config = json.loads(base64.b64decode(next(f for f in files if f["path"] == "config.json")["source"]["content_base64"]))
        labels.append(config["spec"]["doc"]["mc2_targets"]["labels"][0])
print(f"option A is true in {sum(labels)} of {len(labels)} TruthfulQA tasks")
```

The uncertainty calculation follows the prior Exp3 seal and [#10197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197). Each benchmark uses the conservative task-level SEM bound `s = 0.5/sqrt(10*0.9)`, including the 90% valid-trial allowance. With scored fractions `r_b`, means `m_b` and weights `w_b=1/20`, set `mu=sum(w_b*r_b*m_b)`, `delta=sum(w_b*(1-r_b))` and `sigma=sqrt(sum((w_b*r_b*s)^2))`. The Imbens–Manski critical value solves `Phi(c+delta/sigma)-Phi(-c)=0.95`; here `c=1.9381`. The interval is `[mu-c*sigma, mu+c*sigma+delta]`, clipped to [0,1]; benchmark intervals use one cell. spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

`lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_cache.py` currently points GPU ranks within one job to persistent, uncleaned per-process folders (`/cache/xla/per-fusion-autotune/process-{process_index}`) where only one rank per node fetches from FineStore (global rank 0 as uploader-fetcher and local rank 0 on each other node as fetcher; `lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_cache.py:95-100, 111-116, 148-166`, `lib/finestore/src/finestore/fileset.py:76`). Because different ranks compile with differing autotune folder contents, a single multi-GPU job can compile multiple HLO variants under the same JAX `cache_key`.

**Evidence so far:**
- **Per-process autotune folders with differing contents gave mixed programs across ranks and a hang (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11793):** On a 64xH100 default-input compile under one identical JAX `cache_key`, ranks compiled 3 distinct executables (`56 + 7 + 1` ranks): 7 populated first-rank-per-node folders (`184,849–245,228` files) emitted `147` `__cublas$lt$matmul` calls and `182` Triton custom fusions, while 56 sparse folders (`0–1,281` files, including global rank 0 with `206` files) emitted `0` `__cublas$lt$matmul` calls and `329` Triton custom fusions (and 1 rank with `633` files produced a third variant). The two main executables schedule two independent 64-GPU collectives (`all-gather` channel 121 and `all-reduce` channel 1) in opposite blocking order under `--xla_gpu_experimental_parallel_collective_overlap_limit=1`, which is sufficient to deadlock on step 0 when both variants are present in one job.
- **Identical inputs on all 64 processes (empty per-fusion dir, `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`) gave one program, no hang, in 2 of 2 regions, at the slow step rate (~129 s/update):** Setting `--xla_gpu_per_fusion_autotune_cache_dir=` (empty) across all 64 ranks eliminated executable divergence and completed `3/3` updates in both `cw-rno2a` (`64/64` identical `executable_text_sha256`; steady steps `128.7 s` and `121.3 s`, even GPU power within `2.0%`) and `cw-us-east-02a` (`64/64` identical `executable_text_sha256`; steady steps `129.6 s` and `128.6 s`, even GPU power within `0.81–0.82%`). Both fix tests and the hanging control ran at `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`; only the per-fusion dir differed. The ~129 s rate fits untuned default kernels (empty dir); whether a shared tuned dir at level 0 restores the fast rate is untested.
- **Fast-mode runs (~43 s/update, up to ~44–55 s/update) also ran at `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`, with populated per-process autotune folders (checked in recorded `XLA_FLAGS` for two `cw-us-east-02a` fast-mode runs; https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11775, https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11909).**

**Open question (not yet shown):**
- How to make autotune inputs identical across all processes by construction **and** keep the fast rate (~43–55 s/update) is untested and remains open (candidates include one shared, read-only tuned autotune set chosen before the step compiles; whether a shared tuned dir at `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0` restores the fast rate is untested).
- The matched default-input control on `cw-us-east-02a` is still queued.

## Confirmed code defects (`main` `2bf3f721c9`)

1. **Intra-node rank asymmetry (`lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_cache.py:95-100, 111-116, 148-166`, `lib/finestore/src/finestore/fileset.py:76`):**
   - Each GPU process on a node points to `/cache/xla/per-fusion-autotune/process-{process_index}`.
   - `_autotune_cache_role()` assigns `UPLOADER` to global rank 0, `FETCHER` to `process_index % processes_per_task == 0` (local rank 0 on each other node), and `NONE` to local ranks `1..7`. Global rank 0 (`UPLOADER`, which fetches on start via `FineStoreDirectory.__init__` at `fileset.py:76`) and local rank 0 of each other node (`FETCHER`) fetch from FineStore; local ranks `1..7` never receive the fetched file set.
2. **Persistent uncleaned host folders (`compile_cache.py:95-100`, `lib/finestore/src/finestore/fileset.py:34-53`):**
   - `process-{process_index}` persists across jobs and across repository `tree_hash` builds (`makedirs(exist_ok=True)`, never cleared), and `fetch_file_set(root, local)` overlays fetched files onto existing files without removing stale leftovers. Giving `FETCHER` to every rank in shared/uncleaned folders is still insufficient because stale leftovers differ across nodes and ranks (`206` vs. `184,849–245,228` vs. `633` files).
3. **Uncoordinated cross-node snapshot reads (`lib/finestore/src/finestore/fileset.py:39`, `lib/iris/src/iris/jax/init.py:279`):**
   - `configure_jax_compilation_cache()` runs before `jax.distributed.initialize()`, and each node independently opens `ReadView(root)` on arrival. A concurrent FineStore commit during startup can give nodes different store heads.

*(Contained fetch-bound, skip-existing-file, and stop-leftover-upload fixes are tracked separately in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11925; post-compile HLO hash equality checking is tracked in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11917.)*

## Requested fix: identical autotune inputs by construction

Make XLA per-fusion autotune inputs identical on every process of a multi-GPU job by construction (no unshared per-process state that can differ across ranks or nodes):

1. **Launcher-pinned immutable snapshot (`IRIS_AUTOTUNE_SNAPSHOT_ID`):**
   - Have the job launcher/controller resolve one immutable FineStore snapshot ID once at launch time (or `"empty"` if none exists) and pass it via env var (`IRIS_AUTOTUNE_SNAPSHOT_ID`) so all nodes open the same snapshot in `ReadView` / `fetch_file_set()` instead of racing on moving store heads (`configure_jax_compilation_cache()` runs before `jax.distributed.initialize()` at `init.py:279`).
2. **One clean, shared job-scoped directory on each node (no per-process host leftovers):**
   - Replace `/cache/xla/per-fusion-autotune/process-{index}` with a fresh job-attempt directory (e.g., `/cache/xla/per-fusion-autotune/jobs/<job_attempt_id>/snapshot/`) populated strictly from the pinned snapshot (zero pre-existing host files), fetched once by local rank 0 with local ranks `1..7` waiting on an atomic `.ready` marker (reaping finished/expired job dirs).
   - Point **every** rank on the node to that single read-only `snapshot/` directory when `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`, and do not run `FineStoreDirectory` uploads at level 0.
   - **Write check before RO sharing:** Confirm with a controlled before/after file count, mtime, and content-hash check that XLA performs zero writes (new files or in-place rewrites) at `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`. If XLA writes anything at level 0, materialize isolated per-rank directories (`shutil.copytree`, or `os.link` only if writes are strictly temp-file-and-rename) from the verified clean `snapshot/`.
3. **Compatibility keying and non-divergent seeding (`compile_cache.py:119-123`):**
   - Key `_file_set_cache_root()` by XLA-autotune compatibility `(gpu_variant, jaxlib_version, cuda_version)` under a clean prefix (instead of per-`tree_hash`), seeded offline by a shard-autotuned run on the production mesh (`--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=true`), and disallow per-rank unshared `autotune_level > 0` in multi-rank jobs. *(Whether a shared read-only tuned snapshot recovers the ~43–55 s fast band on cold compiles remains open to test once implemented.)*

## Acceptance criteria

- **Unit tests (`lib/iris/tests/`, `lib/finestore/tests/`):**
  1. Legacy `/cache/xla/per-fusion-autotune/process-*` leftovers are completely ignored; all local ranks see only the pinned snapshot files.
  2. Local ranks `1..7` wait for local rank 0's `.ready` marker and receive identical directory paths/contents; cross-node fetches with the same pinned snapshot ID match even across concurrent FineStore commits.
  3. Any fetch failure fails the job cleanly rather than falling back to a divergent empty/local folder on one node.
- **64-GPU end-to-end verification (on dirty hosts holding asymmetric legacy folders):**
  1. All 64 ranks log identical `snapshot_id` and autotune file counts, compile cold (`cache_event == "miss"`) to **64/64 identical `executable_text_sha256`**, pass the post-compile hash guard (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11917), and complete `3/3` updates.
  2. Against a candidate seeded read-only tuned snapshot, measure steady-state step time and per-GPU power (answering the open question of whether a shared read-only tuned snapshot recovers the ~43–55 s fast band).

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

On `main` at `2bf3f721c9`, the GPU cache setup assigns each rank a persistent `process-{index}` directory, but only one rank per node fetches the remote file set. `fetch_file_set()` overlays files onto that directory, and each fetch independently reads the current FineStore HEAD before JAX distributed initialization. A shared path alone would leave stale files and cross-node snapshot races.

**Relevant code**
- [`compile_cache.py#L90-L116`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2bf3f721c9946150a02c3417c4c93e14b273a5e8/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_cache.py#L90-L116) — persistent rank paths and fetch roles.
- [`compile_cache.py#L119-L166`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2bf3f721c9946150a02c3417c4c93e14b273a5e8/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_cache.py#L119-L166) — tree-hash key and role selection.
- [`fileset.py#L34-L53`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2bf3f721c9946150a02c3417c4c93e14b273a5e8/lib/finestore/src/finestore/fileset.py#L34-L53) — HEAD-based, overlaying fetch.
- [`reader.py#L890-L920`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2bf3f721c9946150a02c3417c4c93e14b273a5e8/lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py#L890-L920) — `ReadView` accepts a pinned snapshot, but defaults to HEAD.
- [`init.py#L275-L280`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2bf3f721c9946150a02c3417c4c93e14b273a5e8/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/init.py#L275-L280) — cache setup precedes distributed init.

# Proposed Fix

This needs a coordinated Iris/FineStore change and a 64-H100 run; it is larger than a contained fix.

1. Add a FineStore read API that reopens an immutable manifest by ID, validates that it belongs to the expected archive, and passes the resulting `ArchiveSnapshot` to `ReadView`. Extend `fetch_file_set()` to require that snapshot for this path. Keep the manifest and referenced shards available for the lifetime of jobs pinned to it, including across compaction and temporary-bucket expiry.
2. At job submission, select one snapshot for an explicit `(GPU variant, jaxlib version, CUDA version)` compatibility key, or the explicit `empty` sentinel. Persist `IRIS_AUTOTUNE_SNAPSHOT_ID` in the job definition and propagate it to every task and retry through the common Iris environment; never resolve HEAD independently on workers. Validate the actual runtime tuple before compilation. Seed compatible tuned snapshots in a separate shard-autotuned job, then publish them atomically.
3. For each task attempt, have local rank 0 fetch into a new node-local staging directory and publish a `.ready` marker only after successful completion. Other local ranks wait with a bound, verify the marker's snapshot ID, and use the same clean `snapshot/` directory. A failed fetch or timeout fails the task. Ignore existing `process-*` folders and reap expired attempt directories. At `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`, disable the FineStore uploader; reject unshared `autotune_level > 0` in multi-rank jobs.
4. Before making `snapshot/` read-only, run a controlled level-0 compile and compare file count, mtimes, and content hashes before and after. If XLA writes, copy the verified snapshot into isolated rank directories before compilation and keep the source immutable. The initial file sets must still match across ranks.
5. Test pinned reads across a concurrent FineStore commit, stale host files, local-rank waiting, failed fetch/timeout, and retry isolation. Then use dirty hosts for a cold 64-H100 compile: log one snapshot ID and matching file counts on all ranks, require `64/64` matching optimized-HLO hashes and `3/3` updates, and record steady step time and per-GPU power against a seeded tuned snapshot. A cache hit cannot establish input uniformity. Coordinate the bounded-fetch work in #11925 and the executable guard in #11917 / PR #11923 without duplicating them.

Open measurements: whether level 0 writes into the autotune directory, and whether a shared tuned snapshot restores the observed ~43–55 s/update band. The two uniform-empty runs on #11793 established matching executables and completed updates, but ran near 129 s/update.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
TL;DR: Model merging is a promising direction for Marin: different Grug/Snowball checkpoints have complementary strengths, but we do not yet have a reliable way to combine them while preserving the base model's other capabilities. Cheap weight-space operations could make this orders of magnitude less expensive than on-policy distillation (OPD). We would benefit from expert input on how to make that tradeoff work for our mixture-of-experts (MoE) models.

The policy evaluation tracker illustrates the problem (percentages; higher is better):

| Checkpoint | MATH500 | GPQA-Diamond | HumanEval+ | NUPA | BFCL-Parity/Pi |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [Grug Antidoom Step12](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02) | 95.00 | 67.30 | 72.60 | 0.10 | 5.70 |
| [Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92) | 89.60 | 42.90 | 68.90 | 40.60 | 16.30 |
| [Grug Reference-KL Step20](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04) | 92.60 | 63.00 | 86.60 | 0.30 | 43.90 |

Source: [policy-tracker snapshot](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/inputs/TRACKER.md). These are policy NUPA scores; the merge study instead optimized NUPA200, a 200-task subset of the policy’s 5,000-task panel. BFCL-Parity/Pi is the policy's tool-use evaluation with the Pi agent. No checkpoint in this comparison achieves the best score in every column.

Our [initial study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975) shows both the appeal and the unresolved problem. Static merge construction typically required roughly 1e11–1e12 estimated arithmetic FLOPs per checkpoint, often without GPUs. This supports the prospect of a large compute advantage over OPD, which requires rollout generation and training; we have not run a matched OPD cost comparison. Evaluation and any calibration or expert-selection work add costs beyond static construction.

The best merge scored 36.50% on NUPA200 and 48.78% on BFCL-Parity, versus historical specialist references of 38.00% and 43.90%, respectively. But its recipe copied only 0.76% of all parameter values unchanged from the intended Base (Step12). On non-target benchmarks, it scored 89.80% MATH500 and 52.19% GPQA-Diamond, versus Base’s historical policy scores of 95.00% and 67.30%; these were not matched reruns. That study did not establish capability-preserving transfer into Base.

We would welcome advice from people with model-merging experience, especially on transferring specialist behavior into an existing MoE checkpoint with limited weight changes, handling expert/router compatibility and the tokenizer differences observed in #9975, and choosing retention evaluations that expose damage outside the target benchmarks.

Done when: expert feedback informs a concrete follow-up design with a fixed Base, explicit limits on weight changes, and pre-agreed target and non-target evaluation criteria.

comments.author: craffel
comments.body:
Hi, I can comment a bit on this (also tagging @marcociccone who has been doing a lot of work along these lines).

Anecdotally it seems that merging may work better* than OPD in the MOPD setup when merging RL-trained checkpoints:
- [This paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12566) which seems to have invented MOPD without credit (?) includes merging as a baseline, where it compares favorably.
- The ["MOPD paper"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30406) includes task arithmetic (a weak merging baseline) where it performs roughly on par with OPD
- The [Open-MOPD paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19098) also has some merging results and it works reasonably well.
- [This very recent paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04272) also has some promising results with merging in the MOPD setting.
- The fact that merging can work well in the RL setting is explored in [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22039).

The trouble is that there is some conflicting evidence, which I think stems from the following:
- We generally do not have a precise characterization of how well merging will work in a particular setting.
- Most work that evaluates merging takes the simplest possible method off the shelf (generally task arithmetic). This can work ok (anecdotally especially for larger models, see [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03617)) but there has been a ton of work on more sophisticated merging methods that have been pretty conclusively demonstrated to work better. The additional trouble, though, is that there are details that people often get wrong, for example how to merge the embedding/unembedding matrices, or other nuisance details (see e.g. the discussion of incorrect implementations of RegMean in [our recent work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01329)).
- Underlying merging is the choice of mixing coefficients for the constituent models, which is rarely explored but turns out to be important in practice.
- To get to the asterisk above, there often is only a cursory notion of what "better" means; often it is found e.g. that merging works better than MT/OPD on some tasks and worse on others, but this seems to largely be a consequence of the implicit mixing weights used by a merging method where no mixing weight tuning is done.

As mentioned above @marcociccone is finishing up a project investigating this much more thoroughly; the end product is a method for tuning merging coefficients and strong results using strong merging methods. It's a bit hard to claim "pareto-optimality" in terms of the merged model dominating the MT/OPD model for *every* task, but merging at the very least seems to be on par and also has the huge advantage of being much cheaper to use (and in particular much cheaper to try out new mixing coefficients to balance capabilities to your preferred profile).

HTH.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
Thank you very much @craffel for the detailed comment here! As a Grug-brained newbie in the space of model merging, I would certainly be happy to experiment with the method of @marcociccone if he would like to check something into our monorepo!

Naively, it seems that model merging can produce models that look OK (even strong) under our eval policy but then acquire weird tics / behavioral quirks that would make them pretty unappealing as an official release. So we're looking into how to harden our eval policy against these kinds of failures (and also hopefully get better at merging models)

comments.body:
🤖 A data point on the transfer losses in #9920 and #9984: both experts were trained on targets that never open a reasoning block, and every distilled arm, and the half-strength merge, carries that shape to prompts outside CRUXEval. That fits the off-target losses better than skill interference does.

**Expert data.** The SFT rows of expert E ([`task133-20261007-prepared-v2`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Transfer-Artifacts-2026.10/tree/98c153c05ddd02068c5415144696e01e9a61c0a2/teacher-traces/cruxeval-test-exposed/task133-20261007-prepared-v2)) and expert E2 ([`task162-e2-prepared-20261009-v1`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Two-Expert-Transfer-Artifacts-2026.10/tree/7a96dade2635b0bd76a1a67cb5381fad2d6b2be8/teacher-traces/mopd2/task162-e2-prepared-20261009-v1)) put the reasoning inline: `reasoning\n<|end_think|>\n\nanswer`. The `chat_template.jinja` shipped with them renders assistant `content` verbatim and ends the generation prompt at the assistant header, so `<|start_think|>` is in neither the prompt nor the target. `MARIN_CHAT_TEMPLATE` renders reasoning as `<|start_think|>…<|end_think|>` ([`chat_template.py` L109](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f79686b2185c57d2db32569d9c27f2bcebd04e76/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/chat_template.py#L109)).

| SFT rows | rows | with `<\|start_think\|>` | with one `<\|end_think\|>` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| expert E | 1,454 | 0 | 1,454 |
| expert E2 | 1,359 | 0 | 1,359 |

The counts are the same in `train.jsonl` and in the token ids of `train-prebuilt.jsonl.gz`.

**What E learned.** Of E's 12,800 k=8 samples (`task145-e-k8-20261008`), 98 have one well-formed block; 11,133 have no reasoning before the first `<|end_think|>`, 4,747 repeat the opener and 1,679 reopen after closing. The plain and RS-SFT sets are drawn from these samples: none of the 1,503 RS-SFT targets starts with `<|start_think|>`, and 711 contain two or more. For comparison, #10400 finds two or more thinking segments in 1.9% to 9.1% of the thinking messages of Marin's general checkpoints.

**What the arms carry.** Teacher-forced next-token probabilities on 48 prompts (12 each from CRUXEval, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K and IFEval) for the checkpoints #9920 and #9984 pin, averaged over the 36 prompts that are not CRUXEval:

| | B | E | RS-SFT 282 | OPD 75 | plain SFT 399 | mixed RS 727 | MOPD 100 | merge TA0.5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `/think`, after `<\|start_think\|>\n`: next token closes or reopens | 0.0016 | 0.156 | 0.220 | 0.216 | 0.298 | 0.376 | 0.829 | 0.152 |
| `/nothink`: first token is `<\|start_think\|>` | 0.0000 | 0.051 | 0.288 | 0.041 | 0.373 | 0.274 | 0.420 | 0.115 |

On the CRUXEval prompts under `/nothink` the opener probability is 0.95 for RS-SFT and 0.78 for OPD (B 0.00), in line with the think blocks the #9920 and #9984 panels counted in thinking-off CRUXEval replies (28 and 18 of 30; v0.1 0). B itself writes a second opener after `<|start_think|>\n` on the CRUXEval prompt format (0.91, against 0.0015 on the other prompts), so part of the CRUXEval gap that E closes is format.

**Reading.** The off-target losses sit on format-strict benchmarks (BFCL-Parity, NUPA with 62.8% to 71.9% valid format, thinking-off FinanceBench, length-capped TriviaQA), while knowledge and reasoning benchmarks hold. Every expert row has the shape #11706 describes: reasoning without the opener, then `<|end_think|>`. The probe shows that the arms carry it, not that it causes the losses, and how far an arm shifts does not rank its BFCL loss. A direct test: re-score B on the affected benchmarks with the current panel code (B's panel row is from older code), then compare RS282 with RS-SFT on the same samples rewritten into one well-formed block each, and with an expert rebuilt from the GLM traces rendered with the opener. If the format is fixed and the losses stay, the format is not the cause.

🤖 **Marin Belay intake: post research ideas for [Marin Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/) here.**

Marin Belay is a human-guided, agent-executed experiment loop that hill-climbs the grug `fast_track` scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss).

**Start with the [contributor guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/marin_belay_v1_recipe/experiments/belay/CONTRIBUTING.md)**: how to check an idea against the recipe, pick a Track, follow its runs, and take it up the ladder.

1. **Post one idea per comment**, with a paper link or a short rationale. Add a `Track:` line to pick the baseline; the default is `speedrun` (the 8-minute d512 run). The Belay page lists the Tracks.
2. **A maintainer reviews it** on the Belay admin page and approves it for an agent session, or declines it with a reason.
3. **👀 on your comment means it has been reviewed.** Nothing else is posted here. Plans, results and decline reasons are on the Status page.

**The usual path for an idea:** optionally a `vanilla-*` Track first, for a radical idea or a stronger signal; then `speedrun`, for fast iteration and to check it fits the current recipe; then `hero-mfu` if it will change MFU a lot; then `ladder`. Maintainers promote ideas into the recipe from those results.

**Tracks** (the `Track:` line):

| Track | Runs against | Hardware |
|---|---|---|
| `speedrun` (default) | The 8-minute d512 run of the current recipe; judged at equal data, then equal time if the step time changes | 1× 8×H100 |
| `competitive-d512` … `competitive-d1280` | The current recipe at one ladder rung, compared with its finished baseline run | 8×H100; d1280 on 4 nodes |
| `ladder` | All four `competitive-*` rungs at once, at the baseline's step count. After a `hero-mfu` result, each rung's steps are adjusted for the MFU change (better MFU, more steps). Without one, the verdict is provisional: the idea needs a `hero-mfu` result before it joins the recipe | as above |
| `moe-d512` … `moe-d1280` | A basic MoE at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `vanilla-d512` … `vanilla-d1280` | A dense baseline at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `hero-mfu` | Step time of the hero GB200 stack; a maintainer runs it | 1 GB200 rack |
| `custom` | A study: runs on other Tracks, then an analysis report with no win/loss verdict; needs a node and hours budget | per study |

Wins are judged on Paloma macro loss with a noise band of 0.005 (`hero-mfu`: step time, ±0.5%).

**Example comments**

> Try warming the MuonH momentum up from 0.85 to 0.98 over the first 10% of training, as modded-nanogpt does.

> Track: moe-d768
> Replace the router's sigmoid combine weights with softmax over the top-8 experts.

> Track: ladder
> Take X0221 (CPLM Plus) up the ladder with the settings of its speedrun win.

> Track: custom
> Measure how the stable rank of each attention projection changes over a full d512 run, from checkpoints every 1,000 steps.

**The Belay app** ([public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-…](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/)):

- **[Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/):** the project. It covers the current recipe, the scaling ladder and its projection, the timeline, the gates an idea passes, the Tracks, the data and the starter kit.
- **[Status](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#status):** every idea and its results across the gates (Dense, speedrun, Hero MFU, projection, recipe), live runs and queue, and the agent log with one thread per idea (`#status/X####`).
- **[Hero MFU](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#mfu):** hero-scale throughput, with each MFU change on the GB200 stack and its branch.
- **[Admin](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#admin)** (maintainers, signed in to Marina): review and approve or decline ideas, with instructions and node, hours and priority grants. It also sets the node cap, dispatch and GitHub reactions.

Notice: The majority of our compute right now is dedicated to SFT and RL runs. As a result, runs outside the speedrun track may queue up for a couple days.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:

A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
or
B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt

Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: 🤖 Second intake test (end-to-end on main, scheduled run): this comment should be copied into #9451 within a few minutes of its 👍, then get a 🚀. Not a research suggestion.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.

Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.

But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:

1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting

And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.

The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Attention residuals q embedding:
In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from

exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))

into

exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))

q_e should be initialized as all 0.

Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Reconsider per-element attention gate, and either variant seems viable.

1. a linear projection with the same shape of the W_v projection, followed by sigmoid, like how Kimi K3 does it.
2. a down projection to a smaller vector, followed by a Swish nonlinearity, an up projection, then sigmoid, like how the current GatedNorm does it.

Rationale: the current Marin recipe has reduced the total number of MLA layers, by using a KDA+MLA hybrid, therefore the extra overhead of per-element gates compared to per-head ones becomes smaller.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):

1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.

Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:

1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.

These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).

Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".

Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
where y = s + r

Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.

Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.

Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.

Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body:
**Report the Paloma macro without `ptb` and `wikitext_103` next to the macro, and prefer it for calls near the bar.**

I paired each d512 Belay run (`lc1-*` in `marin_moe`) with its `-s1` twin, which has the same config apart from `trainer.seed`: 404 pairs from Sept 25 to Oct 8. These numbers are for the 305 configs near the frontier, i.e. within 0.01 of their batch median.

- **`ptb` is 1/16 of the macro but carries about a third of its seed noise** (35%). With `wikitext_103` the two carry 42%, by a covariance split.
- **Dropping the two cuts the noise much more than the signal.** Averaging the other 14 subsets cuts the noise SD of a paired Δ by 20%, while real differences between configs shrink by 3%. Signal-to-noise rises 1.4–1.5× (main estimate 1.48×, 95% CI 1.2–1.8), about what 1.5× as many seeds would buy.
- **`ptb`'s differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds:**

| Metric | Seed-to-seed correlation | Noise SD of a 2-seed paired Δ |
|---|---|---|
| Paloma macro, 16 subsets | 0.81 | 0.0016 |
| Without `ptb`, `wikitext_103` | 0.86 | 0.0013 |
| Uncheatable macro | 0.87 | 0.0014 |
| `ptb` alone | 0.10 | 0.013 |

The 0.0016 fits your "two-seed noise of ±0.004" (about 2.5 SD).

**This keeps the objective.** Near the bar, the 14-subset Δ estimates the full macro's true Δ better than the measured macro Δ does: the two-seed RMSE is 0.0009 vs 0.0011. For large changes the two can diverge, so the full macro stays the reference there.

**Two fixed-time calls** (seed 0 / seed 1):

| Call | Macro | Without the two | Uncheatable | `ptb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Batch 174: candidate 11 vs 10 (same math, 3.5% faster) | −0.0058 / −0.0047 | −0.0075 / −0.0067 | −0.0072 / −0.0070 | +0.013 / +0.029 |
| Batch 200: candidate 12 vs 11 | −0.0001 / −0.0000 | +0.0017 / +0.0045 | +0.0043 / +0.0063 | −0.020 / −0.055 |

- In batch 174, `ptb` hid about a quarter of the gain.
- In batch 200, the exact tie was a fixed-time loss on the other 14 subsets and on Uncheatable. Its two sides ran on different clusters, but candidate 11's equal-step runs on the two clusters agree within 0.002 on these metrics.

**Why these two subsets.** They are the subsets with copies in the hero's training data (#9874), and I picked them before looking at Belay. Choosing subsets by their noise would be fitting the metric. Uncheatable works about as well.

**The bar.** You can keep 0.005 on the 14-subset Δ, for fewer false wins. Or you can lower it to about 0.004, which keeps today's false-win rate; with the observed tails the matching value is 0.0042.

Method, code and per-run numbers: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise. I left out 6 pairs whose two seeds differ by 0.03–0.21 on the macro and by as much on Uncheatable (broken or diverged runs). Kept in, they swamp the overall variance, but the near-frontier numbers above barely move: for example, the gain is 1.38× instead of 1.48×.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
**Try numerically stable cross-entropy from [arXiv:2610.31642](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31642).**

The paper identifies a numerical problem with standard softmax cross-entropy called **Softmax Collapse**. When the correct logit becomes sufficiently larger than the others, floating-point rounding makes its softmax probability exactly 1, zeroing its gradient while leaving non-target gradients nonzero. This breaks the zero-sum gradient invariant (the gradients across all logits should sum to zero) and can cause optimization instability, including sudden spikes in training loss.

The proposed fix is simple: exclude the correct class from the log-sum-exp calculation and use `softplus` to combine the result with the correct class's logit.

```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def cross_entropy(logits, targets):
    target_logits = jnp.take_along_axis(
        logits, targets[..., None], axis=-1
    )
    is_target = jax.nn.one_hot(
        targets, logits.shape[-1], dtype=jnp.bool_
    )

    others = jnp.where(is_target, -jnp.inf, logits - target_logits)
    return jax.nn.softplus(
        jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(others, axis=-1)
    )
```

This is mathematically equivalent to standard cross-entropy but avoids prematurely zeroing small gradients.

comments.author: armorfaye

Try replacing top-k routing with ReMoE’s ReLU routing and adaptive, load-aware sparsity regularization. Target the same average number of active experts as the baseline, while allowing the count to vary across tokens. Use the paper’s unnormalized nonnegative routing weights.

Rationale: expert selection becomes continuous as routing weights cross zero, and different tokens can receive different amounts of computation. ReMoe (https://arxiv.org/html/2412.14711v2) reports improved language-model loss across several scales. Track active-expert counts and load imbalance, and include the initially denser training phase in the fixed-time comparison.

comments.author: WhenWen

The archived seed-0 TPU results look promising: Paloma / Uncheatable macro BPB improves from 1.184407 / 0.960857 to 1.181649 / 0.953552 at d512, and from 1.093305 / 0.853946 to 1.091306 / 0.850160 at d768, compared with ordinary CPLM. comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Try causal token-level capacity routing in front of the MoE (Mixture-of-Depths style ([arXiv 2404.02258](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02258)) ), keeping top-k + QB for expert choice.

Following @ClassicLarry's [comment 1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6411175364) and  [comment 2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5862159670) that dynamic compute likely matters more at scale.

Each MoE sublayer gets a small per-token router score. Tokens above a learned threshold go through the routed experts with a larger top-k; the rest go through the shared expert and the residual only. For routed tokens, expert ranking stays as in the current recipe (QB-adjusted logits, same combine weights); only k changes. Mean active experts per token matches the current recipe, e.g. with today's k = 10: 80% of tokens routed at k = 12 or 13, so the average stays ≈ 10.

Rationale: X0220 ([batch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6409675987)) showed ReMoE's failure came from the ReLU gates themselves: dead experts (40–278 per layer), 3–8% drops and load imbalance. Its allocation was already adaptive (easiest loss decile ≈ 7.4 experts, rest ≈ 12). This proposal keeps that adaptive allocation but separates the two decisions: *which tokens get more compute* (new router) and *which experts serve them* (top-k + QB, already stable here), so no expert can die from a zero gate. Mixture-of-Depths uses the same capacity idea for whole blocks.

FYI: the original MoD picks the top-k tokens over the whole sequence during training, so whether position t is routed depends on later tokens. Use a causal version instead: each token is routed by comparing its own score to a learned threshold (or a running causal quantile), with the same rule in training and eval.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Revisit MTP as a low-weight, decaying auxiliary loss computed on a subset of positions, with a block-head variant.

Batch 18 ([comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5843750617)) tried one MTP configuration: a depth-1 head (h_t + W·norm(embed(t+1)) through the shared lm_head), weight 0.3 for the whole run. 

Rationale: MTP results in the literature come from much longer token budgets, so an equal-steps vs fixed-time pair on this ladder says whether the Batch 18 loss came from the configuration or from the objective at this budget. 

Here are some things worth trying:
1. **Lower weight:** 0.05 and 0.1 instead of 0.3.
2. **Decay to zero:** linearly to 0 by 50% or 80% of training, so the late phase optimizes next-token loss only. One extra arm turns MTP off entirely after the first 50%.
3. **Block head:** replace the linear head with one lightweight Transformer block (local attention + dense FFN) that reads norm(h_t) and norm(embed(t+1)) and feeds the shared lm_head, as in DeepSeek-V3 ([arXiv 2412.19437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437)). 
Also, in a recent interview ([video, ~1:30:00](https://youtu.be/V9eI-t3TApE?t=5396)), MiMo-V2.6 leader Fuli Luo said they added MTP in pre-training because it improves the base model, and only later, while designing inference for their hybrid-SWA model, found enough spare decode compute to use MTP for speculative decoding. She also said teams that put too much faith in MLA missed this path; my reading is that MLA leaves less spare decode compute for MTP drafting. That is an inference-side hypothesis without published measurements, and I am not sure if this (spare compute) applies to our situation.
4. **(optional) Subsampled positions:** compute the t+2 logits and loss on a random 25% of positions per batch, still through the shared lm_head. If the cost scales with scored positions, the slowdown drops to about a quarter of 8.6%.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Try adding **spelling-normalised byte embeddings** to the input. Each token's input embedding row gets a learned sum over the first 8 UTF-8 bytes of its surface string, one 256 x d table per byte position. Read the bytes after stripping leading spaces and lowercasing, so " The", "the" and "The" share every byte row. Add two small feature rows to keep what the normalisation removes: leading space (0/1) and case (lower, capitalised, all caps, mixed). Zero-init the tables so the model starts identical to the baseline. Add the byte sum to the vocab table before the token gather, so there is no per-token cost and no extra communication. Input side only: do not share byte rows on the lm_head. Keep 8 byte positions and table width d_model at every rung.

Rationale: tokens that are spelling or case variants of each other start with unrelated embeddings and have to learn their similarity from context. Sharing byte rows gives the model that information directly, and it is information the body cannot compute from token ids. This is close to Spelling Bee Embeddings (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18030); the space/case normalisation is the addition.

For each vocabulary token, normalise its string as in X0226 (strip leading spaces, lowercase), add word-boundary markers, and take the set of character 1–4-grams, keeping only n-grams that occur in at least 2 vocabulary tokens. comments.author: xTimeCrystal
comments.body: Track: speedrun Similar to https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08888, try implementing a Full Bandwidth Transformer (FBT): the trunk runs K parallel passes over the sequence, and pass p's input at token t is fused from that token's embedding and the previous pass's output at token t-1: `x^{(p)}_{t} = norm(x_t + W_fuse norm(h^{(p-1)}_{t-1}))` - Use this formula, not the paper's. This is more stable. - `x_t` is the pass-1 input of token t (its embedding). - `h^{(p-1)}_{t-1}` is the final layer's output of pass `p-1` at position `t-1` (what the LM head reads), not that pass's input. - `norm` is parameter-free RMSNorm. - `W_fuse` is a `d_model` x `d_model` matrix, zero-initialised, so training starts as the plain model. - Position 0 and every document start (BOS) get the plain input `x_t`: no feedback across documents. - Gradients flow through all passes; do not detach or no-grad any pass. - Do not add "jitter" unlike the original paper - Training loss: CE of pass 1 + mean CE of the later passes (ignore as we only test K=2 passes). Evaluation: the last pass only. Sweep the fraction of training steps that use K=2 passes, the rest using K=1: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 (always 2 passes). Never use K=3. Evaluate every run with K=2. Optimise W_fuse with Muon first, at the learning rate and schedule of the other weight matrices. Then sweep 0.7x and 1.4x to bracket the optimal W_fuse lr using Muon. Then repeat the best Muon run with Adam on `W_fuse` (no weight decay), sweeping its learning rate over 0.7x, 1x, 1.4x. With MoE: keep the expert selections different across passes (the router picks again in every pass; never reuse pass 1's experts—we want the model's second pass picks to be adapted to the "enriched" hidden states). Quantile balancing counts the routing margins of all passes of a batch and updates the bias once, after the batch, for the next batch, never per pass: a per-pass update routes pass 2 with a bias computed from the same batch's own tokens, including later positions, which breaks causality. Compare against the dense baseline at matched training FLOPs: K=2 costs about 2x the FLOPs per token. Also, confirm that sequential decoding (token by token, each token fused with the previous token's final state) gives the same hidden-state and loss (within noise) as K=2 parallel passes. In our nanochat run they agreed to within 0.0003 bpb. nanochat results (per-iteration val bpb using the last pass; fbt2 = always 2 passes): This image shows the untuned baseline; it does not quite break even for the extra compute, and more tuning could close that gap.

Track: speedrun

Fix for X0230: belay-X0230-seed0 trained all 3,030 steps and then crashed in the final eval (`dropless_eval_hook`) with `ShardingTypeError: broadcast_shardings got incompatible shardings` inside `previous_token`, called from `RoutedMoE._lag_window`. Exact-match pointer mixture on the output with 8 candidates. For every position t, collect K = 8 candidate next tokens from earlier in the same document: for n = 1 and n = 2, the tokens that followed the 4 most recent earlier positions s < t whose last n tokens equal the n tokens ending at t (candidate x[s+1]). Mix them into the output: p(y) = (1 - G) p_vocab(y) + open * sum_k pi_k [c_k = y], where (pi_0, pi_1..pi_K) = softmax(0, l_1..l_K) over the candidates that exist, l_k = h . w_k + 8 * b[k, a_k] - 2 with h the lm_head input and a_k the number of other slots proposing the same token, G = open * sum_k pi_k, open = clip(8 * o, 0, 1). w [d_model, 8], b [8, 8] and the scalar o are zero-initialised and trained in the plain Adam group with no weight decay, so the model starts as the control. comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

Softcap radial MuonH: give each hidden matrix a learned, bounded radius on top of MuonH's sphere.

(Generated by an automated research harness. Edited to replace the earlier evidence with the completed results; bottom line first.)

**Bottom line**
- On Belay's 8-minute d512 speedrun, softcap beats the recipe's MuonH beyond the 0.005 band (below).
- That edge shrinks with size: on Belay's ladder recipe it is inside the band by d768 (one seed).
- Softcap does **not** beat a fairly tuned MuonW-family baseline. Once MuonW gets a tuned head LR and schedule-scaled decay (MuonC, Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285), that baseline matches or beats softcap.
- So we are not proposing softcap as a ladder improvement on current evidence. d1024/d1280 are still running.

**Update rule (per Muon-group matrix slice W)**
- Write W = r0 · exp(s) · Ŵ, where r0 is the init radius and Ŵ is on the unit Frobenius sphere. Ŵ takes the usual MuonH hyperball step.
- s (a scalar log-radius per slice) is stepped by Adam on the radial gradient g = <∂L/∂W, W>, at the same LR and schedule as the matrix LR.
- Bound: outward steps are scaled by (1 − (s/c)²) and inward steps are taken in full. With c = 2 the radius is capped at e² ≈ 7.4× init.
- Slices whose output passes through a scale-removing norm keep a fixed radius (plain MuonH). Head and fallback groups are unchanged.

**d512 speedrun (Belay recipe, same-commit MuonH control)**
- Equal data, six paired GB200 seeds: softcap − MuonH mean −0.0083, one-sided 95% upper bound −0.0059, 6/6 seeds better. Three H100 seeds agree (mean −0.0082).
- An equal-time check gave smaller margins on the seeds read (about −0.004).
- learnable_qk_mult adds nothing (control + lqk +0.0002). The radius gain does transfer under the recipe's MLA q/k norms.

**Ladder (Belay recipe, one seed per rung; single-run gaps under 0.005 are ties)**
- Against MuonH: d512 −0.0103 (seed 1; −0.0057 on seed 0), d768 −0.0030 (a tie).
- Against the best MuonW-family run (MuonC, head LR ×0.35): d512 tie (−0.0025 on averaged reruns), d768 −0.0049 (a tie at the band edge).
- Same-seed reruns of identical settings at d512 differ by up to about 0.003, so one-seed margins below the band carry little weight.

**KMA d768 target (where the method was developed)**
- Softcap leads MuonW tuned on LR and decays by −0.0044 (seeds 2-11, held-out agreeing).
- That MuonW was under-tuned:
  - With MuonW's AdamW head LR tuned as well (×0.25-0.5), the lead drops to about −0.002, inside noise.
  - MuonC with a tuned head (2.4944, seed 0) beats every weight-normalized variant we tried, including softcap's best (2.5013).

**What we learned**
- Weight-normalized radial MuonH's apparent edge over MuonW came mostly from two things a fair MuonW also gets:
  - the AdamW head LR being too large;
  - plain decoupled decay shrinking the matrices late.
- MuonC's scheduled decay fixes the second, which matches the paper's prediction (flat late weight norm, bounded grad/weight ratio).

Document n-gram count cache mixed into the output. Let q1 = n1 / c1 and q2 = n2 / c2 (each is a distribution over the vocabulary). Gate logits l_n = h . w_n + 8 * b_n * log2(1 + c_n) / 12 - 2 for n = 1, 2, where h is the lm_head input; (pi_0, pi_1, pi_2) = softmax(0, l_1, l_2) over the orders with c_n > 0; open = clip(8 * o, 0, 1); G = open * (pi_1 + pi_2). The model's distribution is p(y) = (1 - G) * p_vocab(y) + open * (pi_1 * q1(y) + pi_2 * q2(y)). w [d_model, 2], b [2] and the scalar o are zero-initialised and trained in the plain Adam group with no weight decay, so the model starts as the control. Train and evaluate on the mixture loss ce - log((1 - G) + M * exp(ce)), where ce is the lm_head's per-token cross-entropy (plus z-loss in training) and M = open * (pi_1 * q1(label) + pi_2 * q2(label)). Implementation: all counts are integer work on the token ids, once per step before the forward pass and outside value_and_grad and any jax.checkpoint region. Per sequence, sort three key arrays stably with the position as payload: the token x_u; the pair id x_{u-1} * vocab + x_u; and the triple as two int32 keys (pair id of (x_{u-2}, x_{u-1}), x_u). A pair or triple that would cross a document start gets a key no other position has. In each sorted array a run breaks where the key or the document id changes; an element's rank is its index minus its run start (a cumulative max); scatter the ranks back to positions. Then c1(t) = rank_token[t], c2(t) = rank_pair[t], n1(t) = rank_pair[t + 1] and n2(t) = rank_triple[t + 1]. comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

At each step of training, we estimate the gradient against the 'weights', where the weights is a weighted sum over all prior gradients. However this weighted sum has a restricted set of options because we only modify it via new_update + modifier*all_prior_updates. A richer set is possible. Try this:

Implement linear init removal in our Hyperball optimizer. For every weight matrix Hyperball constrains (attention and MLP matrices; leave embeddings and norm gains alone), keep a scalar b, the coefficient of the initial weights W₀ in the current weights. It starts at 1.0. Regenerate W₀ from the init seed rather than storing a copy. On every step, keep b updated as b ← a·b, where a = R/‖W − ηV‖ is Hyperball’s projection factor. From step N/3 to step 2N/3, subtract a fixed amount of the init before projecting: W ← W − ηV − d·W₀ with d = min(δ, b), then project back to radius R, and update b ← a·(b − d). Pick δ so b reaches exactly 0 at step 2N/3. A good start is δ ≈ b(N/3) divided by the number of steps in the window, then adjust slightly to account for the shrinking from projection. Outside that window the optimizer is unchanged.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen.

Track: speedrun

**Learned-radius MuonH (nonsi) plus an s(t)² head and late-matrix anneal.** This changes only the optimizer. It adds one scalar per matrix slice and no model change.

**Update rule** (s(t) = lr_t / lr_max of the recipe's MuonH schedule):
1. *Learned radius ("nonsi").* Write each MuonH-group slice as W = r0 · exp(ρ) · Ŵ, with r0 = ‖W‖_F at init and Ŵ on the unit sphere.
   - Ŵ takes MuonH's hyperball step, unchanged.
   - ρ (one scalar per slice) is stepped by Adam (β 0.9 / 0.99) on the radial gradient ⟨∂L/∂W, W⟩, at the matrix LR and its usual (unannealed) schedule. There is no cap.
   - Slices whose output feeds a norm through linear maps only (so ⟨∂L/∂W, W⟩ = 0) keep ρ = 0, i.e. plain MuonH. These are the MLA kv down-projection (w_dkv), the MLA query (w_q) and key up-projection (w_uk), and the MoE latent down-projection (w_latent_down). The KDA write-strength group learns ρ at its own LR.
2. *Head anneal.* The lm_head / output_proj (AdamH) LR becomes lr_max · s(t)² instead of lr_max · s(t).
3. *Late matrix anneal.* From step t₀ = round(0.7937 · N), multiply the MuonH matrix LR by s(t) / s(t₀), so the angular step falls as s(t)² from there and is continuous at t₀.

The Adam groups are unchanged. With ρ ≡ 0 and both anneals off, this is the recipe.

**Evidence** (our own runs, Paloma macro loss)

*8-minute d512 speedrun, equal data, 6 paired seeds, against a same-commit recipe MuonH control (mean 3.0423):*

| Arm | Δ vs MuonH |
|---|---|
| nonsi + s² anneals (this) | **−0.0115** (all 6 seeds; one-sided 95% bound −0.0098) |
| nonsi without the anneals | −0.0079 |
| MuonC (Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285), λ 0.1, + the same anneals | −0.0033 |
| MuonC, λ 0.2, + the same anneals | −0.0161 |

*d512 on the ladder recipe (10,767 steps), seed 1:* this 2.8518; recipe MuonH 2.8697 (+0.018); nonsi without the anneals 2.8604 (+0.009).

**Caveats**
- A tuned MuonC with the same anneals beats this on the speedrun: at λ 0.2 it is 0.0046 better (five of six seeds). The anneals are not specific to the learned radius.
- On the larger ladder rungs, the same anneals helped our capped variant (softcap) less and less: −0.008 at d512, −0.010 at d768, −0.004 at d1024, and +0.006 (worse) at d1280. nonsi with the anneals at d768 to d1280 is still running.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen.

Track: speedrun

**MuonC with an s(t)² head and late-matrix anneal.** This replaces MuonH's sphere with Muon plus schedule-scaled weight decay (MuonC, Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285), and adds the two anneals from our nonsi intake above. It changes only the optimizer, with no new parameters.

**Update rule** (s(t) = lr_t / lr_max of the recipe's MuonH schedule, N = number of steps):
1. *Matrix LR with a late anneal.* lr_m(t) = lr_t until t₀ = round(0.7937 · N), then lr_m(t) = lr_t · s(t) / s(t₀). The angular step falls as s(t)² from t₀ and is continuous there.
2. *MuonC matrices.* Every MuonH-group and KDA write-strength matrix takes W ← W − lr_m(t) · (O + λ_t W), with no projection to a sphere.
   - O is the Muon direction MuonH already computes: Newton–Schulz with the √max(1, fan_out / fan_in) scale.
   - λ_t = λ · lr_m(t) / lr_max, with λ = 0.2.
   - KDA write-strength keeps its 2× LR multiple.
3. *Head.* lm_head / output_proj use AdamW instead of AdamH, at LR lr_max · s(t)², with decoupled decay 0.05.
4. *Adam groups.* They keep their recipe LRs, with AdamW decay 0.05 on rank ≥ 2 leaves, replacing the recipe's annealed gate/router decay.

This differs from X0243/X0244 in the two anneals, the AdamW head, and the decay schedule λ · lr_t / lr_max. Both parts matter on the speedrun. At λ 0.1 the anneals are worth 0.006, and raising λ to 0.2 adds another 0.013.

**Evidence** (our own runs, Paloma macro loss)

*8-minute d512 speedrun, equal data, 6 paired seeds, against a same-commit recipe MuonH control (mean 3.0423):*

| Arm | Δ vs MuonH |
|---|---|
| MuonC λ 0.2 + anneals (this) | **−0.0161** (better on all 6 seeds, −0.011 to −0.020) |
| MuonC λ 0.4 + anneals | −0.0135 |
| MuonC λ 0.1 + anneals | −0.0033 |
| MuonC λ 0.1, no anneals | +0.0025 |
| nonsi + the same anneals (our other intake) | −0.0115 |

λ was picked on these seeds from a grid of λ (0.025 to 0.4) and LR multiplier (0.5× to 1.41×). λ 0.2 and 0.4 are close, and both beat λ 0.1 by far more than picking the best grid cell would add by chance. Every LR change was worse. λ 0.8 is still running.

*Belay ladder recipe, seed 1, λ 0.1 (not yet tuned on the ladder) + anneals vs recipe MuonH:*

| Rung | d512 | d768 | d1024 | d1280 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Δ | −0.013 | −0.009 | −0.010 | −0.010 |

🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen.

Track: ladder

**Law-cap ball: MuonH's matrices take a plain Muon step inside a per-layer Frobenius ball whose radius comes from a closed-form law, plus the s(t)² head anneal and late matrix anneal from our earlier intakes.** There is no weight decay and nothing to tune per rung. The change is optimizer-only, with no new parameters.

**Update rule** (s(t) = lr_t / lr_max of the recipe's MuonH schedule, N = number of steps)
1. *Matrices.* Every MuonH-group and KDA write-strength slice W takes W′ = W − η_t U. If ‖W′‖_F exceeds cap_l, W′ is rescaled onto the ball; otherwise it is kept as is. There is no decay and no projection inside the ball.
   - U is the Muon direction MuonH already computes: Newton–Schulz with the √max(1, fan_out / fan_in) scale.
   - η_t is the recipe's MuonH LR. From t₀ = round(0.7937 · N) it is multiplied by s(t)/s(t₀) (late anneal). KDA write-strength keeps its 2× LR.
   - A slice is a 2-D leaf, or one layer of a stacked leaf.
2. *Cap, from shape and peak LR only.*
   - cap_l = κ · |U_l|, where |U_l| = √(n · min(in, out) · max(1, out/in)) is the Frobenius norm of an orthogonalized update for that slice, and n is the number of matrices in the slice.
   - κ = √(τ · lr_max / (2λ)), with τ = 39 and λ = 0.2. This is the size MuonC's matrices settle at for decay λ (Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285). The ball reaches it directly instead of decaying toward it.
3. *Head.* The recipe's AdamH head, with LR lr_max · s(t)² instead of lr_max · s(t).
4. *Adam groups.* Unchanged.

**Evidence** (our own runs on the Belay ladder recipe, seed 1, Paloma macro loss)

| Rung | this | recipe MuonH | Δ | MuonC (λ 0.1) + same anneals, same commit | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512 | 2.8538 | 2.8697 | −0.016 | 2.8569 | −0.003 |
| d768 | 2.6051 | 2.6148 | −0.010 | 2.6062 | −0.001 |
| d1024 | 2.4045 | 2.4075 | −0.003 | 2.3997 | +0.005 |
| d1280 | 2.2627 | 2.2749 | −0.012 | 2.2656 | −0.003 |

- The matrices sit on their caps from early in training. A checkpoint check confirmed this on every rung.
- The cap level is bracketed around the law. At d512, 0.5× and 1.4× the law's cap are clearly worse, and 0.7× ties. At d768, 0.7× is worse and 1.4× is within noise.
- On the 8-minute d512 speedrun (6 seeds) it ties tuned MuonC + the same anneals (+0.0004 vs λ 0.4).

**Caveats**
- One seed per rung. Seed-to-seed spread of paired gaps is about 0.003–0.006, and a second d1280 seed has been proposed.
- It ties, rather than beats, a tuned MuonC with the same anneals (our other intake). Its appeal is that it gets there with no decay to tune: the cap is set from shape and peak LR alone, and the same formula was used at every rung.
- It also avoids a failure we saw with a learned-radius variant (softcap + the same anneals), which fell 0.016 behind at d1280.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body: Forwarding servers don't serve any queries, so the index building and remote object backups are unnecessary. They should simply collect and forward logs from their locally compacted segments.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Locate Finelog forwarding-server code and index/backup logic
- [x] Determine root cause and scope
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no overlapping PR; #8748 is adjacent object-storage work)
- [x] Post analysis — **out of PR scope: design change, needs human review**

---

**Research**

Forwarding servers are ordinary `Live` stores that additionally spawn a `Forwarder`; the store itself has no notion of a forwarding-only role, so per-namespace maintenance runs the full `flush → compact → sync → evict → index-backfill` cycle regardless ([`run_maintenance`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/namespace.rs#L1934-L2015)). Index building is gated only by the static per-namespace policy [`segment_indexes_enabled_for`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/policies.rs#L164-L167), which is identical on hub and regional servers — there is no server-role input to turn it off for a forwarder. Remote backup is [`sync_step`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/namespace.rs#L1512), uploading L≥1 segments to the object store.

The blocker is that remote backup is load-bearing for **retention**, not just durability. Eviction reclaims only `BOTH` (local+remote) segments via `select_eviction_candidate`, and [`evict_segment`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/namespace.rs#L1644-L1679) refuses to destroy `LOCAL`-only data — the test `eviction_skips_local_only_when_no_remote` (namespace.rs:3987) asserts local-only segments are never evicted. So dropping backup on a forwarder as configured today grows local disk without bound; there is no size/age reclamation path for local-only segments.

**Proposed approach (for review — not implementing as a PR)**

Doing this safely is three coupled changes, not a two-line gate, so it exceeds the self-contained-bugfix bar:

1. **Server-role signal.** Thread a forwarding-only flag from the CLI (`args.forwarding` non-empty, already parsed in [main.rs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/main.rs#L303)) through `Store::new*` into each `Namespace`, rather than deriving indexing from the global static policy. Decide whether this is a new `ServeMode` variant (`Forward`) or an orthogonal boolean — `ServeMode` currently means "what a process may touch," and forward-only fits that framing.
2. **Gate the two steps.** Skip `sync_step` and index backfill in `run_maintenance` when forwarding-only (leaving `cleanup_disabled_index_bundles` to remove stale bundles on a converted server).
3. **Retention for local-only segments.** Since the hub becomes the durable archive for forwarded rows, a forwarding-only store must treat local segments as ephemeral scratch and evict `LOCAL`-only segments by size/age. This is a new eviction path; the forwarder is already best-effort and tolerates eviction removing un-forwarded segments ([forwarding.rs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/server/forwarding.rs#L27-L44)), so at-least-once semantics hold, but the "evict rows that never forwarded" behavior is a policy decision worth an explicit sign-off.

Open questions for a maintainer: (a) is a forwarding server ever queried locally as a fallback (the forwarder docstring calls the local store "the system of record")? If yes, dropping indexes/backup changes that guarantee. (b) Should local-only eviction wait on the forward cursor, or stay purely size/age-bounded? Deploy wiring in [`config.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/src/finelog/deploy/config.py#L219-L241) (forwarders currently also set `remote_log_dir`) would follow whichever shape is chosen.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
Builds of the patched PJRT wheel in `marin-community/xla` cache `~/.cache/bazel` wholesale, about 11.6 GB against GitHub's documented 10 GB per-repository limit. Retention is unpredictable, and the difference is 1m35s of build time versus 3h31m.

| run | restore | build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [33013385685](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/actions/runs/33013385685) | 3m38s | 1m35s |
| [33093433428](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/actions/runs/33093433428) | 0s, nothing to restore | 3h31m33s |

A save at 2026-08-26T21:12Z was gone by the next build at 2026-08-27T16:29Z, which then paid a full cold compile. A save at 2026-08-27T20:04Z is still present a day later. Both entries are the same size, so exceeding the cap does not by itself explain which one survives.

The cached directory holds more than compile output. `external/` and `cache/repos/` carry fetched repositories including the CUDA 13 redistributables, which cost minutes to download again, while `execroot/.../bazel-out` carries the object files that cost hours to rebuild. No size breakdown has been taken, so which part dominates the 11.6 GB is unknown, and that is the first thing needed.

Impact is bounded. Builds run only on pushes to `main` that touch the wheel, so this costs 3½ hours on a refresh or a build-script change, not on routine work. Promotion runs from a published candidate and never compiles.

Done when:

- a size breakdown of the bazel output base is recorded from a build that runs anyway
- the cached content is small enough to be retained between consecutive builds
- two consecutive builds restore the cache, and the second compiles in minutes rather than hours
