spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body: By default Coreweave treats all pods as critical. We can provide hints for non-critical jobs with a CKS label as noted above. Let's adjust Iris to set these as appropriate. Certainly BATCH jobs can be interruptable (sic), INTERACTIVE we could also use interruptible or graceful-interruptible.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue + actionability check
- [x] Locate pod-manifest label stamping and priority bands
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no overlapping PR/issue)
- [ ] Confirm exact CKS label key + values (blocked on screenshot content)
- [ ] Implement band→CKS-hint mapping + test

# Research

Iris task pods carry no CoreWeave workload-criticality hint, so CKS treats every pod as critical and won't drain them for node maintenance/reclamation. Pods are built one-per-attempt in `_build_pod_manifest`; the priority band (`PRODUCTION`/`INTERACTIVE`/`BATCH`) is already resolved there and drives the Kueue priority class and native `priorityClassName`, so it's the natural key for a criticality hint. The `cks.coreweave.cloud/` prefix is already used at the node level (`SYSTEM_CRITICAL_LABEL`).

**Relevant code**
- [`backends/k8s/tasks.py#L888-L917`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L888-L917) — pod `labels`; `effective_band` resolved here
- [`backends/k8s/tasks.py#L1019-L1021`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L1019-L1021) — band → native `priorityClassName`
- [`job.proto#L614-L617`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/job.proto#L614-L617) — `PRIORITY_BAND_{PRODUCTION,INTERACTIVE,BATCH}`
- [`platforms/k8s/constants.py#L16-L25`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/constants.py#L16-L25) — existing CoreWeave `interruptable` toleration
- [`platforms/k8s/nodepool_manifests.py#L15`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/nodepool_manifests.py#L15) — node-level `cks.coreweave.cloud/system-critical`

# Proposed Fix

Stamp a CKS pod-criticality label in the `_build_pod_manifest` `labels` dict, keyed off `effective_band`:

| Band | Hint |
|------|------|
| `PRODUCTION` | critical (default — omit label) |
| `INTERACTIVE` | graceful-interruptible |
| `BATCH` | interruptible |

Define the label key/values as constants next to `COREWEAVE_INTERRUPTABLE_TOLERATION`. Test: assert the manifest label per band via the existing k8s pod-manifest test.

**Blocking question:** the exact CKS label key and its value strings live only in the screenshot, which I can't fetch (auth-gated attachment) or confirm via web search from here. Please confirm before I implement — specifically the label key (e.g. `cks.coreweave.cloud/<?>`) and whether the values are `critical` / `interruptable` / `graceful-interruptible`. This is a production-scheduling label, so I won't guess it.

This is a new scheduling feature touching live CoreWeave behavior, so per policy I'm posting analysis for review rather than opening a PR up front.

### Slurm wrapper used by every command in this issue

All commands submit `run_gpu.sh` from `$WORK/marin` on the AMD HPC Fund cluster. It turns XLA command buffers off; a later `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=...` in `XLA_FLAGS` overrides that. It will be committed to the repo; this comment is the reference until then.

<details><summary>run_gpu.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -o pipefail
cd "$WORK/marin"
export RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=${RAGGED_DOT_IMPL:-xla} PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# Command buffers (HIP graphs) corrupt memory on this ROCm stack: nan gradients and segfaults after a few steps.
export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer= $XLA_FLAGS"
uv run --no-sync python "$@" 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered -v -E "rocm_pcie_bandwidth|rocm_executor"
```

</details>

🤖

# Research

MI350X reaches 3.86% MFU with bf16 Triton `ragged_dot`; its fp16 XLA runs reach 2.59–2.83%. The reported ~10 ms Triton expert matmul is a bottleneck hypothesis; the current MI350X results do not include a pinned-revision profile that attributes the full step. MI300X batch 32 reached 10.3% MFU over steps 2–9 but hung at step 10, which coincides with the trainer's watch interval; the cause and sustained throughput remain unconfirmed.

**Relevant code**
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108) — benchmark flags; no watch control
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166) — trainer uses default watch configuration
- [`train.py#L641-L649`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/train.py#L641-L649) — interval selects watch computation
- [`ragged_dot.py#L341-L367`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L341-L367) — XLA/Triton selection

# Proposed Fix

1. Extend the existing benchmark PR #9693 with a benchmark-only watch interval flag (0 disables watch) and the Slurm wrapper used in the issue. Pin one post-rebase benchmark commit and the ROCm/JAX versions for every comparison. Keep the production watch default unchanged.
2. On 8× MI300X, rerun the full EP8 batch-32 configuration for 20 steps with watch intervals 10 and 0, `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla`, memory fraction 0.90, no profiler, and command buffers off. Record the step-10 outcome, median time over non-watch steps 2–9 and 11–19, tokens/s, MFU, and peak memory. Treat 10.3% as preliminary until a 20-step run completes; if both variants hang, capture the failing step's trace before changing the model.
3. At the same pinned commit, rerun MI350X bf16/Triton batch 8 and fp16/XLA batches 8, 16, and 32 with the same 20-step setup. Profile a separate run of the fastest completed configuration and report time in expert GEMMs, collectives, other kernels, and host gaps. Compare against the MI300X reference only after these reruns.
4. Use that profile to choose one next change: test `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` if communication dominates, or tune the Triton expert GEMM if it dominates. Test command-buffer types separately on a smaller shape with finite-loss checks before a full-model run; the [current ROCm setup](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/559) has produced non-finite gradients and crashes with command buffers enabled. Post each run's commit, exact command, job ID, step time, MFU, peak memory, and negative results here.

Completion criterion: a full 20-step MI350X run with finite loss and a measured improvement over the rerun bf16/Triton batch-8 baseline (previously 3.86%). #9777 already covers ROCm architecture parsing; RCCL ragged all-to-all remains unsupported in its reported test, so it is not a parallel implementation target for this issue.

comments.body:
🤖 ### MI350X bf16 matmul ceiling: 1,229 TFLOP/s in JAX by kernel time (53% of datasheet peak, 97% of PyTorch's sustained 1,261)

Commits: 265ea0f (MAMF jobs 453328, 453329), d733a95 (453334), 52cf1ee (JAX 453412), 08516a7 (JAX 453420, 453421), 6b47d18 (JAX 454529), 370d41d (JAX 454561), 704ceff (JAX 454577-454580) · GPU: one MI350X or MI300X, whole node reserved · Scripts: [`experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling) (PR #9840)

This measures how fast one GPU runs a plain dense matmul, to give the MFU numbers above a measured ceiling. Two tools ran on the same node for each GPU type: k007-002 for MI350X, k002-003 for MI300X. Both venvs install AMD's `rocm-sdk-libraries==10.0.0` wheel, which provides hipBLASLt and rocBLAS; the nodes' system ROCm (`/opt/rocm-7.2.0`) is not used for compute.

- Stas Bekman's [MAMF-finder](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py) (PyTorch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, `PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_ENABLED=1`, which benchmarks every rocBLAS and hipBLASLt solution per shape and keeps the fastest) searches about 2,100 shapes. It reports MAMF (maximum achievable matmul FLOPS): the median of the 5 fastest of 200 iterations, run in bursts of 20 after 250 ms idle. It also reports MSMF (maximum sustainable matmul FLOPS): the best rate held for 2 s under continuous load. It times each `torch.mm` with GPU events recorded just before and after the call, so its rates count kernel time only.
- `jax_matmul.py` (JAX 0.11.0) times `jax.jit(jnp.matmul)` with XLA autotuning on: 1 s of warmup, then the median of ten 0.2 s windows of back-to-back calls. It runs under `rocprofv3 --kernel-trace` and reports two rates per shape. Kernel time divides the FLOPs by the GPU time of the kernels inside each window, which matches MAMF-finder's timing. Wall clock divides them by host time, which also counts host dispatch and the idle GPU time between calls. Both are sustained rates, so MSMF is the PyTorch number to compare with.

Hardware and theoretical peaks:

| | MI350X | MI300X |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture, compute units | gfx950, 256 CUs | gfx942, 304 CUs |
| Memory per GPU (as torch reports it) | 288 GB HBM3E (294,896 MB) | 192 GB HBM3 (196,592 MB) |
| Dense bf16 and fp16 peak | 2,307 TFLOP/s, as in this issue (brochure: 2,309.6) | 1,307 TFLOP/s (datasheet: 1,307.4) |
| Node, Slurm partition | k007-002, `mi3508x` | k002-003, `mi3008x` |

The peaks are AMD's dense figures without structured sparsity. `lib/fray/src/fray/device_flops.py` stores the brochure values; the percentages below use 2,307 and 1,307 to match the tables above.

Software, identical on both GPUs:

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| ROCm user-space libraries | `rocm==10.0.0` wheels (`rocm-sdk-core`, `rocm-sdk-libraries`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx942`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx950`) from `https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/` |
| hipBLASLt, rocBLAS | 100401-8d1ae90e, 5.6.0.8d1ae90e (from TunableOp's results file) |
| PyTorch | 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, with `amd-torch-device-gfx942` and `-gfx950` 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0. `torch.version.hip` is 7.15.26333 and `torch.version.cuda` is None: a ROCm build, no CUDA |
| JAX | jax and jaxlib 0.11.0, `jax_rocm10_plugin` and `jax_rocm10_pjrt` 0.11.0+rocm10.0.0 |
| Kernel tracing | `rocprofv3` from the `rocm-sdk-core` 10.0.0 wheel |
| MAMF-finder | commit [0359db8](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py), benchmark version 4, auto search, default tuning |
| Python, OS | 3.12.12, Linux 5.14.0-611.54.1.el9_7 |
| JAX flags | `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`, `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0`; the Triton-off run adds `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` |

Each run used GPU 0 while the other 7 GPUs on the node were idle.

```bash
cluster "cd agents/<name> && sbatch --export=ALL,MARIN_COMMIT=$sha -p mi3508x -w <node> -t 60 -J <name> \

  --shapes-file experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt"
```

Results in TFLOP/s per GPU, with the share of the dense peak. Shapes are MxNxK. The JAX column is kernel time, with the traced wall-clock rate of the same shape in parentheses.

| GPU | dtype | MAMF (PyTorch) | MSMF (PyTorch) | JAX best | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MI350X | bf16 | 1,445 (62.6%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 (54.7%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,229 (53.3%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,178) | 453328, 454577 |
| MI350X | fp16 | 1,377 (59.7%) @ 4096x4096x20480 | 1,177 (51.0%) @ 8192x4096x14336 | 1,086 (47.1%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,047) | 453329, 454578 |
| MI300X | bf16 | 698 (53.4%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | 645 (49.3%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | not run | 453334 |

The JAX column covers a 125-shape grid (M, N and K each 4096, 8192, ..., 20480), the June model's projection shapes, and, for bf16, the 28 shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted (job 454579). By kernel time, JAX reaches 97% of MSMF in bf16 and 92% in fp16. Without the tracer, the best bf16 wall-clock rate was 1,192 at 4096x4096x16384 and 1,180 at 4096x4096x12288 (job 453420).

Measured against these ceilings instead of the datasheet, the MI350X baseline above (3.88% MFU, 90 TFLOP/s per GPU) runs at 7.3% of the JAX bf16 kernel-time ceiling. The confirmed MI300X batch-16 row (8.66%, 113 TFLOP/s) runs at 17.5% of PyTorch's MSMF; JAX was not measured on MI300X.

The MI300X run reproduces the MI300X bf16 row in [Stas Bekman's table](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/README.md#maximum-achievable-and-sustainable-matmul-flops-comparison-table) (MAMF 676, MSMF 659, PyTorch 2.12.0+rocm10.0.0): MAMF is 3.3% higher and MSMF 2.1% lower. His table has no MI350X row. His MI355X row reads 62.6% of peak, the same share as our MI350X MAMF.

The next table times the same matmul shapes in both frameworks, in bf16 on MI350X, using the shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted. MSMF is PyTorch's sustained rate after TunableOp has kept the fastest rocBLAS or hipBLASLt solution for that shape; the TunableOp column names the library it picked. JAX kernel time comes from job 454579, where XLA's autotuner picked a hipBLASLt kernel for every shape. JAX wall clock comes from job 453412, which ran without the tracer.

| Shape | MSMF | TunableOp | JAX kernel | JAX / MSMF, kernel | JAX wall | JAX / MSMF, wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 | rocBLAS | 1,052 | 83% | 1,008 | 80% |
| 4096x4096x8192 | 1,246 | hipBLASLt | 1,209 | 97% | 1,150 | 92% |
| 3584x4608x8192 | 1,237 | rocBLAS | 1,199 | 97% | 1,137 | 92% |
| 4096x4096x20480 | 1,224 | hipBLASLt | 1,179 | 96% | 1,153 | 94% |
| 4096x2048x20480 | 1,089 | hipBLASLt | 1,111 | 102% | 1,065 | 98% |
| 2048x4096x4096 | 1,080 | rocBLAS | 959 | 89% | 828 | 77% |

An earlier version of this comment read the 2-23% wall-clock gap as XLA choosing slower kernels. Most of that gap was the timing method. Wall clock counts host dispatch and the GPU's idle time between calls: on MI350X a trivial jitted op takes about 43 µs to dispatch, and the GPU idles about 12-15 µs between executions even when the host keeps ahead (job 454529). Kernel time removes that overhead. On 2048x4096x4096 it moves JAX from 77% to 89% of MSMF, and on 4096x4096x8192 from 92% to 97%. JAX's kernels are within 4% of MSMF on four shapes. Two gaps remain: 17 points on 4608x4096x7168 and 11 points on 2048x4096x4096. TunableOp picked a rocBLAS solution for both. Every GEMM kernel XLA picked in these runs carries hipBLASLt's `UserArgs` naming, and we have not checked whether XLA's autotuner considers rocBLAS solutions or whether they account for those gaps. TunableOp also picked rocBLAS for 3584x4608x8192, where JAX's hipBLASLt kernel reaches 97%.

On MI350X in bf16, the June model's projection GEMMs at 4096 tokens per GPU run at 369 TFLOP/s (k and v weight gradients, 2560x640x4096) to 1,058 (lm head weight gradient) by kernel time through JAX (job 454577). 4096x2560x2560 is the shape of the q, attention output and shared expert gate, up and down projections, and of their input gradients. It runs at 972 by kernel time and 826 by untraced wall clock (job 454529). The lm head forward runs at 1,030 by kernel time and 1,029 by untraced wall clock. The k and v projections, 4096x640x2560, run at 427 by kernel time with XLA's Triton GEMM and at 556 with hipBLASLt (next table). By untraced wall clock they run at 257 with Triton. Full list in [`snowball_shapes.txt`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt). The routed-expert `ragged_dot` and the small router, attention gate and GatedNorm GEMMs are not covered.

In bf16, XLA generates its own Triton GEMM for four of the k and v shapes: every shape with a dimension of 640, and 2560x1280x4096. Every other shape uses a hipBLASLt kernel. With `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` (job 454580), XLA uses hipBLASLt for these shapes too, and its kernels run 17-33% faster in bf16. Kernel time in TFLOP/s:

| Shape | Use | Triton (454577) | hipBLASLt, Triton off (454580) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4096x640x2560 | k and v projections | 427 | 556 | +30% |
| 2560x640x4096 | k and v weight gradients | 369 | 490 | +33% |
| 2560x1280x4096 | k and v weight gradients, fused | 514 | 664 | +29% |
| 4096x2560x640 | k and v input gradients | 471 | 552 | +17% |

Of the other 38 shapes in the Triton-off run, 33 used the same hipBLASLt kernel as with Triton on, and their kernel time moved by at most 1.6%. For the other 5, the autotuner picked a different hipBLASLt kernel in the new run (see the variation note). Under the tracer, wall clock moved the other way on the four Triton shapes: on 4096x640x2560 a call took 48 µs with Triton and 61 µs with hipBLASLt, against kernel times of 31 and 24 µs, so host-side work sets the wall-clock rate at this size. We have not measured these shapes with Triton off without the tracer. In fp16 (job 454578), XLA also picks Triton for 4096x2560x1280; we did not run fp16 with Triton off.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- fp16 is slower than bf16 for dense matmuls on MI350X: MAMF is 5% lower, JAX 12% lower by kernel time.
- The best 10 JAX grid shapes in bf16 fall between 1,179 and 1,229 TFLOP/s by kernel time (job 454577).
- Run-to-run variation on k007-002. With the same kernel, repeated runs agree closely: across the 24 MAMF shapes where jobs 454579 and 454580 ran the same kernel, the median difference is 0.3% and the largest 0.6%. Some shapes move more. 4096x4096x16384 measured 1,188, 1,221 and 1,189 by kernel time (jobs 454529, 454561, 454577), and 1,192 and 1,153 by untraced wall clock (jobs 453420, 454529). Treat differences of about 3% as noise. XLA's autotuner can also pick a different hipBLASLt kernel for the same shape in a new run. It did so for 4 of the 28 MAMF shapes between jobs 454579 and 454580 and moved three of them by 7-12% (for example 20480x4096x12288: 1,039 with a 192x320 tile in job 454579, 1,164 with a 256x256 tile in job 454580).
- Under `rocprofv3`, wall clock reads lower for shapes that take less than about 100 µs per call, because the tracer adds host work to every dispatch: 4096x1280x2560 reads 401 traced (job 454561) and 472-550 in two untraced passes (job 454529). Wall-clock numbers above say which kind they are.
- The node matters. JAX on MAMF-finder's 28 shapes ran a median of 3% faster on k007-002 than on k007-004 by wall clock, and faster on 26 of the 28 shapes (jobs 453412 and 453338). The two slower shapes, 20480x4096x12288 (-8%) and 16384x8192x8192 (-4%), may reflect XLA's autotuner picking a different kernel rather than the node: 1,043 on k007-002 matches the 192x320-tile kernel in the variation note, and these two runs did not record kernel names. k007-001 and k007-003 have not been compared. The bf16 grid's best wall-clock rate was 1,156 on k007-004 (job 453314) against 1,192 on k007-002.
- With `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`, JAX ran bf16 matmuls at 15-17 TFLOP/s, 1% of the autotuned rate (job 453316, stopped by its 45-minute limit after 99 shapes). Any hipBLASLt kernel is far faster than that, so level 0 appears to switch to a different GEMM path on ROCm, and it cannot measure hipBLASLt's untuned default choice.
- MAMF-finder's telemetry on MI350X read the wrong GPU. It samples `amdsmi` GPU 0, but HIP device 0 on k007-002 is PCI 0000:77:00, which is `amd-smi` GPU 3; `amd-smi` GPU 0 is an idle GPU at about 308 W. The MI350X MAMF and MSMF runs (jobs 453328 and 453329) predate the fix in stas00/ml-engineering#143, so their power and clock readings, the 38 MHz and 308 W in their logs, and the "not a boost burst" warning from the MAMF boost check all come from that idle GPU. MAMF-finder's TFLOP/s do not depend on telemetry. On MI300X it reads 750 W and 1,315 MHz sustained and 2,096 MHz at boost, matching the 750 W cap in note 9 of Stas Bekman's table.
- Power cap on MI350X (`amd-smi static --limit`, job 453520): the socket power limit is 1,000 W, equal to the maximum limit and to the brochure's maximum TBP. During a sustained bf16 4096x4096x16384 matmul in JAX (job 453523), the GPU held 1,000 W at a 70-73 °C hotspot, below the 100 °C slowdown temperature, and its 8 compute dies ran at 1,332-1,513 MHz, about 1,400 MHz on average. At 1,400 MHz the peak formula (256 CUs x 4,096 bf16 FLOPs per clock) gives about 1,470 TFLOP/s, 64% of the 2.2 GHz figure. Against that power-limited peak, MSMF is about 86%, JAX by kernel time on the same shape (1,189 in job 454577) about 81%, and JAX by untraced wall clock in job 453523 (1,145 TFLOP/s) 78%. MAMF's short bursts may run above the sustained clock before the GPU reaches its power limit, so the 1,400 MHz figure does not bound MAMF.
- With torch imported, the `amdsmi` Python binding from `/opt/rocm-7.2.0` reports no GPUs, because torch has already loaded the ROCm SDK's own `libamd_smi.so.27`. `setup_envs.sh` uses the SDK's binding instead.
- Next: measure a training step with `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` to see whether the faster hipBLASLt kernels for the k and v GEMMs carry over. Separately, check whether XLA can use the rocBLAS solutions TunableOp picked for 4608x4096x7168 and 2048x4096x4096 (`tunableop-*.csv` in the results directory), and whether those solutions close the remaining gaps.

</details>

Edit: first posted with JAX numbers from node k007-004 while MAMF-finder ran on k007-002. All MI350X numbers now come from k007-002. JAX medians now use the true median of the ten windows. The MI350X telemetry note was corrected after jobs 453520 and 453523 showed MAMF-finder sampling a different GPU. Second edit: JAX now reports kernel time from a `rocprofv3` trace next to wall clock, and comparisons with MAMF and MSMF use kernel time (jobs 454577-454580). This corrects the earlier reading that the wall-clock gap came from XLA's kernel choice; XLA's choice still costs 17-33% on the k and v shapes, where it picks its own Triton GEMM. The Snowball shapes now cover separate k and v projections, the k and v weight gradients and the input gradients, and the paragraph names every projection behind a shared shape. Added the Triton-off comparison, the run-to-run variation note, and the TunableOp library choices. Scripts moved to `experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/`, and the grid arguments are now `--m-range`, `--n-range` and `--k-range`.

### MI350X Triton `ragged_dot` rewrite and tuning: batch 64 step 2.634 → 2.426 s, 8.58% → 9.32% MFU

Commit: 8471641 (local, not pushed) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 453565 (A/B), 453564 (microbenchmark), baseline 453384

PR: #9859 (AMD Instinct only; NVIDIA, TPU and megablox unchanged).

```bash
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 \

```

| Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.426 s (was 2.634) | 108,100 (was 99,500) | 9.32% (was 8.58%) | 184.2 GiB (unchanged) |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- Loss matches the baseline to 4 decimals (11.7770 vs 11.7769 at step 19).
- Forward and dlhs now launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a device-side tile map, instead of a full row grid per expert. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. drhs uses an explicit flat grid. Rows past the last group are zero-filled.
- Tuned for MI350X: 256×256×64 tiles, 8 warps, 2 stages for forward and dlhs; 256×128×64, 4 warps, 1 stage for drhs; plus chiplet-aware program order. Blackwell, TPU and megablox are unchanged.
- Per call on one GPU at batch 64 (M=131072), before → after TFLOP/s:

  | Layout | w13 | w2 |
  |---|---|---|
  | fwd | 583 → 722 | 555 → 667 |
  | dlhs | 554 → 760 | 538 → 757 |
  | drhs | 410 → 581 | 396 → 573 |

  A dense `jnp.matmul` of the same FLOPs runs at about 925–958; XLA fp16 `ragged_dot` at 24–98. At batch 8 the forward pass goes from 2.27 ms to 0.36 ms. Jobs 453500 and 453564.
- At batch 64 the tile map alone changes nothing. With the old blocks, w13 forward takes 2.95 ms either way. The gain there is block tuning. At batch 8 the tile map is a 4.6× win.
- `plgpu.CompilerParams` exposes only `num_warps` and `num_stages`, so AMD knobs (`waves_per_eu`, `matrix_instr_nonkdim`, `kpack`) can't be set from Pallas.
- drhs, at 573–581 TFLOP/s, is the remaining gap. Both of its operands are contraction-strided.

</details>

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- Link ceiling (JAX, 1.34 GB bf16): all-gather 392 GB/s bus bandwidth (2.99 ms), reduce-scatter 378, all-to-all 349, f32 all-reduce 366. rccl-tests 7.11 agrees: all-gather 394-396 at 1-2 GB. RCCL uses 112 channels, ring and the Simple protocol. The model's async EP all-gathers take 4.1 ms (about 280 GB/s) because they share compute units and HBM with concurrent compute: next to a matmul, an all-gather hides only 42% of it, even with the latency-hiding scheduler on.
- No change: `NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS=32/64`, `NCCL_PROTO=Simple`, `NCCL_ALGO=Ring`, `RCCL_MSCCL_ENABLE=0`, `RCCL_MSCCLPP_ENABLE=1`, highest-priority async stream, `parallel_collective_overlap_limit=2`, pipelined all-gather and reduce-scatter, collective combine thresholds at 1 GB (all within 0.8% of 2.427 s). Harmful: `NCCL_MAX_NCHANNELS` 64 to 8 (275 to 41 GB/s), `NCCL_ALGO=Tree` (f32 all-reduce at 162 GB/s), the latency-hiding scheduler on the full model (+3%).
- Exposed collective time (profile of steps 10-12, GPU 0) is 317 ms per step with the new kernel, down from 381 with the old one. 198 ms is synchronous on the main stream: 52 EP reduce-scatters (109 ms), 157 per-layer gradient all-reduces inside the scan (71 ms) and routing all-gathers (12 ms). The other 120 ms is async EP traffic not hidden by compute. The `msccl` f32 all-reduce kernels take under 2 ms.
- Pooled-wave moves about half the bytes of ring, but XLA leaves 130 of its 156 all-to-alls per step synchronous on the main stream with none of their time overlapped, and they launch 64 workgroups against 112. Exposed time is 402 ms. It also drops more assignments: 5.4% against ring's 0.9% at capacity factor 1.0.
- Against the old kernel (2.634 s), `save_moe` on the new kernel is 11.3% faster.
- Next, by estimated upside: `save_moe` at batch 64 now (-3.7%, +49 GiB); token-deduplicated EP dispatch (about 58% fewer EP bytes, 100-180 ms); overlap the synchronous reduce-scatters with the shared-expert MLP (50-100 ms); one gradient all-reduce per weight after the layer scan (40-55 ms).

</details>

🤖 Matmul-alone time in the MI350X `--overlap` runs (jobs 453572, 453633, 453651) takes one of two values between runs: about 2.46 ms in `min64`, `ring`, `prio-on` and `lhs-prio-off`, and about 2.88 ms in the other 16. Details: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9886#issuecomment-6047294744

Because the variance is between processes, re-timing the matmul inside a run does not remove it. To compare settings, run each setting in several processes, interleave them, and compare medians of a per-run ratio such as the hidden fraction `(t_collective + t_matmul − t_both) / min(t_collective, t_matmul)`, using the matmul-alone time of the same run.

```bash
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode save_moe
```

| Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.580 s | 165,900 | 14.31% | 206.5 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What it does.** `ring` all-gathers every token to all 8 GPUs and reduce-scatters a full-size output, but with top-4 of 256 experts a token reaches only 3.3 GPUs on average. `ring_dedup` (new module `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring_dedup.py`) sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`, plus a small `all_to_all` of per-row combine weights and local expert ids. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule, grouped layout and Triton `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32 and returns one row per token. All hidden-width movement is a gather (ring's `_dispatch_rows`/`_combine_rows`), so there are no scatter-adds in either pass.
- **Sender capacity** is `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing (0.416 × 32,768 per GPU). At 1.1 it sends 537 MB per collective per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring's all-gather or reduce-scatter (46%), and drops no tokens at the sender in these runs.
- **A/B, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile cache per job, `JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`, median of steps 2-19:**

  | Base | Remat | ring | `ring_dedup` | Jobs |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | merged (gather combine + Triton routing top-k) | recompute_all | 1.798 s, 12.57% | 1.688 s, 13.40% (-6.1%) | 454022, 454026 |
  | merged | save_moe | 1.730 s, 13.07% | 1.580 s, 14.31% (-8.7%) | 454012, 454021 |
  | before the gather combine | recompute_all | 1.865 s, 12.13% | 1.735 s, 13.03% (-7.0%) | 453921, 453922 |
  | before the gather combine | save_moe | 1.842 s, 12.28% | 1.637 s, 13.81% (-11.1%) | 453960, 453968 |

  The two changes stack partly. With `save_moe`, the gather combine alone saves 112 ms, `ring_dedup` alone 205 ms, both together 262 ms. Peak memory changes by at most 0.7 GiB. Step-19 loss is within 8e-4 of ring in every pair. The drop rate is 1.00% vs 0.99% (`recompute_all`) and 1.12% vs 0.93% (`save_moe`).
- **Numerics.** f32 CPU unit tests on 8 shards match ring and a dense reference to 1e-5 in value and in gradients for x, combine weights and both expert weights, including a forced sender-drop case. At full shapes in bf16 on MI350X, one layer differs from ring by 0.2-0.5% relative in value and gradients. That comes from ring's bf16 summation; `ring_dedup` sums in f32.
- **Profile (steps 10-12, GPU 0, ms per profiled step, ring vs `ring_dedup`, both before the gather combine).** `recompute_all`: large EP collectives take 481 vs 311, exposed collective time is 357 vs 288, and MoE dispatch/combine kernels take 150 vs 42. `save_moe`: 386 vs 211, 402 vs 266, and 147 vs 40. Each large `all_to_all` takes 1.6-2.7 ms, against 3.3-4.2 ms for ring's collectives.
- **What is still exposed:** the forward return and backward dy `all_to_all`s are synchronous (about 60 ms each per step), and the small metadata `all_to_all`s take 0.8-0.9 ms per call under `save_moe`, where they queue behind the large transfers.
- The latency-hiding scheduler gave 1.594 s vs 1.637 s before the merge, but 1.591 s vs 1.580 s after it (job 454027), so leave it off.
- One run (454010) hit the step-5 GPU-7 out-of-memory on a 96.6 GiB allocation, the same failure seen at batch 96 in job 453660, and hung. The retry (454021) ran clean. Since diagnosed as allocator fragmentation around the step's temp buffer and fixed by `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` (#9901).
- **Follow-ups:** packing the metadata into the activation rows and chunking the expert MLP were tried and did not help; see the next comment. Not tested on TPU or NVIDIA.

</details>

### One gradient all-reduce per weight after the layer scan: works, keeps gradients, no speedup on MI350X

Commit: bd8e11a · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Job: 453915 (on 60b253d), 454011 (on 67ca557)

```bash

```

| Base | Remat | Variant | Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 60b253d | recompute_all | baseline | 1.844 s | 142,200 | 12.26% | 158.4 GiB |
| 60b253d | recompute_all | deferred reduction | 1.852 s | 141,600 | 12.21% | 158.4 GiB |
| 60b253d | save_moe | baseline | 1.824 s | 143,700 | 12.39% | 205.8 GiB |
| 60b253d | save_moe | deferred reduction | 1.856 s | 141,200 | 12.18% | 205.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | recompute_all | baseline | 1.786 s | 146,800 | 12.66% | 157.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | recompute_all | deferred reduction | 1.786 s | 146,800 | 12.66% | 157.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | save_moe | baseline | 1.748 s | 150,000 | 12.94% | 205.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | save_moe | deferred reduction | 1.741 s | 150,600 | 12.99% | 205.9 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- What the in-scan all-reduces are: on this mesh (`expert=8`, other axes 1), every non-expert block weight is replicated across the batch. Explicit sharding types each layer's weight gradient as replicated, so the backward while body all-reduces it per layer. Per layer that is 5 gradient all-reduces: q/k/v/gate and w_o in the attention `cond` branch, one combined GatedNorm/router/shared w_gate/w_up, shared w_down, and the two RMSNorm weights. The forward body adds one router-stats all-reduce, for 6 × 26 = 156 per step. XLA's combiner can't merge across loop iterations or `cond` branches.
- The change: weights that only feed matmuls are marked `reduced` over the batch axes before the scan (`levanter.grug.sharding.defer_batch_grad_reduction`). Their gradients leave the scan unreduced and are all-reduced once per stacked weight. FSDP-sharded leaves (`data` > 1) are left unchanged. RMSNorm weights keep the per-layer reduction. Stored parameter shardings don't change.
- Gradients match. On CPU (tiny preset, f32, 8 devices) the loss and 26 of 27 leaves are bit-identical. On GPU (medium preset, bf16, job 454079) the loss is identical, and baseline-vs-change errors (at most 0.63% relative L2) equal baseline-vs-baseline. The full-model losses match too.
- The backward loop goes from 5 gradient all-reduces per layer to 1, but the step doesn't get faster. In a profiled A/B (job 453987) the change saves 43 ms per step, but the profiler adds about 0.3 ms to every collective call. Unprofiled, the 130 removed calls cost about 11 ms, and the single 2 GB all-reduce after the scan takes about 16 ms on the main stream. The bytes are the same either way, and the per-layer calls were bandwidth-bound, not latency-bound.
- Not proposing a PR for MI350X. Small collectives should be priced from unprofiled step times, not from trace durations.

</details>

### Hiding `ring_dedup`'s synchronous all-to-alls behind the shared expert: no gain

Commit: 3838b71 (local, on the `ring_dedup` base 91286fc) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 454847, 454872, 454943 (overlap + latency-hiding scheduler); 454865, 454945, 454949 (latency-hiding scheduler only); 454857, 454892 (baseline)

```bash
JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton \
  XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode save_moe
```

| Variant (`save_moe`) | Step | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 1.589 s | 14.23% | 206.5 GiB |
| latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s (best 1.569) | 14.36% | 207.7 GiB |
| shared expert pinned under the transfers + latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s | 14.36% | 208.2 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What was tried.** A `custom_vjp` around `ring_dedup`'s return `all_to_all` runs the shared-expert MLP between the transfer's start and its use. The backward does the same for the dy `all_to_all` and the shared-expert backward. Ordering is enforced with `optimization_barrier`. The shared expert moves into the backend (`moe_mlp(..., shared_expert=...)`). f32 CPU tests on 8 shards match `ring_dedup` plus a separately computed shared expert to 1e-5 in value and in every gradient.
- **The forward return was already hidden.** In the default schedule the forward return `all_to_all` is async and spans the shared-expert forward GEMMs (30 of 45 ms per profiled step run under it). The synchronous forward transfer is the dispatch. The backward dy `all_to_all` is synchronous.
- **Without the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers backfire.** XLA's default GPU schedule doesn't move all-to-all starts earlier, so it placed the shared GEMMs before the start and every large `all_to_all` became synchronous: 1.610 s vs 1.589 s (+1.3%).
- **With the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers work, but the time just moves.** Unhidden ms per profiled step with the scheduler, before → after pinning:

  | Transfer | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | dy | 41 | 26 |
  | dx | 7 | 33 |
  | forward return | 66 | 90 |

  The scheduler was already hiding dx behind the shared backward. It won't split that work across dy and dx, and scheduling-group annotations, which could force the split, crash the compiler on this ROCm build.
- **`recompute_all`:** baseline 1.707 s, scheduler only 1.695 s, scheduler + pinning 1.703 s.
- **The latency-hiding scheduler alone** gives -0.9% (`save_moe`) and -0.7% (`recompute_all`) here, but an earlier run measured +0.7%. That's within run-to-run noise (about 1.5%), so the defaults stay as they are.
- **Next:** profile-guided latency-hiding scheduling (`xla_gpu_pgle_profile_file_or_directory_path`), so the scheduler fills windows by measured transfer time; or find other independent work for the forward dispatch window.

</details>

The 5 are the `ragged_all_to_all` tests, which now fail with `UNIMPLEMENTED` instead of the `gfx950` parse error. With the decomposer, 16 of the 17 ragged tests pass. Commit: none (standalone JAX script, no Marin code) · GPU: one MI350X per configuration, run side by side on one node · Job: 460950

```bash
# $WORK/marin/.venv: JAX 0.11.0, jax-rocm10-plugin, ROCm 10.0.0 from pip.
# Command buffers stay off because hipBLASLt's grouped GEMM crashes with them on (#9904).
# Times jax.lax.ragged_dot (fwd) and its VJP (bwd: dlhs and drhs) by wall clock over 20 calls,
# then sums GPU kernel time by kernel name over 5 calls under jax.profiler.
XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=" python gg_profile.py --dtype bfloat16  # bf16, XLA default
XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=" python gg_profile.py --dtype float16   # fp16, hipBLASLt grouped GEMM
```

Useful TFLOP/s per call (2·M·K·N per pass, counting only each row's own expert). Shapes are per GPU as in #9859 (w13: fused gate/up projection; w2: down projection), with 32 experts and equal row counts. bwd is dlhs and drhs together. The Triton column is #9859's tile-map kernels at the same shapes (job 457866, from the PR description); for bwd it gives the combined rate, then dlhs / drhs.

| Shape (M, K, N) | Pass | bf16 XLA (default) | fp16 XLA grouped GEMM | bf16 Triton, #9859 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| June w13, batch 64 (131072, 2560, 2560) | fwd | 35.6 | 37.4 | 784 |
| | bwd | 29.5 | 38.9 | 743 (806 / 689) |
| June w2, batch 64 (131072, 1280, 2560) | fwd | 36.6 | 52.9 | 725 |
| | bwd | 27.1 | 38.1 | 696 (764 / 639) |
| June w13, batch 8 (16384, 2560, 2560) | fwd | 36.2 | 36.5 | 621 |
| | bwd | 33.5 | 71.3 | 562 (632 / 506) |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **Relaxing XLA's gate is not enough.** XLA lowers `ragged_dot` to hipBLASLt's grouped GEMM only where `CanBeHandledByGpublasltGroupGemm` in `xla/hlo/transforms/expanders/ragged_dot_rewriter.cc` allows it: fp16 and bf16 on gfx942, fp16 only on gfx950 (openxla/xla#38088, unchanged on XLA `main`). The gate follows hipBLASLt's kernel coverage. The gfx950 kernel libraries in hipBLASLt from ROCm 7.1 and 7.2 (the cluster's system installs) and ROCm 10.0 (pip) have grouped-GEMM kernels for fp16 only, and `ROCm/rocm-libraries` `develop` has no bf16 grouped-GEMM tuning logic for gfx950. A plugin rebuilt with the gate relaxed would have no bf16 kernel to call.
- **The gfx950 fp16 grouped GEMM has one kernel.** Each gfx950 fp16 grouped-GEMM logic file in [`rocm-libraries`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/tree/develop/projects/hipblaslt/library/src/amd_detail/rocblaslt/src/Tensile/Logic/asm_full/gfx950/gfx950/GridBased) (about 9 KB) lists a single solution with a 16x16x32 tile. The gfx942 bf16 grouped-GEMM files list 4-7 MB of tuned solutions per layout. In the profiles, that `MT16x16x32` kernel accounts for the whole fp16 call. bf16 and fp16 matrix-core throughput is the same on gfx950, so a bf16 build of the same kernel would not be faster. XLA's setup kernel (`SetUserArgsKernelRaggedIn*Dim`) takes about 6 µs per GEMM.
- **XLA's default bf16 path does 32x the useful work.** It runs one hipBLASLt matmul of every row against every expert's weights at 1.20-1.42 PFLOP/s, then masks the result. The matmul is 68-91% of the call, and transposes and the mask take the rest. fp16 with `--xla_gpu_experimental_use_ragged_dot_grouped_gemm=false` takes the same path at 25-34 TFLOP/s.
- **The possible gain is small.** On MI300X, where hipBLASLt has tuned bf16 grouped kernels, XLA's grouped GEMM took 11-28% less time per call than tuned Triton (#9904, microbenchmarks only). Triton `ragged_dot` was 21% of the MI350X batch-64 step in [this profile](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6026123445), taken before the kernel rewrite and flash attention. If the MI300X edge carried over to gfx950, it would save about 2-6% of step time (21% × 11-28%), and less now that the rewritten Triton kernels are faster.
- **If someone picks this up:** test fp16 first, because it needs no plugin rebuild. Generate large-tile gfx950 fp16 grouped-GEMM solutions from the `rocm-libraries` tag that matches ROCm 10.0.0, and set `HIPBLASLT_TENSILE_LIBPATH` to a copy of the stock gfx950 library directory with the new files added. Add bf16 solutions and rebuild the plugin with the gate relaxed only if fp16 beats Triton. The other route is to ask AMD to ship tuned gfx950 grouped-GEMM kernels in hipBLASLt. Until then, MI350X keeps Triton `ragged_dot`.

</details>

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

- **Motivation:** Long-loop rounds regressed from Exp1 (SFT 746 → RL 16: Micro scored-attempt mean 0.4526, mean of benchmark means 0.5216; SFT 746 alone 0.4023 / 0.4798) to Exp2 (SFT 204 → RL 20: 0.4048 / 0.4829) and Exp4 (SFT 360 → RL 36: 0.3763 / 0.4250; issue 11337), while several SFT settings (along with data and RL) changed at the same time. Isolating which SFT setting change(s) account for the drop directly informs the SFT recipe for Mochi.
- **Goal:** Identify which SFT setting change(s) between Exp1 and Exp4 account for lower general and agentic ability.
- **Data:** Fixed 10/05 SFT full-mixture catalog (216 SFT stores plus pretraining replay) starting from the pre-train Snowball base, held constant across every arm so data-release changes do not confound SFT recipe settings.
- **Method:** SFT only, changing one verified Exp1-to-Exp4 setting at a time from the Exp1 baseline settings; run at one-hour scale first and then 8-hour scale for decisive arms, scoring every checkpoint on Micro210 and the edit-call eval.
- **Results:** None yet; no runs have started.
- **Conclusion:** None yet.

Parent: issue 11535. Related: issue 11337 (Snowball recipe scoreboard) and issue 11793 (first-update hang when running Exp1's optimizer assignment with FP32 stored weights on the current long-loop runtime).

## Verified Exp1–Exp4 SFT settings

Every setting below comes from direct source inspection at each run's commit (Exp2 from its archived consumed config):

| Setting | Exp1 (`9662fdba02`) | Exp2 (`442bf9d878`) | Exp3 (`0f5721bbb4`) | Exp4 (`09ac3d5afd`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Optimizer | `grug_moe_muonh_v1` (`experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py`) | Plain Adam on all parameters | `GrugMoeMuonHConfig` (`moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py`) | Same as Exp3 |
| 4-D routed expert banks | Adam (`adam_lr`) | Adam | Muon-H | Muon-H |
| Norm scales | Muon-H (stacked 2-D) | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `lm_head` / `output_proj` | AdamH (main LR) | Adam | AdamH (main LR) | Same as Exp3 |
| Peak LR | `5e-5` (both groups) | `5e-5` | Muon-H/AdamH `5e-5`; Adam group `1.1538e-5` (`5e-5 × 3/13`) | Same as Exp3 |
| Betas / eps | Optimizer defaults (`0.9 / 0.95 / 1e-8`) | `0.9 / 0.95 / 1e-8` | `0.9062 / 0.95 / 3.83e-15` | Same as Exp3 |
| LR schedule | Linear, decay 475, horizon 4,750, min `0.1×`; stopped at 746 → **constant `5e-5`** | Cosine over all 204 updates to `0.1×` | Linear, decay 475, horizon 4,750; ran 388 of 746 → **constant** | **Linear over all 360 updates to `0.1×`** (both groups) |
| Weight decay | `0` | `0` | `0.1` passed, **inert** (not read; only `gate_router_weight_decay`, default `0`) | Same as Exp3 (**inert**) |
| Gradient clipping | None (`max_grad_norm: null`) | Global `1.0` | Global `1.0` (`global_gradient_clip=1`, per-group `None`) | Same as Exp3 |
| z-loss | `1e-4` | `0.0` | `1e-4` | Same as Exp3 |
| Stored parameters | **BF16, no FP32 master** (`params=bfloat16`, device mode, `offload_opt_state: true`) | **FP32** (`params=float32`) | **FP32** (`p=f32, c=bfloat16`) | **FP32** (`p=f32, c=bfloat16`) |
| Batch / context / updates | `256 × 262k`; 746 updates | `256 × 262,144`; 204 updates | `256 × 262,144`; 388 of 746 updates | `256 × 262,144`; 360 updates |
| Loss mask | **All-token** (all 216 SFT + 1,711 pretrain children `format: text`) | SFT `serialized_chat` assistant-only; pretrain all-token | Per-source sidecar (`source_loss.json`: `chat_assistant_only` or `full_token`; per-source values not checked) | Same mechanism as Exp3 |
| Packing | Pack, block cross-doc | Cap `256` | Cap `256`, lookahead `128` | Same as Exp3 |
| Data catalog | 10/05 full mixture (`2026.10.24.2`, 377 components) | Same 377 components | Launch-input release URI (not visible in source) | V7 option-g |

Notes from the source read:
- **Inert / unchanged settings excluded from arms:** weight decay `0.1` in Exp3/Exp4 has no effect in `moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py`, and z-loss is `1e-4` in both Exp1 and Exp4.
- **Interaction with issue 11793:** Exp1 used the same `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py` parameter routing (`4-D` routed expert banks on Adam, stacked norm scales on Muon-H) that hangs on update 1 under FP32 stored weights on the current long-loop runtime (issue 11793). Exp1 itself stored BF16 parameters with no FP32 master and therefore never exercised that FP32 path.

## Proposed one-at-a-time arms

All arms train SFT only on the fixed 10/05 full-mixture data from the pre-train Snowball base (one-hour scale first, then 8-hour scale), scored on Micro210 and the edit-call eval. Each non-baseline arm changes one verified Exp1-to-Exp4 setting:

| Arm | Single change from Exp1 baseline | Baseline (Exp1) value | Treatment (Exp4 / Exp2) value | Dependency / note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Baseline** | None (Exp1 SFT settings on fixed 10/05 mix) | `grug_moe_muonh_v1` (Adam experts, Muon-H norms), LR `5e-5` constant, no clip, BF16 params, all-token mask, no 256 cap | — | Reference point; precision choice interacts with issue 11793 |
| **1. Stored precision** | Stored parameter dtype | BF16, no FP32 master | FP32 (`p=f32, c=bfloat16`) | Blocked on issue 11793 for Exp1 optimizer routing |
| **2. Optimizer routing** | 4-D expert banks & norm scales assignment | `grug/moe/optimizer.py` (Adam experts, Muon-H norms) | `moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py` (Muon-H experts, Adam norms) | Keep BF16 params for a single-knob contrast vs. Baseline; an FP32 variant can also run immediately (not affected by issue 11793) as a combined precision + routing check, while isolating routing on FP32 waits on Arm 1 / issue 11793 |
| **3. Adam-group LR & betas/eps** | Adam-group peak LR, betas, and eps | `5e-5`, optimizer defaults (`0.9 / 0.95 / 1e-8`) | `1.1538e-5` (`5e-5 × 3/13`), `0.9062 / 0.95 / 3.83e-15` | Tests lower Adam-group LR (most meaningful paired with Arm 2's group assignment as well) |
| **4. Gradient clipping** | Global gradient norm clip | None (`max_grad_norm: null`) | `global_gradient_clip = 1.0` | Direct single-knob switch |
| **5. LR schedule** | Decay schedule across the run | Constant `5e-5` (475-step decay tail unreached) | Linear decay to `0.1×` over the full run (Exp4) | Can optionally include cosine decay (Exp2) if linear moves the score |
| **6. Loss mask** | SFT token loss masking | All-token (`format: text`) | SFT assistant-only (`serialized_chat`), pretrain all-token | Verify Exp3/Exp4 `source_loss.json` per-source values before finalizing |
| **7. Packing cap** | Per-pack document cap & lookahead | No 256-doc cap | Cap `256` (lookahead `128`) | Direct single-knob switch |

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Scale difference from Exp1–Exp4 and Arm 1 dependency**

## Scale comparison

Our one-at-a-time SFT ablations run at 1/8th the per-update batch size of Exp1–Exp4:

| Setting | Exp1–Exp4 runs | Our 64-H100 ablations |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware | 32 hosts × 8 H100 (256 H100 in Exp1) | 8 hosts × 8 H100 (64 H100; mesh `context=8`, `data=8`) |
| Packed rows per update | 256 (`256 × 262,144` = 67,108,864 tokens) | 32 (`trainer.trainer.train_batch_size: 32`; `32 × 262,144` = 8,388,608 tokens, 1/8×) |
| Microbatch / accumulation | — | `gradient_accumulation_steps: 4` (4 microbatches of 8 rows scanned inside one update; loss divided by the full 32-row scored-token count, `_accumulated_loss_and_grads` at commit `3b291b10`) |
| Updates per run (`stop_after_steps`) | 204 (Exp2), 360 (Exp4), 388 (Exp3), 746 (Exp1) | 150 (one-hour size); 500 (8-hour size) |
| Raw tokens per run | 13.69 B (204 updates) to 50.06 B (746 updates) | 1.26 B (150 updates, 4,800 rows); 4.19 B (500 updates, 16,000 rows) |

Because both batch size per update (8×) and total trained tokens are smaller than Exp1–Exp4, effects that depend on batch size or longer training horizons may differ between the one-hour screen, the 8-hour screen, and 256-H100 scale.

## Arm 1 dependency

Arm 1 (changing stored parameter precision from BF16 to FP32 under Exp1's optimizer routing, with 4-D routed expert banks on Adam and stacked norm scales on Muon-H) waits on issue 11793 (first-update hang under that combination on the current long-loop runtime). Isolating optimizer routing on FP32 likewise waits on issue 11793, while the BF16 single-knob arms and an FP32 combined precision-plus-routing check do not hit issue 11793.

🤖

## Research

This is a multi-run experiment with no results yet. The historical comparison also changes RL duration (16 versus 36 updates), so SFT-only scores cannot by themselves explain the post-RL gap. [#11687](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687) documents the BF16 stored-parameter caveat in the Exp1-style baseline; [#11793](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11793) blocks the FP32 plus Exp1-routing comparison on the current runtime. The Exp3/Exp4 supervision sidecar is hash-pinned in [`exp3_recipe.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1be0454367925411db6a432da3f62901881f8152/experiments/post_training/long_loop/exp3_recipe.py#L114-L126), but its per-source loss modes still need to be checked against the intended mask arm.

## Plan

1. Freeze the pre-train checkpoint, 10/05 catalog, source-loss sidecar and hash, runtime revision, data order, update count, and evaluation policy. Inspect the sidecar's per-source modes and verify that each arm changes only its named setting. Split the proposed LR/betas/eps and packing-cap/lookahead arms; separate expert-bank and norm routing if those assignments can be varied independently.
2. Run a matched Exp1-style BF16 baseline and one-hour SFT screens with the same source weights, sampling seed, update count, and checkpoint steps. Record consumed token counts because packing and masking change them. Score each checkpoint on the same frozen Micro210 and edit-call evaluations. Repeat the baseline to measure run and evaluation variation before promoting an arm whose score change exceeds that spread.
3. Keep the FP32 plus Exp1-routing cell gated on #11793. Once update 1 completes reliably, run a matched precision × routing comparison, then take only the decisive settings to eight-hour, repeated SFT runs. Report both Micro aggregates, benchmark-level scores, coverage, edit-call scores, seeds, configs, and checkpoint links, including negative results.
4. For any SFT setting that plausibly explains the gap, continue a matched pair through the same RL recipe and number of updates. Compare the post-RL checkpoints under one evaluation policy before attributing any part of the Exp1-to-Exp4 post-RL difference to SFT.

🤖 **Optimizer routing per recipe: Exp1's expert banks fall through to Adam**

Source-verified parameter routing across five recipes (Exp1, Exp2, Exp3/Exp4 Hero-EP, the 11-19 control at `6164fcbd`, and the 10/05 run). No claim is made here about which routing performs better.

Conventions used below: `learning_rate` drives Muon-H and AdamH; `adam_lr` drives Adam. "Per-group" clip means `max_grad_norm` applied separately inside each optimizer group; "Global" means one gradient-norm clip across all parameters.

## Cross-recipe overview

| Weight group | Exp1 (`9662fdba02`, `bcf85728`) | Exp3 / Exp4 (`facbad18`) & 11-19 control (`6164fcbd`, `1f9bb1af`) | Real 10/05 (`ce7c77a`, `11baea1f`) | Exp2 (`442bf9d878`, `AdamConfig`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Expert banks (`w_gate`, `w_up`, `w_down`)** | **Adam** (4-D fall-through) | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Attention & shared-expert matrices | Muon-H | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Gated norms | Muon-H | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Stacked per-layer RMSNorm scales `(L, D)` | **Muon-H** (2-D match; no norm rule) | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `embed_norm` / `final_norm` scales (1-D) | Adam | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `output_proj` / LM head | AdamH | AdamH | AdamH | Adam |
| `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate` | Adam | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| Clipping | none | global 1.0 | none | global 1.0 |

Every recipe except Exp2 uses mixed routing, with `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate`, and `output_proj` routed the same way across all mixed recipes; Exp2 is the only recipe applying plain Adam uniformly to all parameters.

## Per-recipe routing tables (verified from source)

### (a) Exp1 (`9662fdba02`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_muonh_v1`, blob `bcf85728`; mask at `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:285-307`. The SFT runtime stacks transformer blocks (`Transformer.stacked_blocks: ArrayStacked[Block]`, `sft_runtime/model.py:1251, 1283`), turning `(E, D, I)` expert weights (`levanter/grug/grug_moe.py:389-392`) into 4-D `(L, E, D, I)` leaves.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate` | Adam (`L291-297`) | `adam_lr` `5e-5` | none |
| `output_proj` (LM head) | AdamH (`L298-299`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | none |
| gated norms (`embed`, `attn`, `mlp`, `final`) | Muon-H (`L301-302`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| attention `w_q/k/v/o`, shared expert `w_*`, latent `w_*` (stacked 3-D) | Muon-H (`L303-304`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| **expert banks `w_gate`/`w_up`/`w_down` (4-D)** | **Adam** (`L305` fall-through) | **`adam_lr`** | none |
| stacked RMSNorm scales `(L, D)` (2-D) | **Muon-H** (`L303-304`; no norm rule in this blob) | `learning_rate` | none |
| `embed_norm` and `final_norm` scales (1-D) | Adam (`L305`) | `adam_lr` | none |

`max_grad_norm: null` (`sft.yaml:75`) and blob `bcf85728` has no global clip option. Both `learning_rate` and `adam_lr` are `5e-5` (`sft.yaml:61, 73`), so the Adam fall-through changed the update rule for expert banks without changing their LR value.

### (b) Exp3 / Exp4 Hero-EP (blob `facbad18`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_hero_ep_muonh_v1`; mask at `moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py:308-327`.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L314-315`) | `adam_lr = 5e-5 * 3/13 = 1.1538e-5` | global 1.0 |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L316-317`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | global 1.0 |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L319-320`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |
| any `.weight` (RMSNorm scales, ShortConv) | Adam (`L323-324`) | `adam_lr` | global 1.0 |
| expert banks (4-D) and other 2/3-D matrices | Muon-H (`L325-326`; normalised per expert bank via `expert_normalization`, `L86-92`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |

Per-group `max_grad_norm` is `None`. Global `1.0` clipping is set outside the optimizer (`global_gradient_clip=1`, `exp3_recipe:138`) and applied in `train_lm.py:328-329`.

### (c) 11-19 control (`6164fcbd`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_muonh_v1`, blob `1f9bb1af`; mask at `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:339-363`.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L345-351`) | `adam_lr` `2e-5` | global 1.0 |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L352-353`) | `learning_rate` `2e-5` | global 1.0 |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L355-356`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |
| `.weight` (norm scales) | Adam (`L357-358`) | `adam_lr` | global 1.0 |
| 2/3/4-D matrices incl. expert banks | Muon-H (`L359-360`; 4-D banks use the hero backend with `expert_normalization: all_experts`, `use_syrk: true`, build `L263-297`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |

Clipping comes from `global_grad_norm: 1.0` applied once before all groups (`L329-337`); per-group `max_grad_norm` is `null`. Routing matches Hero-EP `(b)`, and both use `expert_normalization: all_experts` and `use_syrk: true` (`moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py:228, 230` defaults in Exp3/Exp4); they differ in LRs (`learning_rate` `2e-5` vs `5e-5`; `adam_lr` `2e-5` vs `1.1538e-5`), with `1f9bb1af` sending 4-D leaves through the hero backend and 2/3-D leaves through the generic backend.

### (d) Real 10/05 run (`ce7c77a`, HF model card revision `8c76b22a`)

Trainer `experiments/grug_sft/special_token_lr.py` (`use_array_stacked_blocks=True` at `L334`); optimizer `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/optimizer.py` `GrugMoeMuonHConfig` (blob `11baea1f`, not `bcf85728`).

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L306-312`) | `adam_lr` `5e-5` | none |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L313-314`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | none |
| stacked `rms_attn` / `rms_mlp` scales | Adam (`L317-318`, `rmsnorm_to_adam=True`) | `adam_lr` | none |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L320-321`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| 2/3/4-D matrices incl. **expert banks** | **Muon-H** (`L328-329`) | `learning_rate` | none |

Config sets `learning_rate=5e-5`, `adam_lr=5e-5`, `max_grad_norm=None` (`special_token_lr.py:361-373`) with no global clip. One extra rule scales updates to the 7 special-token rows of `token_embed` and `output_proj` by `×√32` after the optimizer (`special_token_train.py:498-505`).

### (e) Exp2 (`442bf9d878`)

Plain Levanter `AdamConfig` (`levanter/optim/config.py:503-535`) with a single group (no mask, no `multi_transform`): every parameter gets `clip_by_global_norm(1.0)`, then `scale_by_adam`, then `lr = 5e-5`. Weight decay is `0`, so the decay mask is unused.

## Evidence that Exp1's 4-D expert-bank fall-through was unintended

- **Docstring mismatch:** The same blob `bcf85728` lists `"MoE MLP"` under `muonh` (`experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:215`).
- **`(2, 3)` rule vs. stacked 4-D banks:** The `ndim in (2, 3)` rule was written for the `grug/moe` template (`grug/moe/model.py`, `blocks: tuple[Block, ...]`), where expert weights are 3-D and match Muon-H. `sft_runtime/model.py` stacks blocks into `ArrayStacked[Block]`, making expert banks 4-D, and the mask in `bcf85728` was not updated for 4-D leaves.
- **Explicit 10/05 comment:** The 10/05 optimizer (`experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/optimizer.py:322-327`, blob `11baea1f`) explicitly guards against this trap: *"plus 4D when use_array_stacked_blocks=True… Without including 4D, stacked expert weights fall through to adam"*.
- **Branch fix not in `main`:** Commit `02c96d8378` (2026-11-17, `"[grug] Preserve Muon state across expert routing"`, no commit message body) adds 4-D routing, the `.weight` → Adam rule, and `test_muonh_groups_match_hero_for_stacked_and_unstacked_models`. It is present in `6164fcbd` but **not in `main`**.
- **Still in `origin/main`:** `origin/main` (blob `81304114`, `L311`) still checks `ndim in (2, 3)`, so any stacked-block run on `main` using `grug_moe_muonh_v1` repeats Exp1's routing (which current recipes on `main` use it was not checked).
- Nothing found in source records the Exp1 fall-through routing as a deliberate choice.

## What Exp1 → Exp3 changed in optimizer routing

Moving from Exp1 (`bcf85728`) to Exp3 (`facbad18`) changed three optimizer behaviors together:

1. **Expert banks (`w_gate`/`w_up`/`w_down`):** Adam → Muon-H (with per-expert-bank `expert_normalization`).
2. **Stacked per-layer RMSNorm scales `(L, D)`:** Muon-H → Adam (via the `.weight` rule, and at `adam_lr = 1.1538e-5` instead of `5e-5`).
3. **Gradient clipping:** none → global norm clip `1.0` (`global_gradient_clip=1` in `exp3_recipe:138`, applied in `train_lm.py:328-329`).

## Unverified detail

How generic Muon (`_grug_scale_with_muon`) handles Exp1's stacked `(L, D)` RMSNorm scales was **not traced or verified**. As a 2-D leaf they may be orthogonalised across layers as a single matrix, so that behavior is left open rather than stated as fact.

## Open question for experiment owners

Was Adam on the 4-D expert banks (and Muon-H on stacked RMSNorm scales) in Exp1 intended, or an unintended result of stacking blocks under the `ndim in (2, 3)` rule?

**Did clipping act, and do the two training curves match?** Read from W&B for both LR 5e-5 runs (150 updates each).

| question | clip 1.0 run | no-clip run |
|---|---|---|
| updates with a pre-clip total grad norm above 1.0 | 17 of 150 (updates 1-10, 13, 28, 31, 71, 101, 117, 144) | 18 of 150 |
| largest pre-clip total grad norm | 4.81 (update 2) | 9.19 (update 79) |
| median pre-clip total grad norm | 0.433 | 0.427 |
| updates where clipping changed the update (a group norm above 1.0) | 14 of 150 (updates 1-7, 9, 10, 13, 71, 101, 117, 144) | none (no clip) |
| train loss, update 150 | 0.4726 | 0.4727 |
| train loss, mean of updates 141-150 | 0.6721 | 0.6721 |

- **How clipping works here:** the optimizer (`grug_moe_muonh_v1`) clips each of its three parameter groups to norm 1.0 separately, not the total norm. In the step-150 checkpoint manifest (`opt_state`), the groups hold these parameters: AdamH holds `output_proj`; Adam holds `token_embed`, `embed_norm`, `final_norm`, the routers, router bias, attention gates and the expert MLPs (`expert_mlp` w_gate and w_up stored as `[26, 256, 2560, 1280]`, w_down as `[26, 256, 1280, 2560]`); MuonH holds the other matrices, the gated norms and the stacked `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp` weights (stored as `[26, 2560]`). So the binding count uses the group norms. In the clip run, the MuonH group was above 1.0 on 8 updates, AdamH on 13 and Adam on none. Nearly all of it is the first 13 updates plus 4 later spikes.
- **Where the numbers come from:** W&B logs `grad/norm/<parameter>` before the optimizer, so these are pre-clip norms. Each group norm is rebuilt from the 27 logged per-parameter norms, using the optimizer's own grouping rule. Their sum of squares matches the logged `grad/norm/total` within 1% on every update.
- **The loss curves are not equal step by step.** They differ on every one of the 150 updates, starting at update 1 by 0.00004 (0.79061 vs 0.79058).
  - Update 1's loss is computed before any update, so clipping cannot explain that first gap. It comes from the different cluster and executable, not from clipping.
  - Clipping can act from update 2 on. Mean absolute gap over updates 2-150 is 0.00034, and 12 updates differ by more than 0.001. The largest gap is 0.0044, at update 79, where the no-clip run had its one large spike (MuonH group norm 9.00 and Adam group norm 1.50, against 0.23 and 0.06 in the clip run).
- **Reading, not a conclusion:**
  - Clipping bound on 14 of 150 updates, mostly in the first 13. Train loss ended the same to the third decimal.
  - On held-out sets, no clip is 0.003-0.005 lower on all, SFT and SFT macro than clip 1.0. Replay pretrain, Nemotron and agenttrove are within 0.001.
  - Identity-data is 0.047 lower without clipping. It rests on 8 held-out packed sequences, and every arm drew 3 identity sequences in training (method caveat: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11783#issuecomment-7056481299).
    - **Correction (21 Nov):** updated the identity draw count from `1` → `3` packed sequences in 150 updates; the earlier realized-mix tool listed data sources in sorted order, whereas training uses config order (`MixtureDataset` insertion order).
  - These are single runs. The clip pair also crosses clusters, so a 0.003 gap is not separable from cross-cluster numeric noise without a repeat.
- **Weights:**
  - control (LR 2e-5): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/base-start-20261118/control-eager/checkpoints/step-150` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fbase-start-20261118%2Fcontrol-eager%2Fcheckpoints%2Fstep-150))

🤖 The public checkpoints test the hypothesis in the BF16-vs-FP32 comment and settle the unverified detail. Exp1 is `open-athena/Snowball-LongLoop-Round1-2026.11.12.7` (`475ba62d`), Exp2 is `open-athena/Snowball-LongLoop-Round2-2026.11.14.13` (`6546ba2d`) and Exp3 is `open-athena/Snowball-LongLoop-Round3-2026.11.17.55` (`8e787c61`). Each is compared with the base `open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8` (`3bbf729f`), so the numbers include each round's RL updates.

**BF16 storage rounded away most of Exp1's Muon-H updates.** After 746 SFT updates at 5e-5, 77% of Exp1's attention values are bit-identical to the base and 17% differ by one BF16 step. The Muon-H matrices moved 0.20%, and most of that is the hyperball re-projection rounding the stored values, `bf16(bf16(x / n) * n)`, which #11755 removes: measured from the re-projected base, they moved 0.125%. With FP32 storage, Exp2 and Exp3 moved the attention matrices 3.26% and 1.02%.

**The unverified detail.** On Exp1's stacked `(L, D)` RMSNorm scales, the Muon-H step left nothing that BF16 storage kept. 13.1% of the 133,120 scale values changed, 95.4% of the changed values equal what the re-projection alone gives from the base, and 99.5% of the values that the re-projection flips are flipped. The re-projection takes `n` over the whole leaf: `input_layernorm` (26 × 2560) needs `n = 336`, and its float64 norm is 335.03. What the orthogonalized step itself did stayed below one BF16 step, so the weights cannot show it.

**Where each round's update landed** (displacement `|round − base| / |base|` per class, then the share of values that changed):

| tensor class | Exp1 (BF16 storage) | Exp2 (FP32, Adam on all) | Exp3 (FP32, Hero-EP routing) |
|---|---|---|---|
| routed expert banks | 9.79%, 85.4% (Adam) | 3.60%, 94.9% | 0.79%, 76.7% (Muon-H) |
| attention q, k, v, o | 0.20%, 22.8% (Muon-H) | 3.26%, 93.9% | 1.02%, 82.1% |
| shared expert | 0.20%, 24.1% (Muon-H) | 3.40%, 94.7% | 1.06%, 83.7% |
| GatedNorm projections | 0.22%, 26.5% (Muon-H) | 3.24%, 95.0% | 1.10%, 83.3% |
| `lm_head` | 1.15%, 9.3% (AdamH) | 3.97%, 96.4% | 1.32%, 78.4% |

Exp1 is the only round whose always-active matrices barely moved, while its Adam fall-through moved the expert banks 9.79%. So Arm 1 (FP32 storage) and Arm 2 (expert banks on Muon-H) also change where the update lands, and a per-class displacement count of each arm's checkpoint against the base shows that before any eval. Method: #11687 and #11639.

spillover_issues.author: WhenWen
spillover_issues.body:
Opened on behalf of @WhenWen for the belay-wn research loop. Updates are posted here as results land.

**Question.** Why does MuonH (fixed-norm hyperball matrices) trail MuonW on KMA d768 fast_track? Can a weight-normalized optimizer beat a *fairly tuned* MuonW-family baseline? The work covers KMA d768 and the Belay ladder recipe (d512–d1280, plus the 8-minute d512 speedrun). All numbers are Paloma macro loss, and gaps under the 0.005 band count as ties.

**Current answer (2026-11-19).** With equal tuning, the weight-normalized forms tie tuned MuonC. Neither family leads anywhere.
- *Baseline.* The bar is MuonC (Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285): MuonW with matrix decay λ·lr_t/lr_max and an AdamW head. Its decay is tuned per length: best λ is 0.2–0.4 on the speedrun, 0.2 at ladder d512, and about 0.1 at d768. Both families also use the same s(t)² head anneal and late matrix anneal ("tl-d schedule").
- *Speedrun, d512, 8 min.* nonsi (learned per-matrix radius on MuonH) + schedule, with its starting size tuned, against tuned MuonC + schedule: +0.0007 over nine held-out seeds (95% −0.0033 to +0.0046). Both beat the recipe's MuonH by about 0.011–0.016.
- *Ladder d512.* nonsi + schedule against MuonC (λ 0.2) + schedule: +0.0033 on fresh seeds 4–7, a tie.
- *Formula-cap ball.* A no-decay ball whose per-layer cap comes from a shape/LR law, with no retuning. It ties MuonC + schedule on all four rungs: −0.0031, −0.0011, +0.0048 and −0.0029, one seed each. It also ties on the speedrun (+0.0004 over six seeds).
- *Mechanism.* Loss is set first by rotation per step and second by how matrix size evolves, not by where size ends up. A fit on MuonC's settings alone predicts nonsi's loss from its rotation to within 0.002. The original MuonH–MuonW gap fits the same picture: MuonH's rotation and size were off the optimum.
- *Open: d1280.* softcap + schedule (tl-d) trails MuonC + schedule by 0.0158 on one seed. Running d1024 width on d1280's recipe does not reproduce this, and a second seed is running.

**Intake posts.** speedrun-track proposals for nonsi + schedule (#9514, comment 7019355085) and MuonC (λ 0.2) + schedule (#9514, comment 7019433555).

**Running now**
- An "unnormalized hyperball" baseline: MuonH's norm-relative step with no projection, plus MuonC- or MuonW-style decay. It is tuned like MuonC and becomes the bar wherever it wins.
- MuonC decay brackets at d768–d1280.
- nonsi + schedule at d768–d1280, with seed 2.
- A second d1280 seed for tl-d vs MuonC + schedule.

Runs log to W&B project `understanding-sam/research-loop-belay-wn`.

---

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Experiment log, part 1 of 3: the KMA d768 gap and the first weight-normalized fixes (2026-11-17)**

Setup: KMA d768 fast_track, batch 128, ctx 4096, 6,930 updates, 8×H100. Metric: final validation loss on the tuning split (plus a fixed held-out set once it was verified). Seeds are paired.

**Baselines reproduced**
- MuonW seeds 0/1/3: 2.51555 / 2.51564 / 2.5219 (four-seed mean 2.5182).
- MuonH seeds 0/1/2: 2.52054 / 2.52530 / 2.52428.
- Mean paired gap +0.0057 (+0.0064 over three paired seeds). On the fixed held-out set it is +0.0054, lower bound > 0.
- MuonW LR ×0.71 / ×1.41 is worse than ×1.
- Checkpoint restore is bitwise exact on H100, and interrupted-vs-uninterrupted continuation matches.

**Where the gap is** (log reads and swap runs)
- MuonH's deficit is front-loaded: +1.8 nats in the first 100 steps, about 0 by step 5000, then a ~0.006 loss in the final anneal.
- Swaps put the whole gap in the hidden-matrix update:
  - MuonW matrices + MuonH head/Adam groups: 2.5164.
  - MuonH matrices + MuonW Adam groups: 2.5218.
  - Gates and fallbacks don't matter.
- Rotation vs size, finals:
  - ShadowH (MuonW's rotation on fixed spheres) ends at MuonH's level: best 2.5273, ×0.5 2.5360, ×2 2.5441.
  - MuonH's rotation with MuonW's size law ends at 2.5112 / 2.5138.
  - So the gap is weight scale, not rotation.
- MuonW for the first 1,000 steps, then MuonH holding those sizes: 2.5078. MuonH's problem is mainly its first ~1,000 steps at the small init size.

**Candidates (MuonH step + some way to set the matrix size)**
- *Fixed bigger spheres* at 0.66× the update size: 2.5178 (seed 0), equal to MuonW's mean.
- *C2* (radius follows MuonW's size law in closed form): 2.5112 / 2.5138 on seeds 0–1. On held-out it is −0.006 / −0.003 vs MuonW.
- *C3* (grow by that law for 1,000 steps, then hold) on seeds 1–5:
  - −0.0057 vs original MuonW.
  - −0.0024 vs tuned MuonW (not claimed).
- *Radial MuonH* (learned log-radius per slice, Adam on ⟨G, W⟩):
  - 2.5047 / 2.5082 on seeds 0–1, about 0.01 below MuonW.
  - But radii ran away up to ~4,600× on slices whose output feeds a norm. Their radial gradient is rounding noise, and Adam with ε≈0 turns it into full steps.
- *softcap* (outward radius steps scaled by 1 − (s/c)², c = 2, capped at 7.4×):
  - Kept all of radial's gain: seeds 0–1 mean 2.5060. Any cap from 2.5× to 15× gives the same result, and 1.5× loses it.
  - Against the original MuonW on seeds 2–7: −0.0091 (bound −0.0056), held-out −0.012.
- *nonsi* (no learned radius on the scale-invariant slices, no cap):
  - Seeds 0–1 mean 2.5064.
  - Learning radii for only the first 500 steps keeps almost all of the gain (2.5084).
- Closed negatives:
  - gradient-gated or slower learned sizes: ~2.517
  - coupled learned size: 2.544–2.552
  - adaptive step rules: 2.62–2.67
  - persistence: 2.520

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Experiment log, part 2 of 3: stronger baselines, the speedrun and the ladder (2026-11-17 → 11-19)**

**The MuonW bar gets tuned, and most of the d768 lead goes away**
- *Tuned MuonW* (step 1.41×, matrix decay 0.05, no decay on head/small params): seeds 0–1 mean 2.5100. Most of the original H–W gap came from this.
- *Head step.* MuonW also gains from a smaller AdamW head step (0.18–0.35× all within 0.001). Against head-tuned MuonW, softcap's d768 lead is about 0.0001–0.001.
- *tl-a / tl-d* (softcap plus an extra s(t) factor on the head step, plus a late matrix-angle anneal ∝ s² from 79.4% of training): tl-d reached 2.4969 on seed 0.

🤖 **Experiment log, part 3 of 3: new weight-normalized forms, the mechanism, and what is running (2026-11-18 → 11-19)**

**Forms that did not beat MuonC (KMA d768, two seeds, same commit unless noted)**
- *Weight-normalized MuonC* (radius follows MuonC's decay law): 2.5121 / 2.5148, which is +0.011 vs MuonC. Changing decay moved the size 5× but the loss only ≤ 0.004.
- *ShadowC* (MuonC's rotation on a sphere): 2.5189 at init radius. With softcap's learned radius it gets 2.5086 (λ0.1), still worse than plain softcap.
- *Learned gain on MuonC* (MuonW family): adds nothing (+0.0007 to +0.0034). A weight-normalized head on MuonC's matrices costs about 0.
- *Four new constraint shapes, all with interior LR brackets:*
  - spectral-norm sphere: 2.4994, ties tl-d, −0.0018 behind MuonC + schedule
  - capped ball: +0.0020 vs tl-d
  - per-row radii: +0.0030 vs tl-d
  - Stiefel/orthogonal: about 0.10 worse; the constraint was verified exact, so this is real
- *Per-family caps* on the formula-cap ball: no gain (−0.0008 to +0.0092). *Caps at a fixed multiple of init:* best +0.003 vs the law cap.

**Forms that tie MuonC**
- *Formula-cap ball* (no decay; per-layer cap = 0.71·√(39·lr_max/(2·0.1))·|U_l|):
  - KMA d768: 2.4978 vs MuonC + schedule 2.4967.
  - Belay ladder vs same-commit MuonC (λ0.1) + schedule: −0.0031 / −0.0011 / +0.0048 / −0.0029 (d512–d1280).
  - Speedrun: +0.0004 over six seeds vs MuonC λ0.4.
  - It beats tl-d by 0.018 at d1280.
- *Ball capped at MuonC's measured final sizes* (explanation only): 2.49695 vs 2.49694.

**Mechanism, measured**
- Rotation per step is the first variable. Across MuonC and nonsi settings it explains loss with R² 0.97 on the ladder; final matrix size explains 0.02. A fit on MuonC's settings alone predicts nonsi's loss to within 0.002.
- Size is second, and it is the path over training that matters, not the end point:
  - Pinning nonsi at MuonC's final per-layer sizes loses ~0.009.
  - nonsi at start ×4 ends at MuonC's size with the same rotation and is 0.008 worse.
- In this recipe MuonC's matrices grow toward a fixed per-layer size and hold, without shrinking late.
- The formula-cap ball behaves like MuonC at about 1.2× its nominal decay, which is why its larger cap ties and its smaller cap loses.
- tl-d's d1280 loss is not radius stranding; tl-d's radii there are larger than softcap's. d1024 width on d1280's recipe does not reproduce it: nonsi + schedule and MuonC + schedule both score 2.3478 there.
- The original KMA H–W gap fits the same picture: MuonH's rotation and its size path were away from the optimum early on.

**Running now**
- *Unnormalized hyperball (uhs).* MuonH's step relative to the current norm (MuonH's tuned angular step, no projection), plus MuonC- or MuonW-style decay, with MuonC's AdamW head (0.35×, s² anneal in the schedule cells). Decay is bracketed per rung around its own balance point. Speedrun first, then the ladder. It replaces MuonC as a rung's bar if it wins.
- *MuonC decay brackets:* λ0.05 at d768; λ0.2 at d1024/d1280, run as H100 and GB200 sets.
- *nonsi + schedule:* d1024/d1280, seed 2, and d1280 head-only / anneal-only splits.
- *d1280 seed 2* for tl-d vs MuonC + schedule.
- *Formula-cap ball:* no-schedule pair at d1280.

All comparisons are now scored on the same hardware type. A difference between hardware types is only allowed as a difference of same-hardware differences.

comments.body:
🤖 **Update, 2026-11-19 23:25 → 11-20 00:45 PST**

**Goal change.** The target is now a weight-normalized optimizer that *beats* tuned MuonC + the s² anneals; a tie no longer counts. New lines should be designs derived from the measured mechanism, not new grids on existing forms (tuning only as much as a fair comparison needs).

**New results**
- **d768 ladder, MuonC decay (lml3):** λ 0.1 is best both with and without the anneals; 0.05 and 0.025 are worse.
- **d1280, seed 1 (lna):** nonsi + anneals trails same-code tuned MuonC by **+0.0086**, like tl-d. The cause is a smooth exponential drift of matrix size with no restoring force. The law-cap ball held at d1280 (−0.0029), so it is the only weight-normalized form that has kept pace on every rung. New designs will be confirmed on it.
- **Train-vs-Paloma offset (tdg, 308 speedrun runs, 260 pairs):** weight-normalized forms trail MuonC 0.005–0.008 more on training loss than on Paloma. This tracks the head's end size and logit scale (R² 0.75–0.80), not matrix size (0.15) or rotation (0.23), and is spread evenly over the 16 Paloma domains. It is a head trait, not a cost of weight normalization, and no held-out gain is hidden behind it.
- **Momentum echo (derivation, then a check):** each Muon update points back along its own recent steps through momentum, so ⟨Ô, Ŵ⟩ ≈ −κθ with κ ≈ 10.7. This accounts for the radial drift of the unnormalized hyperball and for the KDA w_beta runaway. It predicted the d512-ladder neutral decay at 0.152; the smoke run measured 0.166.
- **Direction noise (KMA d768):** about 80% of each Muon step goes along the momentum's noise-like directions, which hold only ~20% of its energy.

**Now running:** soft orthogonalization (sod), MuonC's per-slice rotation on nonsi (pss), a logit-scale intervention (lgs), and the unnormalized hyperball on the d512 ladder (uhl), all against same-code tuned MuonC.
